div.head: PRIZE WINNER.
div.p: A PRIZE WINNER.

An old Scotswoman had a reputation far and near for her fine fowls, and had often been awarded prizes at the neighbouring • shows A man living near her house, hearing her poultry so highly praised, resolved to give her a trial, and sent an order for the finest capon she had. After a little delay he was delighted to receive as splendid a specimen as could be wished for. This delight, however, was short-lived, for on trying to ,carve the bird be found it extremely tough. Enraged, he set out to tell the woman she had swindled him. "Hoots, man," she cried, • after listening to his outburst of wrath, "why ye canna tell a guid fowl when ye see aned. That. bubblyjock's ta'en th' first prize at th' show for th' last seeven years! "

div.head: DISEASES OF THE CROP.
div.p: DISEASES OF THE CROP.

Catarrh, or ,rnmon cold, is very frequent in the draught3 Jowl-house, much more so than among fowl ,vhich roost in trees and take the weather as it comes all the year round; but catarrh of the crop is not so generally recog- nised, although quite common under certain circumstances. Among these may be named decomposing food, more particularly animal food, overloading with hard, indigestible sub- stances, the accumulation of sand, and the presence of parasites (Filaria uncinata and others). Several cases of the first-named kind have been receized within the past few weeks, and the senders h,ave always suspected poison. They were right in a way, but their suspicions of ill-disposed neighbours were unjustified. In such cases the lining membrane of the -crop is intensely inflamed, and after a short pre- liminary period of dryness and loss of appetite a profuse secretion of ill-smelling fluid follows, and the bird is almost sick—does, in fact, vomit, but not in such a conspicuous manner as the dog or cat or

Dangers Of Putrid Flesh. When the catarrhal crop is caused by putrid flesh, one should examine the spleen of a dead subject as well. It will be found enormously enlarged and dark in colour: Those who do not know the spleen may be told that it resembles a membranous bag attached to the stomach by a loose, thin membrane. We do not suppose that poultrymen deliberately feed. folds on corruption, but the fowls find it. There is still so much carelessness in the disposal of dead animals and birds. A rabbit that has been snared an& forgotten, or left there because the man Who set the snare thinks it is not safe to collect results, has 'often been the cause of crop trouble to birds They seem somehow attracted to decaying carcases, and will return. A warped calf or a dead rat or mole, or other' of the many cadavers that are carelessly left hbout the farm or fall into ditches, serve as poison bait for 'fowls. They are the more likely to sample such things if already suffering from indigestion as a result of eating ,their full capacity of hard maize, peas, or beans. A hard-packed or crop-bound bird is recog- nised by most people, and many henwives attempt its cure by drenching with warm oil and manipulating the crop, producing an artificial vomition or squeezing upwards of the obstructing material, but a windy crop is more likely to go unnoticed.

div.head: Soft Crop.
div.p: Soft Crop.

In some 'districts what is known as " soft- crop "is recognised, but the cause is not. A crop partly filled with wind and made up with slimy mucus is due to a catarrh which has led the fowl to leave off eating. One absent hen among fifty or more is not missed, and she may be " humping " in a hedge with feathers standing up and wings drooping for two or three days without attracting attention. Irri- tants, such as sheep-dip containing arsenic, have the same effect on the crop, and it is the part one should not fail to examine whenever a bird dies from an unknown cause. Of course, a fatal dose inflames the proventiculus or mediate portion between the crop and gizzard as well, but enough of some paint in an old tin may be taken to cause inflammation of the crop without killing the fowl it the time. Whether a hen is suffering from soft crop or is crop bound in the usual sense of the term, she should receive immediate atention, as she can be cure4V generally if taken in time, but chronics do not pay for doctoring. In either of these crop troubles it is important to empty the contents. Reference has already been made to oil and the fingers as a means of evacuation, but the operation is often a failure because it is hurried, and too much attempted at one time, when packed with hard stuff. The membrane is further injured by too much force. Repeated oilings are needed. It is not a bad plan to use butter and allow an interval for it io permeate the mass, and make two or three "goes" instead of one supremeeffort. There is physiological and practical efidorse- meat for this manner of proceeding. If a distended bladder has to be emptied, it is found by surgeons that the walls of the viscus can better contract upon about one-third of urine than when collapsed by ~complete evacuation by fhe-catheter. Cutting open and suturing should only be resorted to in such extreme cases that no stuff can be got up by way of the mouth.

div.head: POULTRY PEN.
div.p: POULTRY PEN.
HINTS AND INTERESTING FACTS AND CHAT FOR AMATEURS.

bird upside down, when very much will be poured out from the mouth. Some of the fluid comes from the nostrils, and makes breathing difficult, and for this reason the fowl should not be held up very long, but the performance repeated after clearing the nostrils. When the crop is emptied, it is not ready for the immediate work of digestion or as a simple reservoir alone Five drops of dilute hydro- chloric acid mixed with an ounce of water is the most suitable medicine, and of this a tea- spoonful- should be giveft night and morning. At midday a few spoonfuls of milk may be drenched, and this will sustain the patient for two or three days while the digestive mem- brane is recovering. Cordials are helpful, but they must not be irritating, so that mustard and pepper, cayenne, and the like are barred. A few drops of peppermint water with the first small feeds or boluses of meal seem to answer as well as anything for a beginning, antl then a gradual return to ordinary food. Valuable stock are well worth the trouble, and the average hen will immediately 'repay such treat- ment- at the hands of a person who cares more to succeed • than to appraise time.—Harold Leeney, M.R.C.V.S., in "New Zealand , Farmer." •

div.head: VALUE OF POULTRY MANURE.
div.p: THE VALUE OF POULTRY MANURE.

The value of poultry manure is not appreciated as it should be by farmers and gardeners. Practically not one farmer in a thousand understands what he is throwing away through neglect. Each year shows more cleatly the value of this class of fertiliser, while the elimination of horses from large towns becomes a more and more serious matter. Poultry droppings must be kept under cover, removed from the roost; granted, yet two or three corrugated sheets will often remove that difficulty. Treated thus, it is so light as to be easily moved and spread, 'can be taken uphill with a minimum of labour and 'exertion. The old man in the light cart can shift it to the awkward corner, or the steep 'bit which some- times goes short. Cattle feed greedily on the young grass which comes up rapidly after it. Garden and orchard all prosper vigorously. There is only one drawback—you get it for nothing, which to ignorance is just a short road to contempt.
BUFF Rock Eggs, 3/6 dozen; unfertiles re- placed or 15 sent; Chicks double.—Mrs. Mar- son, Kemberton, Shifnal.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 20, 1915.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
POND AND RIVER MUD AS MANURE.

Is river mud of any value as a Manure? asks a correspondent in "Farm and Home," who say 3 it seems to him to have a very rich appear- ance, and as seaweed is so valuable for potatoes, river mud may possibly have some manurial value.

River mud and pond mild may be used with advantage for dressing land, provided certain precautions are observed, but its composition will vary greatly according to circumstances, and no precise information on this point could be given without an analysis. The character of the soil through which the stream runs will have a good deal of influence in the matter. When ponds are cleared the mud should be heaped up, mixed with lime after it has re- thained in heap for some Time to drain, and it is best turned a few times. It may contain the germs of many water-borne diseases that affect stock, and the lime and turnings will help to render them harmless. While, as we state above an analysis is necessary to determine the precise value of any particular sample, it may be useful if we state that mud containing about 40 per cent. of water has been known to contain 1.37 per cent. of nitrogen, 0.22 per cent. of potash,, and 0.26 per cent. of phosphoric acid. Obviously it is best to use such material as near as possible to the source from which it is ob- tamec, as cartage to any great distance will make it costly.
HAVE YOU PIT-WOOD?

The Board of Agriculture and Fisheries desire to draw the attention of owners of *oodlands and others to the fact that some collierjes are still finding it difficulty in securing adequate supplies of pit-wood. In consequence of the situation created by the European War, supplies from abroad are considerably curtailed, and it is necessary to have greater recourse than usual to home-grown timber. Landowners may find this a favourable opportunity to sell, at a re- munerative rate, timber of which they have hitherto found it difficult to dispose to advan- tage. As a rule, however, collieries are not pre- pared to buy standing tfinber unless the woods are in their immediate neighbourhood. Informa- tion as to the kinds of timber required, market- ing, and other matters in this connection will be found in Special Leaflet No. 17, copies of which maybe obtained post free on application to the ,Secretary, Board of Agriculture and Fisheries, 4, Whitehall-place, London, S.W.

div.head: FUTURE FOR JAM.
div.p: A FUTURE FOR JAM.

The fruit-grower has little to be afraid of during the coming seasoh. Owing to the large quantities of jam which our Government, have purchased for the troops there are, we under- stand, a number of jam factories which are pretty well cleared of stock. We think it will prove that out of this war may come much good

to the fruit-grower in the future. The Govern- _ raent have found that the men composing our lines of defence have appreciated jam very highly. If is certainly infinitely better than a good deal of the vile stuff often given to troops, and wrongly, we think, called "butter." It may be that in the future years fruits, as jam and preserves; will enter much more largely than they have ever done before into the dietary of- our soldiers and sailors. This being so, the outlook for the future is distinctly good for the fruit-grower. We urge therefore that every care be taken both in manuring and working the land in due time, that all may be done that is possible to ensure good crops of fruit in 1915. The Fruit-Grower."
POTATO GROWING IN ALLOTMENTS AND SMALL GARDENS.

At the present time many householders will be especially anxious to curtail' their domestic expenses by devoting increased attention to the cultivation .of vegetables ..in their • gardens and allotments, and all available land may in some cases be used for growing vc.-,etables. In such circumstances few vegetables can be planted more piofitably than the potato. Growers on a small scale can .seldom choose the soil in which to plant, but they may do much to enable such soil as they have to pro- duce a satisfactory ,crop. Potatoes do best in Moderately light Soil with good- drainage. 'When heavy laud must -be used it 'should be Alter- oughly dug over during the autumn and winter, and should be prevented from becoming water- logged by being thrown up in ridges or narrow stretches if necessary.. If the soil is in reasonably good condition, potatoes may be planted as soon as mild weather arrives in spring. If, however, wet weather has made the preparation of the soil difficult, plant- ing should be defe,rred for a time. It is better to plant at the end of April with the land in good condition than early in March' with the land in bad order.

The potato is a gross feeder, and a liberal supply of soluble plant food is necessary for the production of a large crop. When it can be obtained, perhaps the best source of such food is farmyard manure, or, failing that, town stable manure.

The depth and distance apart at which pota- toes shoUld be planted vary according to the soil and the climate, but, generally speaking, pota- toes should be planted fairly shallow.—Extract from Special Leaflet of the Board of Agricul- ture, No. 18, which can be had free on applica- tion.

div.head: FRUIT TREES AND SUCKERS.
div.p: FRUIT TREES AND SUCKERS.

When fruit bees throw up a quantity. of .suckers, it is quite evident that the roots have, by digging, or some 'cause, been badly bruised, the suckers springing up from the injured places. The proper way to -treat all trees- from which such suckers Spring is to *bare the roots and find, out .the position' of the ',suckers, cut- ting these clean off and paring back close to the roots; then to refill the space cleared With fresh soil. It may be that some of these suckers may have small roots, in which ease they may be planted up in a row, where they will in time he, sufficiently large for budding or grafting.

div.head: PRUNING BLACK CURRANTS.
div.p: PRUNING BLACK CURRANTS.

Amateurs do net, as a rule, prune their black currants sufficiently, hence sun and air fail to reach the fruit, which is consequently small and of poor quality. As the fruit is borne on the wood of the previous year, this, if good crops are looked for, must be well ripened, and this can only be by freely thinning out the old and useless wood. The shoots must stand clear of each other ,and the centres of the b4shes be kept well open. Another great mistake is digging among the bushes, this leading to the loss of many of the surface roots. The better way is to lightly loosen the surface of the soil with a fork, and then to give a good mulch of cow manure, and, should the weather he dry during the summer, frequent heavy waterings to wash the goodness of the manure down to the roots. In this way both the weight and quality of .the fruits will be much improved. Black currants succeed best in a moist position, and deep, rather retentive soil, but in any sunny position, and, given good soil, they will do equally well, provided the bushes are well mulched and freely watered during a dry time. Cottagers often make a good sum out of their black cur- rants, and they might realise much more, as they are always in demand for puddings, pies and jams, and are often' used for making jelly and wine. In° most houses in the North the good wife's cupboard invariably contains 'a good store of either black currant jam or jelly. I may be wrong, but I am of opiniml that were more attention paid to the pruning and feeding of the black currant we should hear far less of the ravages of the mite. Of the varieties, the best, I think, is the old and well-known Lee's Prolific. Black Champion has very large indi- vidual berries, but, so far as I have seen, it does not crop so freely as Lee's Prolific. Black currants are often planted too thickly, and the trees in a few years become quite overcrowded. --" Farm and Home."

div.head: CHURCH LADS IN WAR.
div.p: CHURCH LADS IN WAR.
PLAY THE MAN.
Rev. H. Ogden's Call To Free
Church Lads.

The quarterly church parade of the War- rington Free Church Lads' Brigade was held at Golborne-street Baptist Church on Sunday, when four companies paraded, under the com- mand of Colonel Grounds. The companies represented were Latchford Baptists, Gol- borne-street Baptists, Bank Quay Mission and 11111 Cliffe Baptists. Each company was under the command of its respective officers, and both officers and boys were very smart in their appearance. It was noted that three captains are serving with the colours—Captain Davis, Captain Appleton and Captain Dale.

div.head: UNREQUITED KINDNESS.
div.p: UNREQUITED KINDNESS.

The Rev. 11. Ogden conducted the service, and preached the sermon. The preacher based his remarks upon the text 11. Samuel x. 12, "Be of good courage, and let us play the men for our people, and for the cities of our God; and the Lord do that which seemeth him good." The incident revealed the fruitful source of all wars. Wanton insult was an evidence of vulgarity. David, as the narrative tells us, was intent upon performing a kindness to a sister nation. They repaid his kindness by wanton insult. The children of Ammon sus- pected the ambassadors of David and regarded them as spies. The result was, that in sus- picion they insulted the servants of King David, and he believed that the only course that was honourably left to him was to declare war. He called all the people together and exhorted them to play the man. Thus are all wars made. Neighbourly kindnesses are dis-

torted by suspicion. Suspicion leads to in- sults. Insults lead to war. The European War was all an outcome of suspicion pf one nation by another. _ The preach& urged the boys to act like gentlemen, and said it was easier to return in- sult for insult than to return courtesy for rudeness. Playing the man required any man who would be a hero in any walk of life to

exercise self-suppression. When boys were young their parents were apt to indulge them and the corrective, hard and severe, had to come later in life. Discipline was a necessary part of human life, and even the rod played a useful part in the development of a boy.

div.head: An Unseated Deity.
div.p: An Unseated Deity.

Forty years ago the rod and the birch were deified; now there has been a rush to the other extreme, and the birch has been neglected. A ound thrashing did some boys all the good in the world. The right system was to under- stand the boy. Temperament played a most important part in determining the manner and amount of punishment.
Need for Self-sacrifice.

"Playing the man called for the exercise of the noblest qualities. One writer said it was easier to chase a German up a trench with a fixed bayonet than to go on self-sacrificing day by day; It , would be quite possible to find even a British soldier who would bayonet Germans in a wild charge, who would refuse to allow any of his pay for the old folks at home To play the man there must be a 'steady and persistent self-sacrifice. The most difficult man in the world to please was the man who was bent upon pleasing himsdf. , He pines for other pleasures he could never have. There was real happiness and pleasure in helping 'others. Old Scrooge became reallty happy when he fed the family of Bob Cratchet, helped Tiny Tim, and took an interest in life. Whoever saved life was a greater hero than he who destroyed it."

During the service one of the lads, Stephen Lees, sang a solo, and the hymns were of such a ousing kind as "Stand up, Stand up, for Jesus !" "Onward, Christian Soldiers!" and "'Fight the good fight." The appreciation of the boys and their work was evidenced by the fact that the church was crowded.
After the service a retiring collection was taken on behalf of the funds of the brigade.

div.head: AN IRISH IMPOSTER.
div.p: AN IRISH IMPOSTER.
Man Who 'Listed and Ran Away.

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, the Bench (over which Mr. R. T. Fairalough presided), complimented the police officers who succeeded in bringing to justice an Irishman who now called himself Thomas Barry, but (who was said to have used as aliases the names Thomas Coleman and Patrick Coffey.—There ;were four charges against the man, viz.: being an absentee from the Army, attempting to obtain ss. lid. from the recruiting authorities by 'false pretences, stealing an overcoat belong- ing to the recruiting authorities, and making a false attestation to them.

From the evidence it appeared that the prisoner first presented himself at Warrington las Thomas Coleman, and, enlisting in the Royal Enniskillen Fusiliers, he received_7s. 3d. and his travelling papers (and an overcoat) to go to Ireland. This was on February 26th. The next heard of him was at Widnes on March sth, when he presented himself for enlistment in the Connaught Rangers; and would have succeeded had it not been for his having to come to Warrington for attestation. It was then that he was identified and given in charge tor being an absentee from the Royal Enniskillen Fusiliers. Whilst in custody, on remand, inquiries revealed the fact that he was travelling from place to place defrauding the military authorities. Prisoner admitted hav- ing come from Glasgow to Liverpool. It was, said the Chief Constable, whilst in Glasgow that prisoner first tried to enlist. His finger prints resulted in the discovery that he had been con- victed at Connaught Assizes on December 4th, and sentenced to three months for theft. After the Court had heard the evidence of half a dozen witnesses as to identification, prisoner persisted that he had never been in Warrington in his life before March 6th, The Chairman said the Bench had come to the conclusion that prisoner was a thorough imposter. They had no doubt about the signa- tures of Thomas Coleman and that of Thomas Parry being written by one and the same man. They believed the prisoner had been carrying on the game in various parts of the country, and he would have to go to prison for six months.

div.head: PUBLISHED IN THIS PAPER. Did you see it P
div.p: PUBLISHED IN THIS PAPER. Did you see it P

Six years ago an Earlestown resident Made a statement which was published in our local papers, and which aroused great interest, not only here, hut for many miles around. Our readers will, we are sure, be gratified to know that the facts are enthusiastically endorsed to- day—years after: ' '

On May 22nd, 1907, Mr. A. Williams, of 58, Houghton-street, near the Station, Earlestown, said: "I suffered with my back for three years. I 'could get no, peace for- the shooting pains which attacked 'me across the kidneys. If I attempted to lift anything the 'pains would seize me, so that I could ;hardly izet my back straight again. The urinary excretions caused pain, and contained a dark, heavy sediment. "I' tried various remedies, but the medicine that, cured me was Doani's Backache Kidney Pills. div.head: VALUE OF DISCIPLINE.
div.p: VALUE OF DISCIPLINE.
Lieutenant Henshall's Message To His Company.

Members of the Church Lads' Brigade are playing a notable and honourable part in the defence of their country; and it is pleasing to know that the keenness of those who have been left behind to keep the flag flying at home while they are "doing their bit" at the Front is meeting with every success. The St. Paul's Company, of which Lieutenant Sydney Henshall is captain, is a case in point. Lieutenant Henshall is on active service, but the company he was largely instrumental .in bringing to a high state of efficiency goes on building on the foundation he and his col- leagues laid. The company, which started five years ago, gradually grew until last August its membership was 100. Some passed through that period and retired on reaching the age limit. The war deprived the company of a; number of the older members—four officers and 35 N.C.O.'s and lads. In addition there are about 25 past members serving their King and country—surely a very proud record. On mobilization of the Territorial Forces the commanding officer of the company (Captain Sydney Henshall), invited Lieutenant Bunch to take over the command in his absence. By steady •recruiting the strength of the company has been raised to near the figures prior to the war, and every effort is being made by the officers and the new N.C.O.'s and lads to•keen up the high standard which was reached before the war broke out. Although the lads are much younger than usual, they are all very keen, and the 'weekly parades are well attended.
There was a special treat for the lads at their usual weekly parade on Thursday night, when a letter was read to them from their Captain.

div.head: LErrEit FROM THE TRENCHES.
div.p: LErrEit FROM THE TRENCHES.
Territorials Were Fit For Immediate Duty.
Writing from "The Trenches" to "the mem- bers of my Church Lads' Brigade Company 7 Lieutenant lienshall says :--

"I thought perhaps you might be interested to hear something from me now that I am with the Warrington Territorials at the Front. These few notes I am writing whilst sitting in the trenches. It may have surprised you when you heard that the Battalion was practi- cally sent straight from the port of disem- barkation to the firing line: it was a great honour to know that our course of training was thought by the authorities to have made us proficient in military practice." Having thus shown his pride in ids battalion. Lieutenant Henshall explains in detail life and work in and out of the trenches, a topic which had a lively interest for the boys. "I have," continued the Lieutenant, "several old C.L.B. lads of the St. Paul's Company with me here, arta they along with the others are really sporting fellows, and the stiffer the work the more cheery they are to tackle it. I am given to understand that over 500 old and pre- sent members of the C.L.Be were reported in the dispatches for Special Service Medal, and in. the C.L.B. Magazine, which all boys ought to buy. In the next monthly you will find a full list. I often give thought to the company and wonder how you are all going on. I hope everybody is trying to keep up the good repu- tation which I think we made. Of:course, the upset arising from the' war has made a great change, and many of the -older members have left you for a short time to join the colours, but •there is no reason why the company should not continue to advance with its regu- lar work. If all are loyal to their officers and realise it is an honour to be a .meniber of the C.L.B. then when. we'tecturn to you we hope to find a stronger and more -united company than ever. , Remember that the Members who are over , here have felt the benefit of their drilling, their ambulance training and their signalling work. The drudgery of drill is the root of all discipline—it is only by implicit obedience and willing subordinafion to those in command of you that success is achieved. "Any successes which our Army has obtained in this war have had discipline at the root of them. The discipline of our original Expeditionary Force was marvellous. It enabled them to recover from many tight corners and to turn what the enemy thought was failure into victorious offensive."

div.head: ENOWAIMENT ASSURANCES AS INVESTMENTS.
div.p: ENOWAIMENT ASSURANCES AS INVESTMENTS.
Endowment Assurance grows in popular favour. An endowment assurance in the Pru- dential possesses five qualities which make it ideal from an investment point of view.

div.head: (1) The Security is Absolute.
div.p: (1) The Security is Absolute.

There is no other business institution in the country which can offer to its members more abundant evidence of security than the Pru- dential. Even in the abnormal financial situa- tion created by the European War the Pruden- tial can look ahead with quiet confidence. Owing to the fact that current income exceeds current expenditure it has no necessity to realise depreciated investments, but can calmly await the recovery in prices.
(2) It Relieves Policy-holders of Income Tax and Super Tax.

Everybody in this. country can escape income tax on one-sixth of his income provided he invests that one-sixth ,in :life assurance. This is an advantage .not possessed by any other investment, and as income tax is now doubled, endowment assurances are rendered doubly attractive. In this connection it should be _borne, in mind that a' man who invests from income in the ordinary way has to suffer tax from two sources. Thus, suppose your income is £3OO per annum, then if you wish to invest £5O each year in an ordinary investment you must set aside 4;54 is. Id. because £4 is. Id. will be required for income tax on the assumption that you pay only the lowest rate of tax. In .addition, income tax at 2s. 6d. in the e will have tq be paid on the interest yielded by the investment.

To those with large incomes life assurance presents further attractions, for in returning incomes for super tax, the amount paid in premiums may be deducted, and is therefore not subject to tibis tax.

div.head: (3) There is No Risk of Depreciation.
div.p: (3) There is No Risk of Depreciation.

Recent events have brought home to investors in,a striking manner the extent to which prices of securities may fall. The holder of an endowment 'assurance is certain of a minimum return in any event, and if the policy be "with profits" he has the satisfaction of knowing that the aniount ultimately to be received can only move in an upward and never in a down- ward direction.

div.head: (4) It Assists Small Investors.
div.p: (4) It Assists Small Investors.

Those who are able to save only a small amount annually can, by effecting an' endow- ment assurance, invest that small amount with- out the recurring difficulty of selecting an investment, and they are furthermore relieved of all expense on 'account of brokerage, trans- fer fees, government stamps, &c.
(5) It Affords the Protection of Assurance.

The fact that the full sum assured it 4 payable should death occur at any time within the term of yeari4, selected, constitutes :ane of the gregtest advantages possessed by an endowment - assurance over other forms of investment. If money is saved in the ordinary way only the amount so saved is available for the dependents of the invtestor, and in the event .of his early death this amount may be very small. By effecting an endowment assurance the investor is saved much anxious thought con- cerning those for whom. he has .to Provide. Mr. S. Brocklehurst, whose offices are at 69, Sankey-street, .ia the Superintendent of AM) Prudential Co. for the Warrington district,. and will be glad to give all information.

div.head: FOR HE WAR CHARITIES.
div.p: FOR HE WAR CHARITIES.
TO-NIC,HTS CONCERT IN
PARR HALL.
SOME ATTRACTIVE MUSIC.

As will be seen from an announcement in our advertising columns, the Warrington Musical Society is co-operating with the Infirmary Working Men's Committee in the giving of a concert this (Saturday) evening, in aid of the local War Fund and the Raddon Court Red Cross Society. With so worthy an object in view it is hoped—we should like to say, expected— that the promoters will be accorded a generous measure of public support. It is a matter for congratulation that the Society's choral and orchestral members, along with two local solo vocalists, will sustain the bulk of the programme, variety to which is being given by the solo playing of a Belgian 'cellist in the person of Mr. Henri Van Demme. The programme reveals a wealth of good things in store for the audience. While much of the music has been heard at previous Musical Society concerts, a great deal of it will well bear repetition, and there are, on ,the other hand, some items that are quite new and that abound in points of interest. Much of both the old and the new is, as befits the time and the cir- cumstances, of a distinctly martial, when it is not actually of a warlike, kind. Our popular townsman, Mr. J. Rabbitt, will, for instance, sing "Sound an alarm !" from Handel's "Judas Maccabeus," and so stirring a theme will -serve as a foil. to Mde. Sara Silcock's singing of some songs entirely peaceful and of graceful senti- ment. The chorus, too, will put forward the sweetly pathetic, yet timely, part-song, "Rest, soldier, rest !" by Roberts, in close association with two in strongly contrasted march rhythm entitled "Our Empire 'Flag" by Mackenzie, and "The Viking Song" by Coleridge Taylor. Choral members will, however, be more seriously con- cerned in two big Elgarian choruses—" Britons alert !" from " Caractacus," and "It comes from the misty ages" from "The Banner of St. George "—both of which, it will be gathered, appropriately breathe the spirit of the strenu- ous period through which we are passing. A quite recently composed work of some import- ance, which will be heard for the first time in Warrington, is a setting for chorus, of inixed voices, organ and .brass instruments, by Mrs. Meredith, of Rudyard Kipling's well-known poem "Recessional," and, as this deeply devo- tional work has been favourably commented 'upon in high places, considerable anticipatory interest is naturally felt in regard to. the man- ner in which our Musical Society will,present it. Not the least interesting items in the pro- gramme are those in which the orchestra are entirely, or chiefly, concerned. .By request the selection will be repeated of "Nautical Tunes," the performance of which was so well received at Mr. A. 11. Crosfield's concert last December. Some, much more serious things will, however, engage the at- tention of the Society's orche,stral members. The Polonnaise for orchestra and chorus from Glinka's opera, "-A Life for the Tsar," may be instanced as affording the bandsmen a fine op- portunity of distinguishing themselves, while it incidentally finds the chorus 'something rousing to sing. Its composer (born 1803, died 1957) is regarded as having signalised in his 'Arson the birth of a genuine school of Russian music. Himself referred to as the "prophet-patriarch" of Russian music, Glinka; in early maturity, conceived the idea of composing a national opera project which was consummated' in the per- formance of a brilliant work under the above- mentioned title in the presence of the Imperial Family in 1836. Its success is said to have been: immediate and unequivocal, the freshness and originality of the music, as well as the patriotic sentiment of the opera's story, greatly endear; big it to Glinka's admiring countrymen. After an interval of less than two years the orchestra will again perform the " Valse Triste" of Sibelius. Readers who listened to this COM- poser's " Finlandia" just over twelve months ago, will recall the strong and fascinating quali- ties of the music of this highly esteemed Finnish composer. Whereas, in " Finlandia " Sibelius i is strong in racial characteristics, we find him, in the " Valse Triste," in quite a spiritual mood.l The qualifying word in the title is equivalent to "full, of grief" or "sorrowful." So that, bear-. ing in mind the nature of the work from which it is an excerpt, the peculiarly ethereal quality of the music will be seen to be as apt as it is highly emotional. In a note in the programme of the concert alluded .to we are told that the " Valse Triste" is a number from the music to Jarnefelt's drama " Kuolema " (meaning death)." and is a characteristic example of the work of the Finnish composer, who has recently come much into public favour. The music is laid out for strings and flute;‘clarionet, two horns and drums. The author of the drama is a' brother- in-law of the composer. The work is thus described by an authority: "The scene is a room at night. A woman is dying on her bed. Her son, who has been watching her, has fallen asleep. Gradually the room becomes suffused with a red glow. There 'comes the sound of dis- tant music in waltz rhythm. To its strains the dying woman rises and begins to move slowly and silently to the dance measure. She waves her hands as though beckoning invisible dancers. They appear. The woman mingles with them. She tries to make them look at her; but they avoid her glance. The weird gaiety reaches a climax. There is a lirnock at the door! The spectral guests vanish. Death stands on the threshold. The music deepens the weird- ness of thescene, and to say this is, perhaps, the greatest witness to the composer's genius." The overture to. Auber's opera, "The Bronze Horse," is one of the brilliant things of its kind. It is, of course, characteristically French in being gay . and vivacious—captivating melody and a careless impetuosity being its *notable features. Its composer (born 1782, died 1871) is spoken of as the last great representative of the French opera comique. Although he owed much, in the course of his early studies, to Cherubini, who was at that time the ruler of the operatic stage, Auber may be more truthfully regarded as ,the follower of Boiedieu and Herold, as is attested by the charm and piquancy of his melo- dies and the brilliance of his orchestral effects. The opera, "Le Cheval de Bronze," was com- posed in 1857, when Auber 'was getting on in years, yet the work is a signal instance of the unimpaired exercise of his genius. The solos to be.given by Mr. Van Damme in- clude a group of three, in which there is an- nounced a " Melody " by Mr. Crossley, the society's conductor, first, heard at its concerts many years ago, when it was played by Mr. Carl Fuchs. The solo 'cellist will, however, be heard apart from these morceaux. in the more exact- ing " Kol Nidrei " of Max Bruch.. This deeply moving composition, 'for 'cello and orchestra, based on an ancient Hebrew melody, calls for some concentration of attention right!y to appreciate its beauties, and listeners would do well to miss none pf them by liipreparedness.. Max Bruch is one of the most eminent of German composer. Born in Cologne in 1838, he came of a family already distinctly gifted Musically on his mother's side. After studying at Frank- fort and Munich he rapidly came to the front, distinguishing himself particularly in the vast field of music scored for chorus and orchestra, wherein he proved himself a master of lofty melody and of the effective treatment or masses of sound. It is noteworthy that, in 1880, Max Bruch was offered the direction of the Liverpool Philharmonic Society, and that he was, conse- quently, at thie time, for some three years resi- dent in England. The-honorary degree of Cam- bridge University Was conferred upon hini lii 1893. • • B. •

div.head: 3s. A WEEK FOR LOWER-
div.p: 3s. A WEEK FOR LOWER-
PAID MEN.

At a special and little more lhan formal meeting of the Warrington Town Council, held in the Town Hall on Tuesday evening, approval was unanimously given to a scheme of war bonuses for employes of the Corpora- tion. The matter had previously been dis- cussed by the General Purposes Committee— which consists of 'the whole Council—and con- sequently there was no need for debate in pub- lic, and the proceedings lasted a bare five minutes. ,

SOLDIER-SERVANTS' WIVES TO HAVE THE BONUS. The terms on which the bonus should be given, as drawn up by the General Purposes • Committee, were as follows : A war bonus shall be allowed to the employes of the Corporation (of *both sexes, and including clerks, teachers and members ' of the police force, but excluding the indoor hospital staff) in receipt of wages of and exceeding £l, but not exceeding £2 per week, subject to the conditions herein set forth:— Married men in receipt of £1 and not exceeding SOs., 3s. per week. Married men in receipt of wages above s 305., but not exceeding £2, 2s. per week. Unmarried men in receipt of wages of £1 and upwards but not exceeding £2, is. jer week. The bonus will be paid on the standard -- rate of wages (exclusive of overtime and allowances) in force immediately before ' the commencement of the war. The bonus will be payable from the Ist March, 1915. Where the hours of labour and the rate of pay vary the bonus will be paid on the average rate of wages as calculated by the manager. If :by reason of employment on Sunday the wages exceed £2 per week the bonus will be calculated on six days' pay. Where a complete week's work does not comprise six full days the bonus will be paid on the wages earnV in each week. The bonus will not be paid to any employe who loses more than one quarter in each week's work unless he satisfies the manager that the loss of time is due to siekness or other, unavoidable cause. Casual labourers shall be allowed instead of the bonus an extra id. per hour. The bonus will be allowed to the ,wives and other dependents of employes serving ' with H.M. forces. The bonus will cease on the termination of the war without prejudice to the con- sideration of all applications for increases made since the commencement of the war. The brief meeting was presided over by the Mayor (Alderman Peacock), and there were also present: The Deputy-Mayor (Dr. Joseph). Aldermen James Evans, Smethurst and Tinnion, and Councillors Henshall, Osborne, Locker, Cunnington, Hawthorn, Wilkinson, Skelland and Firth Lindley, with the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) and other officials. The MAYOE-said that-the Council had already met as a General Purposes Committee, and had agreed to the principle of the bonuses. Alderman JAMES EVANS thought that in order to shorten the meeting the proposals might be taken en bloc, as the matter had been fully discussed at meetings of all the com- mittees affected, and the full sense of the opinions of those committees had been ex- pressed at the meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee. - (Hear, hear.)

div.head: NO INCREASE FOR THE TWO-GUINEA

That meeting had been dilly held, and the resu'i of the deliberations thereat was now bgore the Big Wor:hip werr on to refer to the clause, which read:—" The bonus will be paid on-the standard rate of wages (exclusive of overtime and allowances) in force immediately before the commencement of the war," and suggested that ,it would be better if that clause were omitted altogether and the following substituted:—" Married men whose wages are above. 30s. but under 315., and above 40s. but under 425. per week respectively shall have such bonus as may be necessary to in- crease the wage to 335. per week or 425. per week as the case may be." The addition had the approval of the heads of departments, and he had been asked to include it in the clauses. COutrillor .W.loxixsoN : How will it affeet the case of a man with a salary of 435. 6d.? The MAYOR: Not at all; 425. is their:3A ililUlll. His Worship then moved the confirmation of the conditions as set out above subject to the amendment he had suggested.

Alderman JAMES EVANS seconded, and the proposition was carried, the MAYOR remarking "I think w shall be able to get on with our work smoothly, and I hope all will be satis- factory to the men and also to the Corpora- tion."

div.head: PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE, CO., LTD.
div.p: PRUDENTIAL ASSURANCE, CO., LTD.
Highly-Successful Year in Spite of Unprecedented

div.head: War Conditions.
div.p: War Conditions.
THE STRENGTH OF THE COMPANY.
Mr. Thomas C. Dewey (chairman), presiding at the sixty-sixth annual general meeting of the Prudential Assurance Co., Ltd., on March 4th, at the Chief Office, Holborn Pats,Lut.klu, said :--

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— When I had the pleasure of addressing you twelve months ago, I had not only the .3atis- faction of presenting a very favourable report Upon our business for the year 1913, but I was also able to express the hope that the com- mercial depression we ,had been experiencing had well nigh reached its limit, and that the Prospect for 1914 was BO far of a most encourag- ing character. In the first half of 1914 ray hope was fully justified, and our returns :dur- ing that period pointed to a most successful and indeed a record year. But to-day we meet under the shadow of that terrible struggle which, during the past six months has shaken Europe to its very founda- tions, and we have not only to mourn the loss of so many of our bravest and our best, but we have to prosecute at an enormous cost, such a war as the world "has never before seen, a war characterised on one side by unspeakable brutalities, wanton destruction, and an abso- lute disregard of all those laws of humanity kwhich have hitherto been respected by civilised nations in the fiercest of their struggles. Such an enemy as we are fighting must be. crushed at whatever cost to our Empire, and we can only cheerfully recognise our share of responsibility, hoping and believing that we shall successfully accomplish the great task set before us, and eventually ensure the peace and prosperity of the world for many a long year yet to come.

It is lathe time of stress and strain that true strength becomes apparent, and anyone !who will study the really remarkable report .now presented will readily see how great is the strength of the Company and will, I feel sure, appreciate the conservative course which we have adopted with the view to preparing for Still greater strains on our resources if such should arise as a result of this great war. During the first seven months of the year our results were phenomenal., business was constantly increasing in volume, and had this continued we should certainly have had a record in every department. The business of the Company is National in its character, and it was impossible that it Should escape the effects of the dislocation ensuing on the outbreak of hostilities. I am Pleased to be able to say, however, that once the first effects of the shock had passed away Ol' business was, dtt the whole, of normal volume.

Th—e —total income of the Company was £17,196,088, being an increase of £628,479 over that of the previous year. The most note- *orthy item in this increase is that of the industrial weekly and monthly premiums received, which amounted to £301,746 more than in the year 1913. Only twice before in the history of the Com- PanY has this increase been exceeded, namely, ill 1883 and in 1906; in which years, however, Owing to our method of collection there was 4n extra week, that is to say 53 weeks instead of 52 weeks' collections. In a normal 52-week Year we have never before had so great an increase. Of the total income, no less than £13,211,827 Caine from premiums. For the first time the Premiums received in the Ordinary Branch t,Xceeded £5,000,000, and the premiums in the industrial Branch exceeded £8,000,000. , In the Ordinary Branch 65,751 new policies were issued producing a new premium income of &.,421.,353, and assuring £6,318,843. Of this one- sixth, or more than £1,000,000, was under poli- cies assuring sums ranging from ..t5OO to ,220,000. _ With the doubling of the Income Tax and aSnuper Tax, it is to be expected that life assur- ance, ,b branch of receives special concessions under dem o_f taxation, will be in even greater and in number the future than in the past. The of large policies which- were effected with the Prudential during 1914 indicates that the results in this class of business during the current year will be still more enCouraging. The total number of Ordinary Branch is 922,505, Policies in force in the bonus £102,940,771. assuring with

charged on the excess over £250. For existing policies on the lives of all other members of H.M. Forces, including Territorials and Kitch- ener's Army, it was agreed that no extra pre- mium should be charged. In order to provide facilities for those on active service who desired to obtain either assurance or additional assurance we introduced a special table for sailors and soldiers. Under this table the sum assured is payable at the expiration of 15 years, or at previous death, whether caused-by)the War or otherwise. The policy is issued for amounts of £lO and upwards, the annual premium for each .210 sum assured being twenty-five shillings for the duration of the war and twelve shillings and sixpence after. As there is no maximum limit to the amount for which policies will be issued, the table is suitable for all classes and all ranks.

For some time past very great difficulty has been experienced. in obtaining assurance where the war risk is involved, and our new policy has therefore received very favourable comment and met with considerable success.

The generous treatment of its policy-holders on the sea and at the front has up to the pre- sent time involved .the payment of claims in both branches, amounting to upwards of ...e150,000 on ever 7,000 lives. The concessions that have been made in regard to war risk must in any case costthe Company many thousands of pounds sterling, but I feel sure that in so acting we shell have the hearty support a all shareholders and policy-holders. Our efforts to render effective national assist- ance at this time of stress have, however, to some; extent been discouraged owing to the pro- visions' which were inserted in the Courts (Emergency Powers) Act. The Act forms part of the emergency legislation due to the war, and has added in so small degree to the diffi- culties of the future as regards Industrial Assurance.

Under the provisions of the Act certain sec- tions of Industrial policy-holders whose circum- stances have worsened owing to the war, are given the option of deferring payment of their premiums until after the termination of hostil- ities. On Claims arising under policies where this option has been exercised the Company is called upon to pay the claim as though the assured had continued payment of premiums in the ordinary way. While the Act may entail very serious losses on the Company, it is a very doubtful advan- tage to the policy-holder, for the effort required to pay off the arrears which will have accumu- lated will certainly be much greater than that required to pay the few pence weekly in the ordinary course, and he may in consequence be forced to sacrifice his policy. For obvious reasons the full effect of the Act is not yet apparent, but the contingent liabilities which may arise are SQ serious that a special reserve of .2300,000 has been set aside to provide for them. We do feel that its effect was not pro- perly understood at the time the Bill was before Parliament, and we trust that the Gov- ernment will take the earliest Opportunity of removing what appears to be not only a dis- advantage to the policy-holder, but an unfair burden on Industrial Assurance.

div.head: TWENTY-MILLION MAI-IK
div.p: THE TWENTY-MILLION MAI-IK

In the Industrial Branch the total number of Policies has turned the 20 million mark, the exact number in force being 20,085,010, assur- ing, exclusive of bonus, the sum of £263,739,424. The' number of new policies issued during the Year again exceeds 2,000,000, assuring a maxi- raum sum of £32,291,598. A feature of the new business has been the large number of monthly Premium policies which have been issued. You Will remember that I referred to the notable increase in this class of business last year. The repetition of the experience this year shows that monthly business has passed out. of the experimental stage and is definitely established as an important part of our Industrial Branch. The claims for the year amount to £7,388,508, qf which over £2,800;000 were due to maturing endowments. The claims paid exceeded those for 1913 by £482,690, but were, • nevertheless; eonsiderably below those expected in both Branches.

It itz;---- very satisfactory to be able to tell you that the expense ratio in both branches has again been reduced. In the Industrial Branch the ratio of expenses to premiums received was 38.86 per cent, and the ratio to the total in- come of that branch was 32.6 per cent. In the Ordinary Branch the ratios were £8 48. 2d. per te,t• to premiums, and £5 16s. 7d. per cent. to lotal income. 1_ The year's business must be considered as nighly satisfactory in view of the exceptional .?enditions. To the casual observer accustomed o the enormous figures of the Prudential it l'erhaps presents but few striking features. I 4.,_331a3" impress upon you, however, the fact that Te premiums received in the Industrial Branch nring a year, of which five months were occu- l'led in warfare, exceeded those of the previous Year by over .000,000. This is a great achieve- 112,ent and a wonderful tribute to the outdoor of the Company. outbreak of the war was of momentous -Jtorest to the Company. With 21,000,000 poll- on lives comprising all classes of the popu- Pion and drawn from all parts of the United 'fllngdom, and with invested funds of over 91,000,000, the difficulties which faced the Com- nY at the outset can hardly be over-estimated. L4hat a large number of its policy-holders would °a engaged in the actual fighting was inevitable. There was every reason to believe that the 'angPrs which would be incurred by combatants ,00ld be much greater than those experienced in previous wars. With these facts before us it Itciia-c; a. grave responsibility to 'decide whether condition on the policies excluding war lilska was to be waived or not. The directors, owever, considering the question from a enational standpoint, decided not to charge any Lltra premium to existing Industrial policy- 401ders.

div.head: WAR TIME CONCESSIONS.
div.p: WAR TIME CONCESSIONS.

That the Company should voluntarily have 11,,,,ade this concession, which may affect some •'.°oo policies, is evidence that it is shoulder- ing its full share of the burden that has been east upon the country. „ In the Ordinary Branch it was decided that for existing policies on the lives of members of the Regular Army and Navy, the first £250 of assurance should be subject to no extra Premium, and that £5 ss. per cent. should be

div.head: CONSERVING RESOURCES.
div.p: CONSERVING RESOURCES.

It will be seen from the valuation report that the stringency of out valuation basis has been maintained. Net premiums only have been valued, and the rate of interest assumed has been -three per. cent. When it is remembered that the actual rate earned on the whole of our funds was four per. cent,- after deduction of Income Tax, it will be seen that the surplus interest available for future profit must be very considerable. The sickness assurance business, which, it will be remembered, is carried on in Connection with members of the Prudential Approved Societies, has been valued on the same basis as -last year. The sickness rates have been favourable, and the funds in hand are fifty- eight per cent. in excess of the estimated lia- bility; it has, however, been considered advis- able to carry nothing to profit, but to continue to strengthen the fund until it is beyond any reasonable possibility of loss. The surplus in the Ordinary Branch is £1,794,953, and after, deducting the amount brought forward, viz., X 153,230, the profit for the year is shown as .21,641,723. This surplus would have been more than sufficient to provide a bonus at the same rate as last year, but in view of the uncertainty of the outlook it was decided that a substantial amount should be allotted to the investments reserve fund and an increased amount carried forward. Having thus so far as possible guarded against all con- tingencies it was felt that a bonus of one pound ten shillings per cent on the sum assured could be safely declared. Should the course of events prove as favour- able as our belief in the justice of our country's cause leads us to anticipate, the conserving of our resources must be a source of additional profit in the future.

The total asset; of the Company as shown in the Balance Sheet are £91,202,344, being an in- crease of £4,209,341 during the year. For some years past I have referred to the subject' .of depreciation in investment . prices, and last year I added that the depreciation in 1913 was greater than in any year I could re- member during an experience of half a century. The depreciation in market values had been practically continuous since the year of record high prices, viz., 1896. At that date we had accumulated substantial surpluses in the form of appreciation on our book values, and for a number of years these surpluses were more than sufficient to meet the subsequent depreciation which took plate. We had, however, in the meantime carried large sums to Investment Reserve Funds in both branches for the pur- pose of protecting our funds against the con- tinued fall in prices, and this policy we have pursued down to the present time. We have on several occasions adopted the policy of apply- ing portions of these reserves to writing down such of our securities as we thought advisable, and in this way we have been enabled to main- tain a satisfactory comparison between market prices and the value at which our assets appear in the balance sheet.

By the methods indicated we have during the last six years written down our securities by more than £5,000,000, and we ended the year 1913 with investment reserve funds of £1,000,000 in the combined Branches.

You may remember that last year I referred to the recovery of prices which began in the early part of 1914, and suggested that this _confirmed the opinion I had expressed, that, apart from international complications, Fe were reaching the end of the persistent fall. The outbreak of war has, however, entirely altered the outlook,, and we are now faced with further serious depreciations. As to the future, it is, of course, dangerous to prophesy, but I feel that, apart from a pos- sible temporary improvement in prices on the commencement of peace negotiations, we may expect a period of low values for several years, although I feel confident that the much delayed recovery will eventually take place.

div.head: SUBSTANTIAL RESERVES.
div.p: SUBSTANTIAL RESERVES.
The question as to the best method of deal- ing with the, depreciation is one to which your Board has given much careful consideration.
It will be remembered that on 31st December, 1914, the Stock Exchange was still closed, and any dealings that were actually effected afforded no criterion of the true values which

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 20, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 20, 1915.

obviously can only be ascertained by free deal- ings in an open market. It is also a factor of importance that in a Life Office such as our own, depreciation in many classes of securities does not represent a ~realised loss, but only a temporary reduction of nominal values. This is particularly the case with our large holding of terminable securities, the majority of )which are redeemable at a substantial premium on the existing book-values. In view of these considerations,' your Board considered it was not advisable to write down the values of our funds again this year, but that all available profits should be carried to the In- vestment Reserve Funds. We were strength- ened in coming to this conclusion by the fact that the Board of Trade has suggested that the market prices ruling on 31st December, 1913, might be taken as a criterion. Moreover, all our permanent securities were already standing in our books at the low prices ruling at that date.

A sum of £500,000 was accordingly added to the Reserve Fund in the Ordinary Branch, bringing it to the total of £1,000,000, and the sum of 2250,000 to the reserve fund in the industrial branch, bringing it to the , total of £750,000. Our total Investment Reserve Funds taus stands at the substantial sum of £1,750,000, and, in addition, a further reserve of £300,000 has been set aside in the Industrial Branch to meet certain in- definite liabilities caused through the passing of the Courts (Emergency, Powers) Act, to :which• I have already alluded. The Company has set aside this year the sum of no less than £1,050,000, or nearly £1,200,000 if the• increased amount carried forward is taken into account, to meet the altered con- ditions induced by the war; and as I have endeavoured previously to explain, the Corn- patty has decided to adopt a most generous course to' the Policy holders who have answered their Country's call, an& has put aside reserves which it is hoped will be sufficient to enable this course to be continued. The accomplishment of these results must necessarily involve some sacrifice on the part of both shareholders and policy-holders, and some departure from the high standard of bonus distribution we have aimed to attain. I have already mentioned that the Bonus on Policies in the Ordinary Branch will be reduced from £1 , 16s. per cent. on the sum Assured to £1 10s. per cent. The amount of Bonus distributable under our Profit Sharing Scheme will be reduced from £600.000, the amount distributed last year, to £300,000.
each area in the hands of one agent for atten- tion.
When we met last year we had gained the ex- perience desired by our,expprimental_ proceed- ings, and had decided 'upon a general adoption of the scheme.

There has been no departure from our inten- tion to avoid arbitrary interference with exist- ing agencies, but the improved system has pro- gressed rapidly during the past year, with the result that nearly one-eighth ,of our.lndustrial Branch income, representing over; one million pounds a year, has already been concentrated in more than 1,300 blocks. We are confident that the results will prove of advantage to the company, and that the ad- vantage is not limited to the company is suffi- ciently indicated by the fact that diving the past three yeirs the number of changes in the Agency Staff has very sensibly diminished. The change of system has rendered it unneces- sary to replace many of those who have left us owing to promotion, retirement, or other causes, and the reduction in numbers has been accom- panied by a satisfactory increase in the earn- ings of those remaining in our service. It is necessary in. considering the remunera- tion of our Staff -to have regard to the increased cost of living, and you will be interested to know that the average earnings of our Agency Staff advanced by more than seven shillings per week in the last two years. The promotion of the welfare or our Staff as a whole, which has been a marked and consist- ent • feature of the policy of the Board, has always been responded to most loyally, and never, has it been more abundantly justified than in recent years. The constant development of our business, as well as our participation under the National Insurance Act, have made demands on the Staff, not only for energy, but for enterprise, which could only have been met by men thoroughly imbued with the spirit of the Company and de- termined to add all possible distinction to its records.

We have had-no difficulty whatever in select- ing capable men for any new responsibility— men who have looked ahead And spared no effort to qualify themselves for the performance and control of unprecedented undertakings—men who have become expert authorities on new sub- jects of the first importance to the success of the Company. The capacity thus shown has been well seconded •by the devotion of their colleagues, and the work has been carried out to our com- plete satisfaction in spite of exceptional diffi- culties. COMPANY AND STAFF PATRIOTISM.

We cannot all join the Expeditionary Force; some are outside the acceptable limits of age, and some have not yet succeeded in passing the recruiting standard, though they.hope each new attempt may be rewarded with success.

Those who are left behind are willingly work- ing extra time to' make up so far as may be pos- sible for the absence of their colleagues who have joined the Colours. It has never been a bar to employment with us that a man was a Reservist, and by giving extra leave and in other ways, we have always encouraged our Staff to serve in the Territorial Army Our help has not been limited to our own men; the Courtyard of this building has frequently been placed at the service of regiments who have desired the opportunity of drilling there, and since War was declared our Rifle Range, which was opened by that distinguished Soldier, Lord Roberts, in 1906, has been kept busy during most hours of the day. We determined that members of our Staff elc.uld suffer no knanrial losp because of their engagement on active service, and we are con- tinuing the propOrtioll of their civilian pay necessary to make them as well off when serving the Colours as when serving the Company; in the case of Officers a contribution on a more generous scale has been made in order to secure the same result,

We have also underta tc find them ap- pointments not less important than those they relinquished, on their return to civilian life—a return which we,alL hope May be quickly. and happily accomplished. We have taken the view that. they are not serving the Company less.well.or less effectively because they are clothed in khaki, or because they have changed the collecting book or oen for more offensive *eaponfi. In the revision of Salaries, and in the -distri- bution of the bonus to the outdoor Staff, we have disregarded their absence from their normal duties ;AsfAstaut Superintendents whose Salaries are considered to some, extent on results achieved, have been credited with the figures they would probably have accomplished had they remained at home, and in a vacancy for promotion the fact that the man of our choice was fighting in the trenches in Flanders, tio far from standing in his v. ay was regarded as an additional recommendation.

- I cannot hope to place before you all the services which have been rendered to the Nation by Prudential men, but I cannot pass by the excellent work undertaken by our Voluntary Aid Detachments of the British Red Cross Society. Our men are on duty for this purpose throughout all hours of the day and night here in this Office, , and have received all the wounded soldiers arriving in London, sub- sequentli transferring them with all possible care to the destinations chosen for them by the War Office.

in my judgment the record of the Prudential and the work of its Staff during the present National crisis may well form the subject of profound thankfulness and satisfaction on the part of all who are associated with the Com- pany, and I submit this summary of our activities with every confidence that it will receive your cordial approval. The shareholders will miss to-day the pre- sence of our genial friend and. colleague, Dr. J. Irvine Boswell. ' Since November last • year, with the full approval and good wishes of his colleagues, he has been at the seat of war, giving his services and his highly trained skill to the help of the wounded and suffering, as he also did in the South African War. He has been at the front exposed to the attendant dangers and deprivations, and I need hardly say that his • welfare is followed , by. the affection .and regard of his colleagues, and I know you will allow me, on behalf of the shareholders,' to send him our good wishes and hopes for his safe and successful return.

div.head: INDUSTRIAL BRANCH BONUS.
div.p: INDUSTRIAL BRANCH BONUS.

The Industrial Branch bonus was founded in the year 1907: you will remember in that year the Shareholders resolved that in future they would be content with the then rate of Dividend, save for a proportion of any future new profits in order to assure and sustain their interest in the progress of the Company. The large sums they had in the past voted for the extension of benefits to Industrial policy-holders and the proportionate gifts they had made to the Outdoor Staff, were to be placed on a more definite basis, and thence- forth all increase in the profits was to be divided into six parts; four of these parts were to be given to the policy-holders, one part to the outdoor staff, and the other part the Shareholders were to retain. •

Six years later the devisible profits in this Branch had increased by £600,000, of which amount in 1913, and again in 1914, £400,000 went to the Industrial Policy-holders, £lOO,OOO to the outdoor Staff, and £lOO,OOO to•the Share- holders.

If the necessity for creating additional reserves causes the amount of, profit available for distribution to be reduced, it follows that the reduction should, and indeed must, be made in the proportions established in 1907, when we adopted the principle of profit-shar- sing, which since that date, has formed part of the Regulations of the Company. Therefore, as the amount of devisibla profit in the Industrial Branch is 000,000 less than in the previous year, £200,000 has to be with- held from the policy-holders, £50,000 from the outdoor staff, and £50,000 from the share- holders. This amount of £50,000 represents a reduction of is. in the Shareholders' Bonus, and is equivalent to a reduction of 5 per cent. per ..t1 share.

Since 1907, when this Bonus Scheme came into operation, the amount set aside for the Industrial Branch Policy-holders has been £2,260,000. The method of distribution adopted in previous years will be continued, and for policies of long duration the percent- age additions to the sum assured have either been maintained or reduced as little as possible in comparison with the rates/for the past year. I feel convinced, Ladies and Gentlemen, that the sacrifice you are called upon to make this year will not be in vain; for a purely Life Company such as ourselves, which values annually, which has already severely felt the strain of the war, to still maintain substantial bonuses, and to place itself in such a strong position to face the future, is one of the most conclusive proofs of financial stability it is possible to show,

I said last year that it was the policy of your Board to make adequate provision to meet any emergency. When I used these words,. I could not foresee that the emergency ,was so near or would be so severe, but the test having come we have met it unflinchingly. When better times come, and they will come, the sacrifices we are now making will be repaid in full measure.

div.head: SECURITIES AND INVESTMENTS.
div.p: SECURITIES AND INVESTMENTS.

With regard to our purchase of securities during the year 1914, the amount invested was rather less than. for some years past, owing to the fact that after the war commenced we re- frained from investing to any great exterit. Despite this,. we invested over .1:6,500,000, to yield on the average well over 5 per cent., while the end of the year was marked by our purchase of £BOO,OOO War Loan. As a result of holding our hands, we concluded the year with the very large cash balance of £1,250,000. While the maintenance of such large cash balances .of necessity ihvolves some loss to the Company, we feel: in • the- circumstances it was and is the wisest—and I may say most patriotic —course to adopt. The Government has ex- pressed in no uncertain voice -.its desire that the financial resources of the country should be preserved for the purpose of successfully conducting the war. • The Prudential has al- ready shown that it is prepared loyally to do its share by its large participation in the War Loan. When further loans for our own Gov- ernment or, for our Allies are required, we shall not be behindhand in our participation. You have doubtless noticed that there is a somewhat unusual feature in the balance sheet, viz., a reduction in the "Loans on Company's Policies." I should like to explain the reason for this. When the war broke out our funds were fully invested,. and any undue amount of loans 'might have necessitated a temporary overdraft at the very high rate of interest pre- vailing. We therefore increased the rate on our loans solely with the view of self-protec- tion. The danger has now .passed, and we pro- pose to reduce the, rate for new loans to the usual one of 5 per cent.

' I ,feel. sure that you will be pleased to hear that less than 2 per cent. of our funds are invested in the securities of enemy countries. It may also interest you to know that abOut 88 per cent. of the funds are in securities of the United Kingdom and her Colonies and the United 'States of America; the remaining 10 per cent. being in the securities of the rest of the world.
The distribution of the investments is also very varied, as you may judge when I tell you that we hold over 1,250 different Stock Ex- change securities. •
REMARKABLE RESULTS OF THE YEAR.

To- sum up the remarkable results of the past year, the income of the Company in the com- bined Branches has increased by the large sum of £628,000, and the assets of the Company by £4,209,311. The reserves in co-nsequence of the war have been increased by £1,200,000, but this has necessitated a reduction of £500,000 in the. amount of bonus divided amongst the policy- holders, the outdoor staff and the share- holders.
The shareholders will be pleased to hear that the Staff Provident Fund now amounts to 1160,000.

I am glad to be able to report a continued in- crease in the number of shareholders. During the last ,seven years the number has more than doubled, and at the present time we have 1,580 shareholders' accounts open, 166 being with the minimum holding of 25 shares. • On two previous occasions I have referred to our efforts to secure greater efficiency in our premium collections by *cumulating our busi- ness into areas of limited extent and placing
