div.head: THEY ALSO HELP WHO ONLY KNIT.
div.p: THEY ALSO HELP WHO ONLY KNIT.

Writing in a recent number of the Burton- wood .Parish Magazine, the Vicar •(the Rev. A. M. Mitchell) says: "To the women, so many of whom would dearly like to form a brigade or brigades of their own for service at the Front, knitting and needlework have provided oppor- tunity for sacrifice in all ranks, in the cottage, the villa, the mansion, and the palace. The revival of hand knitting is one or the few blessed results brought about by this terrible European conflict.. Our women have been on the knit day and night, at home and abroad, at meals and at meetings, in trains and 'buses. All, indeed: do not knit with the- same expedi- tion, nor do all put out work of equal quality. Some work slowly—but still they knit; some knit indifferently, but still they work. Some buy wool, providing their Own material, others knit wool, supplied to them for which they can- not afford to pay out of their own pockets!'

div.head: COMFORTS FOR SOLDIERS.
div.p: COMFORTS FOR SOLDIERS.
WOMEN LIBERALS.
" Ever Be Remembered," Say
National Reserve.
PILES OF LETTERS.
At the Crosfield Memorial Hall the Women Liberals' Sewing Class,continues work for the comfort of the soldiers with unabated enthu- siasm.

Captain Dunn recently wrote: "I have the pleasure to inform you that No. 2 Company of the National Reserve, 2/4 South Lancashire Regiment is now full strength, and awaiting marching orders. Any gifts it should be your intention to present to the men from your Association would be most gratefully accepted and appreciated." Immediately the class despatched a large consignment of shirts, hel- mets, socks and scarves to the captain, who now writes: "On behalf of the officers, non-commis- sioned officers and men. . . . I beg to thank you for your kind gifts. They are very accept- able, and all are exceedingly grateful. Your 4sociation will ever be remembered with feel 7, ings of gratitude."'

div.head: CHERBOURG HOSPITAL.
div.p: THE CHERBOURG HOSPITAL.

Meanwhile the Eva McLaren Hospital at Cherbourg—at which, as is well known, Miss Truda Crosfield is rendering such valuable ser- vices as nurse and interpreter—has not been forgotten. Two more valuable parcels of shirts, body-belts and bandages have just been for- warded—the second consignment. The follow- ing acknowledgment to Mrs. Osborne speaks for itself: • •

"The Warrington W.L.A. has been very kind to the hospital at Cherbourg, and I am sure Mrs. McLaren is very grateful to your members for all the useful garments they have supplied. Will you kindly convey her thanks for this latest gift? The boxes arrived safely this morn- ing.—Yours truly, A. L. DOUGLAS, assistant secretary, Liberal Women's Suffrage Union."

div.head: "TOMMY'S" PERSONAL THANKS.
div.p: "TOMMY'S" PERSONAL THANKS.

Then the class is also acting most generously towards the soldiers directly—Warrington sol- diers, of course; and letters of grateful thanks arrive in floods as regularly as the tide. "I have received . the .shirt and socks, and thank you very much," writes Pte. W. Ren- shaw, National Reserve Guard, from the South. "I May tell you we are having funny weather— rain, wind and frost. My part is guarding three bridges and points on top and underneath. It is very cold in the night, hut we're here ready for arything, and as men over forty years of age there are none better. "A little incident happened the other day. While. I was resting my four hours, a horse in a lurry came galloping Awn the lane. We. saw it coming, and said, ` it must be stopped" the corporal and I stopped its career—for the benefit of school children. So you see we are not particular what it is so long as we are doing gobd for our country. . • ." Pte. W. Rose, 4th Connaught Rang-?rs, vaites from Ireland: _ _

"I cannot fully, express . my thanks for ,the. shirt and socks I received on Monday. They come in very useful, as it is very cold and rainy here. I wish the women workeys of the Liberal Association every luck." "I hope you may long he spared to work for so good a cause, for King and country," is the wish of Pte. Thomas Critchley,% South. Lanea- shire National Reserve (in the South). Pte. J. Feeney, 10th Battalion King's Royal Rifles (in the South) is "sure it is very good of. the ladies to think so much about us. We need all the warm things we get, and I ninst. send you my best thanks."
"WISH THEIR TOWNSPEOPLE WOULD-"

The loyal. Inniskilling Fusiliers are in Ire- land, and Pte. Edward Coyne says his parcel will come in very handy. "For," he.continues "we are expecting to be drafted out at any time now. All the boys mire jealous'when they saw me open it, and said they wished' their townspeople would look after them the same." Lance-Corporal T. 'Coyne sends from the same place many thanks for rue "splendid gilt." which was a "welcome surprise." ' He closes with "best. wishes to the Women's Liberal Association." "WILL GIVE GERMANS 'SOCKS.'."
Pte. W. Hennessey, who is in Hampshire with the Loyal North Lancashires, declares that "the useful gifts were wanted badly after all our marching. I hope we will give the Germans socks!" he adds.
Sergeant R. Caslin, of the 4th South Lanca- shires, finds the shirts, muffler and socks "very twarm this cold weather," and joins in the general wish for the Association's success.

div.head: IN FRENCH HOSPITAL.
div.p: IN FRENCH HOSPITAL.

Mr. E. A. Sanders, the Liberal agent, hears from Pte. T. Sauce, of the Ist Cheshire Regi- ment. Pte. Sauce's home is at 3, Lythgoe's-lane, but he writes from Boulogne France, as fol- lows : "I am very thankful to the committee for being so good and kind to send me a parcel of clothing, but I regret to say that I have not received them as yet—l have been in hospital wounded these four weeks, and am getting on very nicely. . . . You can't believe how very grateful I am. "How good of you to think of us poor fellows in the cold wet trenches in Belgium. We had a heavy fall of snow, and I can't describe the sufferings we had to go through. I could tell you a great deal, but I am not allowed to. . . . I am resting, in a convalescent home in Boulogne, and when I am fit again I am going back to my mates in the tren :hes. . . . lam the only one in my regiment that comes from Warrington. I would let them know -what you have done for me. . . . May the old club prosper! Good-night." Later, Private Sauce, writing to acknowledge receipt of "a welcome parcel," says he is recovering from his wound in, the side very nicely.
A COMPARISON. I

From Mid-Wales, Pte. A. Spencer, of the Royal Army Medical Corps, sends his hearty thanks. "At present I am billeted out in a boarding-house," he says, "and those things which you kindly gave came in very handy. So what must the parcels be to the poor souls in the trenches?"

A wish similar to that of Private Critchley is expressed by Private A. Warburton, now in Surrey with the National 'Reserve.—Privates P. and H. Marsh, of the 6th South Lancashires, write gratefully from the same county, and hope all at home are in the best of health. Like many others, they ask that their kind regards may be given" to all inquiring Britishers." __ _ _

l'rivat; J. Barnett wrifes from North Wales to say how he "greatly admires" the parcel of clothing—" especially at a time like the pres- ent, while the weather is so cold and miser- able." He concludes: "I think all the men who have received parcels will appreciate the full value of the contents. . . . I again thank you one and all for your kindness towards me." "CUTTING-OUT" COMMITTEE.

The few extracts given from letters selected at random from a huge pile will serve to indi- cate the value of the work being done by the Warrington Women Liberals.s In conversation with Mrs. Osborne, the popular and valued secretary, "The Examiner" representative learned that a special tribute should be paid to the " Cutting-out " Committee—Mesdames Pem- berton, O'Brien and Hill—who, assisted by other members of the Association, had "cut out" thousands of garments with unflagging energy and enthusiasm.

div.head: TOOTH BRUSHES AND RED HANDKERCHIEFS.
div.p: TOOTH BRUSHES AND RED HANDKER- CHIEFS.

What Wounded " Tcmmies" Specially Want. Mrs. Edelsten reports: Many gifts of warm and useful garments have been received at the Town Hall during the last few weeks, including large parcels from the Training College, Friars' Green Church (per Mr. Hudson), the Stockton Heath Council School (per Miss Bainbridge), the Hamilton-street Infant School, Mrs. Alli- son, Mrs. Birtles; Mrs. Bracecamp, Mrs. Lang- dale, Miss Gorse, Miss Leigh, Miss Timewell, Miss Woods and many others. Large bundles have been despatched to the Military Hospital at Fazakerley, the First Base HoSpital of,' the British Expeditionary Force, and the Warrington Infirmary. There is an especial demand at this time, from the Fazakerley Hospital for new tooth- brushes, coloured pocket handkerchiefs (red for preference), glass cloths and kitchen towels.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.

Before Messrs. R. T. Fairclough (in the chair), A. J. Jolley, T. Pemberton and J. Upson. Lightly Clad.—James Carney, a discharged soldier, who was under remand from Wednes- day, on a charge of having been found drunk and incapable—he was on the footpath in Battersby-lane—was again placed in the dock. —The Chief Constable explained that the adjournment had been made in order to get the drink out of prisoner's system. He sug- gested that the balance of prisoner's Army pay be handed over to Mr. Laws (the police court missioner), to be paid to the man periodically. —Prisoner said he wanted to go to St. Helens to work.—The Chief Constable said that prisoner was the man who was found on the footpath at 1.30 in the morning, with only his shirt on. A doctor's fee of ss. had been in- curred.—Prisoner was fined 10s., and the course suggested by the Chief, with regard to the balance of his money, was adopted. Prisoner's Vain Boast.—Frank Roberts, of no settled abode, who told a constable it would take twenty " coppers " to lock him up, was placed in the dock on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly on Friday evening.—He was, it was stated, lying on the footpath, help- lessly drunk.—The Chief Constable said filo" man was there four weeks ago, and was then fined ss. He was a stranger to the town, and a sailor.—Prisoner, who said he worked at Cros- field's, was fined Bs. 6d., the alternative being seven days.
41P MONDAY. Before the Mayor (in the' chair), Aldermen Bolton and Smethurst, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. W. Furness, G. Pilling and S. Wright.

I Must be Guilty."—Margaret Jones, widow, of 32,. New-road, appeared for having been drunk in Bridge-street on Saturday night.— Asked to plead, she said: "I must be guilty or' I shouldn't be here."—A constable stated that at 9.40 he saw prisoner lying across the footpath, helplessly drunk. He had to get assistance to bring her to the Police Station.— The police had no record against her, and the case was dismissed on payment of costs. " What The Hangment Are You Doing?"— John Heaton, loafer, of no settled abode, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Market-place on Saturday night at 20 minutes to eleven. He admitted "having a drop of drink."—A constable said he was called to Heaton, who was using _bad language and creating a disturbance.—Heaton .said he was at a stall, buying some flowers for his sister's funeral, when an officer came and took him by the shoulder. He asked the officer: " What the hangment are you doing?" (Laughter.)— The Chief Constable said the man was beastly drunk. This was his 98th appearance, and he said that if the magistrates would give him a chance he would turn over a new leaf and "take up" the Army. For his own sake, how- ever, Strangeways at Manchester was the only Army he ought to join."—The Mayor (to Heaton): "The, magistrates are sorry they cannot give you more than a month."— Heaton: "So am I." (Laughter.) " Kaiser's Last Journey To —."—John Brown or James Hogan, labourer, of no settled abode, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street on Saturday.—He pleaded guilty to being drunk, but denied disorderliness.—lt was stated that when questioned he had not been able to give any account of himself. He was lying across the footpath.—The man said he had not been drunk for, five years. lie was upset at having heard that a companion was going back to the Front the next day.—The Chief Constable said prisoner had been standing on the way to the football field on Saturday, selling postcards about " The Kaiser's Last Journey to He could. not .say these postcards were indecent, but they were certainly unfit for anybody to read—especially children.— Prisoner, told he would be fined ten shillings and costs or fourteen days, appeared to be deaf and replied "Yes, sir; I'll go in the Bantams now." (Laughter.) Police As Bankers.—John Shea, fireman, of 72, Stitt-street, Liverpool, was summoned for having been drunk on Sunday, in Crown- street.—The Chief Constable remarked that owing to the police having taken care of it for him, Shea would have the sum of £2 4s. 334. handed to him that morning,—The man was fined ss. and costs (9s. 6d.) in all. As Good As Constable.—Andrew Moran, of no settled abode, pleaded not guilty to having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, at 2.30 on Sunday afternoon.—A constable described how Moran took off his coat, waved his arm about, and wanted to fight him, say- ing he was a better stable was.—The Chief said the man was a stranger, and the police had taken care of the sum of £5 2s. 4d., which they found in his possession.—Moran was fined ss. and costs (3s. 64.), or seven days.

Man Defends " A Terror."—Mary Jenkins or McPaul, of no settled abode, stated to be a' married woman, was charged with having been drunk in charge of her child—under the age of seven years—in Ship-yard, at a quarter past one in the morning.—A constable said he found the woman lying in an outbuilding, help- lessly drunk, with her child aged two years. He brought her out. She used filthy language, and refused to give her address. He took her to the Police Station, and conveyed the child back to a Ship-yard lodging-house--where the wcman afterwards said she was staying.—The Chief Constable said the woman admitted cen- victions at Bolton. It was certainly "a very bad state of affairs."—The prisoner called he r "husband," who begged the magistrates' pardon on his wife's behalf. It was not very often, he said, that she got a drop of drink— hut when she got it she was a terror; he him- self had to keep away from her. He !ie:ped they would give her a chance.—The Chief Un- stable remarked that the couple were not married—though he was not saying anythz.ng againbt that.—The case was adjourned fill Friday in order that-the woman's record :1" i?ht 1:1-! inquired into.

' charges, one of threatening his mother and the °awe of assault on P.S. Holland.—Prisoner, it was Ftated , had just come out of gaol, and, after hearing the evidence, he was committed for another month, besides being required to keep the peace towards his mother for six months.— Mary Harris said she was a widow, residing in Beswick-street. On Wednesday of last week her son used bad language to her because she told him to go and get lodgings. He threatened her and she went to the Police Station and took out a warrant.—P.S. Holland stated that he went to apprehend prisoner, and it was while on the way to the Police Station that he became vio- lent, made his escape once, and also assaulted the witness.—Prisoner said 'he was about to leave home and was to have been married in three weeks. He was in regular work.—The Chief Constable observed that all he could say was that prisoner was an absolute monster, and was never out of trouble. He had fifteen pre- vious.convictions against him.

Fell in a Ditch.-Jane Smith, a rag-sorter, re- siding at 9, Town Hill, was charged with hay- ing been drunk in Arpley-road on Monday.—A constable stated that he saw the prisoner com- ing in the direction of Arpley. She was wet through, and he thought she had fallen' in the river. She was drunk.—Jane said she had fallen in a ditch when crossing the fields.—She was fined Bs. 6d. or seven days. " Not Wisely, But Too Well."—George Pritchard, labourer, 60, Golborne-street, was charged with having been .drunk at Bridge Foot on Monday.—A constable said that he saw the prisoner drunk at 3.35 in the afternoon. He took him into custody and asked him some questions, because he thought he had seen him in military uniform about seven weeks ago.— The Chief Constable said that in 1912 the Bench let prisoner off when he was up on a similar charge.—He was fined Ss. 6d. or seven days.

"Owned U p."—Thomas Llewellyn, labourer, 63, Catherine-street, pleaded guilty to having been drunk and disorderly in Market-street at 8.45 on Monday night.—Prisoner had nothing to say, and having 14 previous convictions against him, was fined 10s. and 3s. 6d. costs, or 14 days.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.
Before Messrs. J. W. Hayward- (in the chair),
C. Jackson Holmes an W. I. Williams.

Worst Woman " Linguist " in Town.—Mary Fisher, of 10, Dolman's-lane, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Dolman's lane, on March 16th, and also with having assaulted P.C.'s John Willis and John McDonald, whilst in the execution of their duty.—lnvited to plead, she, said "I expect I am guilty."—P.C. Willis said the woman was behaving in a disorderly manner and was making use of filthy language. When he attempted to arrest her she threw herself on the ground and commenced kicking, catching him on the leg several times. He was surrounded by a crowd of people, who were trying to pull the prisoner away, and he had to send for assistance. P.C. McDonald camo in response to the call and prisoner kicked him several times. Inspector Foster then arrived on the scene and between the three of them they got the prisoner on to a handcart and, kicking, shouting and using most disgraceful language, she was conveyed to the Police Station.—P.C. McDonald having given cor- roborative _evidence, Superintendent William- son told the Court that that was the woman's forty-first appearance, the last time being on December 24th, when she was fined for using indecent language. "There is not the slightest doubt" added the Superintendent, " that she has been 'using the worst language of any -woman in town. She is not fit to be at liberty." —The Chairman, remarking that the woman seemed to be incorrigible, announced that she would be sentenced to three months' hard labour. • .

div.p: THURSDAY.
Before liessTs. J. Rymer Young (in the chair), A. J. Jolley, W. Roberts, W. T. Williams, and Dr. Naden. •

" Keeping St. Pairick's Day."—John" McDon- ald, a stranger, who was found drunk in Barbauld-street, and supporting himself by holding on to a window-sill at 12.30 in the morn- ing, said he had been keeping St. Patrick's was fined 3s. 6d. or seven days.

Cheaper to Have Got a Licence.—Patrick Lynn, of no fixed abode, was charged with hawking in Wilson Patten-street on Thursday, without having a licence.—The prisoner, said the Chief Constable, had three different names, Last time he called himself Smith.—He was fined 10s. and 3s. 6d., or 14 days in prison. div.head: Leather Trade Brisk.
div.p: Leather Trade Brisk.

"There was a much stronger tone about the local trade -last week," says the Warrington correspondent of "The Leather Trades Re- view." "Inquiry was on a generous scale, and .for suitable goods there was a reedy mar- ket both for prompt and deferred delivery. In particular the demand for all heavy goods was more pronounced and pressing than ever, and over and aboVe the supply already contracted for, there appear to be large requirements still uncovered. This toning up is probably to be traced to the new Government orders lately placed, and also to the better tone in the purely home trade. The inquiry from the latter has been much stronger of late than at any period since the outbreak of war."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 20, 1915. WAR STORIES: BY LETTER AND INTERVIEW.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 20, 1915. WAR STORIES: BY LETTER AND INTERVIEW.
GOING. TO THE TRENCHES DAILY.
West Lancashire Engineer Writes To
His Sister.

Pte. William Webster, who belongs to the Ist I West Lancashire Royal Engineers, and who is ' well known in London, has written a long letter to his sister, Miss E. Webster, who is at pres- ent resident in Winwick. He begins by express- ing his thanks for a parcel ,of good things for- warded him. "They are real luxuries at pres- ent" he says, "and Make a lovely change from bread and jam. I have just had the turkey and tongue for tea, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. The tinned cafe au lait is a very good pre- paration. It is very easy to make, and is just the thing for us chaps. . . . All our cornpany are still in the land of the living, and are looking well and fit. We are going up to the trenches each morning and returning again each evening, and we have had a little more experi- ence of shell fire. . . .

div.head: Died Like a Hero for King and Country.
div.p: Died Like a Hero for King and Country.

"No doubt you will have tieen from the St. Helens papers that there have been casualties amongst the volunteers from that town, amongst the names being that of A. Mather. I was talking to some of the St. Helens chaps the other day, after the company that Mather was in came out of the trenches, and was told about him being killed. . . . He has died like a hero for his Sing and country."

div.head: "LOST A FEW GOOD LADS."
div.p: "LOST A FEW GOOD LADS."
"Terriers'" First Night In The Trenches.

Mr. and Mrs. E. Marsden, of 21, Alder-lane,. Warrington, have received an interesting letter from their son, Drummer Elijah Marsden, who is serving at the Front with the Warrington Territorials, being in No. 3 platoon; A Com- pany. _ .

The letter was written on March 6th, and in it Drummer Marsden says that up to the time of writing he was in the best of health, and adds: "A lot of things have happened during the last few days that I shall never forget. We have been fighting the Germans, and we have lost a few good lads, but on the whole we must consider ourselves very lucky. . .. The first night we were going into the trenches the bullets were flying all round 'us and I expected to be popped off' any moment, but I got through all right. . .. The worst thing we had to put up with in the trenches is the snow and frost, and on one occasion when I was in them, it snowed all night. My feet were awfully cold; in fact they got that bad that I thought they were frost-bitten, but I am glad to say that they are all right. I have seen hundreds of dead Frenchmen and Germans, who have been lying about for months, because we can't get to them to bury them. On one occasion when we were in the trenches we were only

about 80 yards off the Germans, who took good care/that they did not give us a chance to have a shot at them. They are a proper feared lot,' and when we get them on the move the majority of them will not live to see Germany again I was having a drink of tea with an officer in the trenches the other day, and five minutes afterwards he was shot through the head and killed. .. . It is very hard to see one's chum shot down by one's side, but I am getting quite used to it now. . . I am very glad that I led a clean life at home, for one needs to have a strong body and, strong nerves to stand the life out here One night I and some others were lying in a 'dug- out' when the Germans sent over some shrap- nel shells. They dropped all round us, but none of us got hit." The plucky drummer concludes his letter with a request for "- a few cakes,"

div.head: "THE MEN ARE SPLENDID."
div.p: "THE MEN ARE SPLENDID."
‘Varrington Officer's Testimony From
The Field.

A Territorial officer,-writing home, says : Sent from the Trenches, "Mudland," Thurs- day, 11th March, 1915. One finds it harder to get the time to write. When not actually in the trenches there is a succession of duty and, work. that keeps one on the move. There are so many things to be done and provided for. I receive your parcels safely. The last one came as a gift from the gods when most needed. Yesterday was bitterly cold. Our pantry was bare. We had run down to biscuits and bully. We had no fuel for our braziers, so spent a pretty miserable day. I sent a note to our headquarters for a little chocolate and some cigarettes, and the reply came that they had none; but fortunately I had asked if any par- cels to hand they might be sent up, and you can imagine the pleasant surprise your variety parcel gave to us in the trenches and how we appreciated your forethought. We enjoyed them thoroughly, and such parcels cannot be repeated too often. Great Things Ahead.

The papers you are sending are most inter- esting to us all; the daily arrives two days after issue, Tuesday's I received on Thursday, and it is interesting to get our own local papers to read and to learn for the first time of some of our own doings.

Preparations ar-e afoot for great things when the ground it fit to move over. Of course, I cannot indicate what form they are taking. At the moment there is activity all around us. A battalion that should have relieved us has been moved up and the indications are that we shall follow up. The fighting is hellish up North. Tuesday night seems to have brought about some successful work in this locality. We could hear and feel that something important and unusual was astir, both Artillery and Infantry giving the Germans all they deserve. The fearlessness of the Indians is giving the Germans pause for thought and not a little anxiety. No doubt you have 'read in the papers what has happened. From all reports there is a concensus of opinion that we have the Germans absolutely strung up in this district; they fear and hate the man in khaki, who, no doubt, sooner or later, will make them rue the day when they held him in such contempt. Killed and Wounded in Dangerous Work. Last night we had another of those trying experiences, digging bang up against the firing line. We were unfortunate and lost three men killed and two wounded, and I had my own thrill and shock. I was instructing a corporal and was practically closing in our task and getting the trench squared up. He was stand- ing on one side of the trench and myself on the other. The bullets had been pretty lively about us, when, without visible sign, this poor chap was hit clean in and through the stomach; he dropped, but was quite conscious. With a couple of his comrades I helped to bandage him, and do what we could to make him easy, and to await the stretcher-bearers, who had been busy with the other cases. We got him back to hospital, but he died in the morning. A painful and abiding experience, but we all try to take these affairs as a matter of course, however tragic they may be. Here is much that is not ,pleasant to either the eye or mind.

To-night we are on duty for more fatigue work at the firing line. These duties are much worse than the occupation of the trenches. Once in the trenches you can guard agAinst certain risks. The other work is done in the open. You can form no idea of this night-work unless,you experience it; it is nerve- racking. The most simple things and noises take on eminomi shape and fancies, and little things happen that only end in alarm, though they might equally portend something serious, and the tension of watchfulness cannot be slackened, and the agony of concentration is exhausting.

div.head: Roast Chicken!
div.p: Roast Chicken!

By the way, I am very proud of a small field kitchen and oven, which my section have built for our company. Just fancy, when we re- turned in the early hours of this morning they had a chicken roasting in the oven, waiting for us! A sort of christening for the opening of the bakery! The kitchen is built from logs and brushwood, and thatched with willow twigs. The oven is made out of a little scrap sheet-iron, the chimney from biscuit tins, and the whole encased with the inevitable mud. I wish you could see it.

The men are splendid—the harder the task, the more cheerfully they try to do it. Things are much the same as in my previous letters—mucked to the eyes in mud—though the weather is a little warmer and the signs are for drier weather; then our next trouble will be dust. .

div.head: HALF A MILE UNDER FIRE.
div.p: HALF A MILE UNDER FIRE.
Territorials' Thrilling Walk.

Private J. W. Schule, who is serving with the Warrington Territorials at the Front, has written a short letter to his old friend and spiritual adviser, the Rev. H. Ogden, in the course of which he says, under date, March 6th: ," I am keeping in the best of health. We have just finished six days in the trenches, and are having a short rest. We are having fair weather, only it is very cold. I am sorry to say we have had one or two casualties, but thank God for carrying me through all right so far We had to walk about half a mile under rifle fire. It is awful to see the ruin that has been caused out here by the war. Recently we went through a place that looked as if it had once been a very fine village, but it is now all ruined. When we see these things it bucks us up and makes us want to get into the trenches so that we may try and make the Germans suffer for it."

div.head: " 4th SOUTH LANCS. DOING FINE."
div.p: " 4th SOUTH LANCS. DOING FINE."
A.S.C. Driver Tells of Place the Germans "Knocked About.'
Writing to his old friend and Bible Class leader, Mr. Rupert Jones, of 44, Baxter-street, Warrington, Driver R. Wilkes, a Warring-

tonian, whose parents live in Thewlis-street, and who is now serving with the 2nd Company of the A.S.C. (Supply Section), which is at- tached to the 3rd Division of the 7th Infantry Brigade of the Expeditionary Force, says: "I am still keeping well. We are doing very well out here, considering the weather. We have had all sorts of climatic conditions lately—rain, snow, sun and fog—but, unfortunately very little of the sun. lam now with the 4th South Lancs., and they are doing fine. They are going in the trenches again to-night (March 12th), and so they will be having a bit of a rough time for a few days. . . . The place where we are now had been occupied by the Germans, and they have knocked it about a bit. . . .

While I am writing I can hear the shells burst- ing and the big guns banging away. . . . I am a transport driver and I can assure you that we have some trouble sometimes, owing to the slushy state of the roads." Prior to enlisting, Driver Wilkes• was em- ploYed by the St. Helens Cable Co.mpany. and he is an old member of the Young Men's Bible Class in connection with the Working Men's Mission.

div.head: WARRINGTON "TERRIER'S 4' RECORD.
div.p: WARRINGTON "TERRIER'S 4' RECORD.
Something The Men Are Very
Proud Of.

By entering the trenches only fifteen days after leaving England, the Warrington Terri- torials have achieved a record among Terri- torial Battalions, and it is one of which they are justly proud. The fact i recorded in a letter written to friends in Warrington by Private James Ilinde who, prior to being accepted for active service with the 4th South Lancashires, was employed at Messrs. J. Cros- field and Sons' works.
His Baptism of Fire.

"I am still living" he writes on March 4th, 'rand in the best of health. I have just come out of the trenches for a few days' rest, after being in for §ix days; so I have received my real baptism of fire at last. It is not so bad in the trenches; it is the going in and out that does the mischief. We are up to the knees in mud and under heavy fire all the time. At

about dinner-time On Saturday last the Germans poured shell after shell at our trenches, some of them falling only a, few feet off, but, thank God, we had only one man wounded. The Germans are only a distance of forty yards away in places, so you can guess how risky it is to put your head up, for they are extra at shooting. You must only look over in one place once; you Amst change your position the next or they will have you. On our way to the trenches we passed villages that had been totally destroyed. On Tuesday a shell caught a row of houses that were tenanted and set fire to them, and the next thing I saw was the people being driven away to safety. It is a pity the Huns have nothing else to do!
Food Supply " Fine " Under the Circumstances.

"Please don't worry about us being put into the trenches so soon. We entered them exactly fifteen days after leaving Southampton. Such quick work has constituted a record for a Territorial Battalion, and it is a thing of which we are all very proud. The food we are getting is fine, under the conditions I think there will be a big change in the situa- tion soon. You would hardly think there was a war on if you were here at times, for night concerts are held and some of our men form 'a band,' using their mess tins, &c., for instru- ments, and go parading about as if they were on a picnic. This is the sort of spirit which will pull England through."

div.head: TRENCH AND SHELTER.
div.p: TRENCH AND SHELTER.
Officer Tells of Hair-breadth 'Seapes and Casualties.
A Warrington Territorial Officer writing under date March 7th, says:—

Just a hurried letter. it is Sunday morning and the rain, as usual, is soaking everything. We are babk in what is called ou-: rest camp. We came out of the trenches last Thursday night and turned in here about midnight, after the half battalion doing its duty for the six days. We emerged with light casualties, the total being two killed and five wounded. Officers came off free, though not without some narrow shaves. One officer - had a miraculously nar- row shave, a bullet actually going through his trousers and even touching hTs shirt and under- pants without even scarring him. The bullet passed right through his pocket book. Rather a near shave! We were supposed to come to the Rest Camp ( ?) for six days' rest, but on Friday night we were ordered again right up to the firing line to dig trenches. We turned out at dusk and returned at 5.3 e on Saturday morning.

div.head: Plenty of Fireworks:
div.p: Plenty of Fireworks:

It was a bad tramp out through a sea of mud and under fire, and once there plenty of fire-, -works. But we were comparatively safe, although digging within 500 yards of the enemy's lines. We were just under a crest line and the bullets whizzed harmlessly over our heads. We had, I think, four casualties during this expedition, one poor chap passing away the next morning. I had a few men back in a ruined farm. The Germans ranged on to this to a nicety, and they burst shrapnel jtist over the particular building these men were in; they had to clear out. One man brought in a shrapnel bullet which stuck in the mortar of the wall a few inches above his head, and he thinks he has been lucky. In moving about one sees how the country everywhere has been pounded by artillery, roads damaged by Jack Johnsons and houses and buildings in ruins, but it is curious to find isolated cottages untouched, and even in- habitate,d by Belgians within range of the firing lines.

div.head: Parcels Arrive Satisfactorily.
div.p: Parcels Arrive Satisfactorily.

_ Letters and parcels come through quite satis- factorily, and your rule of always enclosing , writing paper and envelopes is a good one, and might be observed With advantage by every- body writing to the Front. We are now billeted in huts, specially built; they are good !weather shelters, but very damp. The only way to' keep clothing aired is to wear it, and when you get wet they dry sooner when worn, It was like a holiday visit returning to shelter after the exposure in the trenches. The first night the hard bed boards felt more comfy I than the home luxuries of spring mattresses. You would scarcely have recognised me on my turn out from the trenches to have my first wash and shave for a week. We enjoyed a bath in the afternoon at the convent. The village which you appear to know is in German hands, and absolutely in front of our position, and is one of the places our artillery delight to range upon. During the six days I only. saw two Germans. I saw them through my sttsses.cookini brcattast one morning. By"-
the time you get this we shall be about to return to the trenches. ,
Recognise the Need for Care.

Our sister Battalion fared rather worse than we did. They lost a subaltern, curiously enough a Tunbridge Wells man. Perhaps you remem- ber me telling you of the incident of a man being saved by his whistle in his pocket, and my having seen the jacket he had been wearing. Well, that is the man; he was with me last Friday, and, poor chap, he was killed early last Saturday morning. He was a really good sort, and it grieves us when we hear of the loss of highly-trained men. Now please don't get anxious about me. We are all in the best of health and spirits, and recognise that we are all more likely to be useful if we exercise care and watch our movements. We all know too well that to be careful is one of our best safeguards.

div.head: SOUTH LANCASHIRES.
div.p: THE SOUTH LANCASHIRES.

The South Lancashire Regiment, as in moat of the campaigns that have made the Empire what it is, have been figuring often and prominently in the great war that now holds Europe in ,its grasp. The regiment has added to its laurels on many a hard-fought field from Mons to the present; it has necessarily suffered, for military glory only comes as

the result of effort and daring, and the South Lancashires have always been willing to pay the price. ,But in their experience we see the experience of the whole war condensed into a small compass, an experience which brings home to us the need for more men and still more men. The Army is calling as a whole for reinforcements that must fill up the gaps, if .we are to make good our victories, such as that of Nouve Chapelle. Warring- ton and district will most assuredly do its share in making good these victories; but we have a special interest in the South Lan- cashires, the pride that attaches to a thing that is our own. To no regiment did GENERAL FRENCH'S Order apply with greater force when, upon the beginning of the war, he stirred the blood of his men by asking them to remember the traditions of their individual regiments and the honours shown upon their colours. Local me,n will be specially proud to join their local regiment, to which entrance has been made easier in the matter of measurement. The regiment calls for recruits to maintain the honour of this part of the county. This part of the county must honour the call. The South Lancashires stand at the very top of the Infantry regiments that have made history; they will round off their grand record on the way to Berlin, a plentiful supply of recruits assisting.

div.head: NO. WORKS COMPETITION.
div.p: NO. WORKS COMPETITION.

A while back there was a division of opinion as to whether fqotball should be discontinued or not for the period of the war. It was felt that, on the whole, it would be better that the game should proceed, and there is reason to believe that its continuance has been for the general good. That the most ardent foot- ball authorities are practical patriots, ,when the real test comes, is proved by the decision made this week by the committee of the War- rington Football Club. The town club have for several seasons run a works competition for the purpose of fostering the game, and at the same time providing recruits for War- rington. The competition has been surpris- ingly successful in both respects. The games have been played at the end of the season, as the light nights come alon, and the struggles of the champions .of the works of the town have been witnessed by thousands of their shop mates, whoSe interest in the Rugby game has been maintained by the personal ele- ment thus imported. On the other hand, the works have developed- many players for War- rington—players who have reached the very top of the ladder the Rugby climber climbs. This year there is to be no works competition. Many of the works are engaged on war work, and others are acting for feeders of war work firms. In other cases works are short- handed through enlistments, and most of the men remaining are on overtime. The Foot- ball Committee, thinking it would be wrong to attract men away from their work in the evenings during the week time, have aban- doned the competition with all its advantages from so many points of view. That is a deci- sion that should, we think, be a complete answer to the t.,w who still believe that foot- ball should be banned altogether.

div.head: TO AN ANONYMOUS COWARD.
div.p: TO AN ANONYMOUS COWARD.

CCiward, who dare not thine own name to write, But hide behind a nom-de-plume to smite, And with the pen to wound a gentle heart, A fiend of blackest dye thou surely art. -oh, shameless brute, thy cruel words have

stung A sweet, pure soul, thou ruthlessly hast wrung; But, be assured, thy sin shall find thee out, A heavy debt thou'lt pay, without a doubt. 'Tis such as thee pollutes God's lovely earth, And SOWB the canker-seed at happy hearth; It pleaseth thee to crush the bloom most choice And at thy handiwork laugh and rejoice.
Coward, beware! The One who sees and hears Shall yet require of thee thy victim's tears; When secrets are revealed at Ills command, Before Thin, slanderer, condemned thoult M.B.

div.head: "THE GAME IS GOING NICELY."
div.p: "THE GAME IS GOING NICELY."

Lance-Corporal A. S. Page, who is with the Warrington Territorials, writes to a friend: "The game is going nicely here. We are frozen and soaked—so feel very `snice'! Everywhere is covered with snow, but you can trust the South Lancashires to stick it."

div.head: MELANCHOLY, BLT WAR.
div.p: MELANCHOLY, BLT WAR.
" Terriers " Behaved Under Shell and Rifle Fire Like True Britons.

The following is the continuation of an officer's letter we received • last week too late for publication, in view of the formalities through which it had to go : We have had six days' duty in the trenches, divided up into 24 hours in and 24 hours out (thus covering 12 days). Last night the other half of our Battalion went out with 200 men from 'A Company to dig a trench. There were three men wounded. This is melancholy writing and reading, but it is war. All behind the trenches we were in and round about them there still lie dead French soldiers. The sight is gruesome, but it is impossible to bury these brave men owing to the dangerous nature of the work.

The feeling here is most optimistic. Yester- day the Prince of Wales and Sir John French and staff were here. We have been under shell fire and also under rifle fire, and my men have behaved like true Britons. They face these risks with a joke and a smile, and their spirits are wonderful. The health of the men is excellent. I am, person- ally, very fit, and so are all my junior officers, and we are a very happy meis of six. We dine off bacon boxes covered with newspapers. Our food is excellent.
We are all getting parcels now from England, which add very materially to our comfort, and for which we are very grateful. Letters are particularly eagerly asked for and very wel- come.

div.head: SANGUINE "TERRIER." ' Looking Forward To Being Home In A Month or Two.
div.p: A SANGUINE "TERRIER." ' Looking Forward To Being Home In A Month or Two.

Private J. V. Podmore, whose father carries on a hairdressing business in Golborne-street, and who is serving with the Warrington Terri- torials, writes a brief letter to Mr. Rupert Jones, of 44, Baxter-street, in the course of which he says: "1 Sul Still keeping 'in the pink' and still doing fine. We are now (March 13th) resting from the trenches, but expect to go back into them in a day or so. . .We have had lovely weather the last few days, and As are resting about 51,- miles behind the firing-line and are billeted in huts. I don't think that anyone has cause to grumble at the way we are being looked after whilst we are resting.
Twenty Casualties Up To March 13th.

Of course, we have to rough it a bit when we are in the trenches, but when we are relieved we get a jolly good hot bath and a clean change of clothing, and, believe me, that makes a chap feel a new man altogether. We have Mid a few casualties—seven killed and about 13 wounded. May the poor chaps who have 'gone west' rest in peace! They have done their duty! Most of the bhoys ' are still keeping in good fettle and there is very little sickness amongst us." "I am looking forward to seeing you in a month or two from now !" concludes the writer.

div.head: TEA IN THE TRENCHES.
div.p: TEA IN THE TRENCHES.
" Tommy " Asks For Fragrant Leaf
In Tabloid Form.

Private J. Jones, D Company, Ist Gloucester Regiment, a Cheshire Lines employe under Mr. Geo. Walker, was at Mons, was wounded, came home, returned, and is now fighting near La Bassee again. Writing to Mr, S. H. Walker, he thanks that gentleman for a parcel of scarves, mittens and cigarettes, which he shared among his chums and himself.

div.head: Seventy-two Hours in the .Firing Line.
div.p: Seventy-two Hours in the .Firing Line.

"We are back again in the land o-f mud and water," he adds. "We do forty-eight hear, in the firing line, as a general rule, and forty- eight hours out, but we had to do seventy-two hours in it the last H&c; . . . During the last ten days we have had a rare mixture of weather—hail, rain, snow and thunderstorms. r6iis part of the country is largely under water, and we do our firing .from behind breastworks of sandbags. The Germans do the same. The sandbags are dry for the feet, but very cold, especially at nights. . . . The Germans made another attack on the right of our position the other day, but were driven back by the in- fantry and our machine gun fire. Their artil- lery sent us a few shells the other afternoon, just to show us that they were still alive! But they did no damage. We have been very, lucky this time, and have only had two men in our lot killed in ten days. . . . The Germans seem very keen on breaking through this part of the line, but they have not managed it yet; and I don't think they will do." "The Cup That Cheers."

Mr. Walker had kindly written, asking Private Jones if there was anything he would like sent out, and after expressing his thanks for the offer, the gallant " Tommy " writes:-- " I would be very thankful if you could send me a box of tea in tabloid form. There are about a hundred tabloids in a box, aud the weight is about two ounces. Of course, we get tea night and • morning, but there are a good many hours in between when a drink of tea would come as a God-send to a good many of us and it is very scarce out here."

div.head: COUNTY COURT JUDGE & COUNCILLOR
div.p: COUNTY COURT JUDGE & COUNCILLOR
PE M BERTON—continued.
17th, 1915? Have you ever made a single complaint about it in writing? Defendant said be never made a domplaint in writing. •
Mr. St(Tel rose to cross-eiamine defendant, but the Judge intimated that there was no necessity.

Florence Pemberton, sister of the. defendant, stated that the bookcase produced in Court Was not the one delivered to the plaintiffs to repair. Two of Weaver's men brought it back. She said to the man who brought it that it was not theirs, and the man said she must see Weaver's about it. The glass was not the same; 'nor the shelves. She could not get the quantity of books in as before. She went to town after the bookcase had been delivered and went through plaintiffs workshop. She went after the man had been with the web- bing to. put a bottom in the oak eettie. His Honour: Why did you keep the cushion? Witness: It was not mine. JUDGE'S SEVERE COMMENT.

His Honour: I do not belle-ve--; -single word of the evidence of Mr. Pemberton or his sister. —Continuing, the Judge said there was no serious complaint by either of them until they were pressed, three years afterwards, to pay, and then they came forward with this defence. It was a pity they did not consent to judgment. instead of going into the witness-box and deliberately perjuring themselves. Judgment would be for the plaintiffs for the ambinie claimed, with costs.

div.head: COUNTY COURT JUDGE
div.p: COUNTY COURT JUDGE
AND
COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON.
SEVERE REBUKE.
Story of a Repaired Bookcase.

At the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day, before His Honour Judge Gurner, Messrs. G. and J. Weaver, cabinetmakers, Bridge- street, brought an action against John Pem- berton, Stockton Heath, to recover an account of £lO 15s. id. for work done.—Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for plaintiffs and Mr. A. E. White defended.

, THE CASE FOR MESSRS. WEAVER. , Mr. Steel said that since the matter had • been entered into Court defendant had paid in ' .R 7 14s. 10d., leaving two items in dispute, viz., ' repairs to a bookcase and making a cushion for an oak settle. With regard to the bookcase he understood the defendant alleged that the bookcase he had sent for repair had not been returned, and counter-claimed £lO for it. The plaintiffs on December 29th, 1911, were en- trusted to repair a bookcase. This was done and returned to defendant on February 17th, 1912. His sister signed the receipt book and nothing was said. On the 31st of March, 1912, a bill was sent to the defendant, to which there was no reply. On the 4th May the plain- tiffs' manager, at the defendant's request, ' attended at defendant's house, where the de- fendant gave him an order for a cushion for an old oak settle. Although it was now alleged that the bookcase wilich was returned was not the plaintiffs', no complaint was then made. Plaintiffs heard nothing till Julie 7th, when defendant's sister called and said the cushion was not suitable, and casually remarked that the bookcase they had sent back was not the one defendaut sent to be repaired. Defendant himself never called at plaintiffs' shop. On June 9th plaintiffs wrote to the defendant ask- ing him to call with reference to the bookcase. As he did not call, Mr. Weaver, on the 16th , August, went to defendant's house and there saw him. Mr. Pemberton said the bookcase returned was not his, but Mr. Weaver insisted that it was, and invited him to call at the shop with a view to convincing him through the workmeti that the bookcase re- turned was the one received from de- fendant's house. Mr. Pemberton prom- ised to call on the following Monday, but, as a matter of fact, never called at all. A further letter was written to the defendant in September and another in October, but to neither of these letters was there a reply. Mr. Weaver's son had seen the defendant two or three times in the street and had reminded him that he .had not vaned as promised.,-.. On the last occasion he told Mr. Pemberton that unless the account was paid the matter would • be placed in the county Court, to which de- . fendant replied: "Yes, that is exactly what • I want you to do." He (Mr. Steel) would ' prove conclusively by the plaintiffs' workmen that -this bookcase was the one received from the defendant. The suggestion of the defendant was preposterous. The plaintiffs' firm had been established in Warrington for fifty-one years and this was the first dispute of its kind they had ever had. Defendant's counter-claim,, had I never been mentioned until after these pro- ' ceedings were taken.

div.head: EVIDENCE FOR THE PLAINTIFFS.
div.p: EVIDENCE FOR THE PLAINTIFFS.

William Henry ,Baker, the shop manager in the employ of plaintiffs, said he went to the defendant's house at Stockton Heath, where the defendant showed him a bookcase and in- structed him as to its repair. He sub- sequently instructed one of the workmen to bring the bookcase from the house to the work- shop. The repairs were completed and the bookcase returned February -17th, 1912. He , produced the delivery book signed by defend- ant's sister, who acted as his housekeeper. By Mr. White: The defendant had done busi-- nes,s with plaintiffs for several years. He was not aware of any previous complaint—Witness was cross-examined in detail with a view to showing that the bookcase produced by the defendant in Court was not the bookcase received by the plaintiffs; but the witness insisted that it was, and pointed out certain repairs to the bookcase that his firm had carried out in accordance with Mr. Pember- ton's instructions. He denied that defendant had ever complained to him regarding the alleged changing of the bookcase.

JUDGE WANTS DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE. His Honour asked Mr. White if he had any documentary evidence in support of defendant's case. Mr. White said he had not. His Honour said that in view of the evidence outlined by Mr. Steel, Mr. .White would appreciate the difficulties in his way of making out a case for the defendant, and asked whether it was worth while continuing the defence.

Benjamin Deeley, cabinetmaker, spoke to going to defendant's house for the bookcase. It was always in the workshop until the necessary repairs had been completed, and it was then delivered to defendant. By Mr. White: The man who delivered the bookcase to Mr. Pemberton was now, he under- stood, at the Front.

Joseph James, works foreman, said he had been in the employ of the plaintiffs for 27 years. He was the one who received the book- case on its arrival at the works and fixed a new pane of glass in it. He identified the bookcase in Court as the one received from the defendant's house.

George Weaver statad that he was a member of the firm. They had been in business 51 years in Warrington. It would be about the end of May, 1912, when Miss Pemberton came and complained that the cushion was not long enough for the settle. He told her it, had been made in accordance with the order given. She mentioned in a casual way that the bookcase returned was not the one her brother had sent. "If you say that" replied the witness. "you cannot see." He wrote as stated by Mr. Steel, but defendant did not call to see him. On August 16th he went to defendant's housa and defendant said it was not his bookcase which they had sent back.

He (Mr. Weaver) invited Mr. Pemberton to call at the shop and see the workmAn, who would prove to him that it was the right book- case, and he promised to do so on the following Monday. He, however, failed to do so and, so far as he (witness) kne'w, he had never called. Thomas B. Weaver, book-keeper, said he had seen the defendant twice. Mr. Pemberton had passed their shop many times. Witness hat sent several accounts without response.

div.head: DEFENCE.
div.p: THE DEFENCE.

Mr. White, for the defence, said he had no documentary evidence. When the bookcase was delivered at defendant's house the atten- tion was called to the man who delivered it, that it was not the same bookcase. He did not attempt to say that Messrs. Weaver had know' ingly sent the wrong bookcase. It was a pity* the man who delivered the bookcase was not present, as Miss Pemberton alleged that she told him it was not the right bookcase.

NO DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE. His Honour here intimated that he wanted to have some documentary evidence. Mr. White said he had none. He proposed to put the defendant and his sister into the wit- ness-box. His Honour: Defendant may go into the box, but I should not believe him.
COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON GIVES EVIDENCE.

Defendant then gave evidence. He said the bookcase he sent to repair had' ground-glass 1.11 the doors. There was no ground-glass in this bookcase. He had seen Mr. Baker several times in the street and had told him the book- case was not the one he sent for repair. Ff. e was an expel;t in glass and he had sat opposzte the one he 'sent and had seen it for years, When he saw the bookcase at the time it vias returned he said it was not the one he sent.
His Honour-: Answer me this question: Yo 4 had this repair from February, 1912, to Marcia'
(ConMitred in preceding column.)

div.head: Emmanuel Fellows' Study Cirele.
div.p: Emmanuel Fellows' Study Cirele.

On Sunday Miss N. Gandy spoke to the mem- bers of the above on the subject of " David— 'ithe Refugee," and remarked that David, flee- ing from the persecution of Saul. and in fear of his life, and left to the mercy of the world, 1. rusted implicitly in God and bound himself in true friendship with Saul's son, Jonathan. Living in caves and anywhere, sometimes with- 'nut shelter, David all this time was guarded by his heavenly Father and was brought -through the terrible ordeal unharmed, ' and h o w ed Saul, his persecutor, how little he -really was in the world. Miss Gandy said that 'even nowadays there were hundreds of Davids, and if they were to be, persecuted and driven :from their only safeholds they should endure it, and at last overcome it. Therefore in the Present times, and even if it should come to .their being persecuted and .east from all their loved ones, the trusting iinplicity in God would have a great deal to do with their losses being restored, for it was when they we're in trouble "that God - showed His strength. Concluding. 'Miss Gandy urged her hearers always to re- 'lnesmber the motto "God is our refuge."

div.head: Russian Church.
div.p: The Russian Church.

This was the. subject of a lantern lecture given on Monday -evening in the Patten Hall, under , the auspices of the English Church irnion. There was a large attendance, and the Rev. W. Stanton, who presided, observed, in introducing the Lecturer, the Rev. E. Davis (Vicar of St. Mark's, Low Moor. near Brad- :ford) that this country had had , many dis- agreements with Russia in the past, which Oisagreements arose chiefly through ignorance of each other. But now the English people 'were beginning to see the wrong they had done Russia consequent upon their not understand- ing each other. England and Russia must jearn to know each other better, and it Was inipossible for them to understand each other iinless they understood the Russian Church.— itttroducing the subject of his lecture, the Rel' E. Davis said that now there was en Alliance between England and Russia, and that the latter country, like ourselves, bad -taken up arms to fight for right against might. Russia, he said, was composed of large to.vns and small villages, but there were no large industrial towns as in England. They found that in religious matters Russia was nearer to them in the perception of Church doctrine than was the Church of Rome.—The pictures shown included views of Moscow—with its 700 churches—and of St.. div.head: Self-denial Record.
div.p: Self-denial Record.

Mr. Joseph Beaumont, 25, Froghall-lane, the local adjutant of the Salvation Army, writes to say that the Warrington Corps raised .2135 during the recent annual self-denial effort, which was an increase upon last year's amount of .05. He wishes us to express his warmest thanks to all who have contributed to this record total—which we have great pleasure in doing, knowing the work the Army does in so many directions—and concludes by thanking us "for the splendid help given by the fine paragraph in your paper, which I am sure did us a lot of good."

Fatal Forge-Yard Accident. John Tynan, 60 years of age, a forge labourer, who resided at 39, Napier-street, met with a fatal accident on Wednesday morning at the Dallam Forge. It appears that he was crossing the yard, at 7.30, when he was knocked down by a "bogey," which was loaded with pig- iron. He was found to be badly crushed, whilst his right arm was also dislocated. He was conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary, where death took place about an hour after- wards. The matter was reported to the Coroner, who will hold an inquiry this after- noon.
