div.head: Wearin' o' the Green."
div.p: Wearin' o' the Green."

Wednesday was St. Patrick's Day, and aq line walked the streets one noticed sprigs of the "dear little shamrock" in many a buttonhole. The annual St. Patrick's Day dance in con- nection with the "John 3laginn " branch of the United Irish League took place at night This year the promoters were unable to secure the Parr Hall, and had to be content with the Gymnasium, and a limited number of patrons. There were, however, upwards of two hundred present to take part in the 22 dances, to the accompaniment of Irish music- provided by Master T. Blake's band. Messrs. P. Marron, B. J. Kelly and A. Sankey were the M.C.'s, and Mr. D. Mahoney ably carried out the secre- tarial arrangements.

Latchford -Wesleyan Band of Hope. On Monday evening, a concert was given in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, Latchford, by the children of the Young Abstainers' League, or Band of Hope. Mr. F. Blease occupied the chair, and the following were the soloists : Eliza Eccleston, Florrie Bate, Kathleen Raw- lins, Edna Willett, Rita Brookes, Connie Ditch- field and Nellie Statham. Recitations were given by Elsie Houghton, Morrie Dakin, Eva Statham and Mona Lorney.. An amusing item was a recitation in Lancashire dialect, by Mary Lythgoe. The programme concluded with the singing, by a large number of the mem- bers, of the French, Belgian, Russian and British National Anthems. Flags of the Allies were carried by each singer, and as they marched off the platform the pianist struck up "It's a long way to Tipperary," in the singing of which the children and i adults present joined. _ _ _

div.head: Lancashire and. Yorkshire Bank.
div.p: Lancashire and. Yorkshire Bank.

The Lancashire and Yorkshire Bank, whose annual meeting was recently reported in "The Examiner" and showed how the difficulties of the most anxious financial year in living memory had been triumPhantly. met, was one of the first of the great banks to institute a savings bank department. The rules of this department—a direct incentive to thrift—are advertised in this issne. The bank, which has a strong Board; representative of the two counties, has a subscribed capital of £1,725,000; paid-up capital, £862,000; reserve fund, £660,000; callable capital, £862,000; and a sur- plus security to the public of £2,385,000. There are Lancashire and Yorkshire offices in most business centres, including Warrington (34, Horsemarketestreet, manager Mr. F. W. Gilbert), Lymm (Dam Side, manager Mr. Gil- bert), and Widnes (72, Victoria-road, manager Mr. W. Arnell).

div.head: Overcrowding of Schools Entails Loss
div.p: Overcrowding of Schools Entails Loss
of Grant.

It was reported to the Education Committee on Monday night that a letter had been re- ceived from the Board of Education, drawing attention to the excess of the average attend- ance over the recognised accommodation at the Parochial, Hamilton-street, St. James', St. Barnabas', Ladies' School of Industry, St. Mary's, and Silver-street Schools. It was noted that, although the Board do not, in the present circumstances, desire to inflict serious monetary loss on the authority by making considerable deductions from the grant, the infringements of the code had been so many and SO serious that they were not prepared to pay the grant in full in all the cases now under considera- tion; that the Board noted that the proposed schools at Oakwood-avenue and. Parr-street were well advanced, and that, therefore, they had decided to limit the deduction to made to the nominal sum of .220 in all, viz.: £lO in the case of the St. Barnabas' School, and .1:10 in the case of the Silver-street School.

div.head: Bro. Steel, V.M.
div.p: Bro. Steel, V.M.

There was an exceptionally large attendance at the installation, on Tuesday, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, of Bro. Thomas S. Steel, the well-known local solicitor, as Worshipful Master of the "St. Elphin's" Lodge (No. 3,287) of Freemasons. The other four Warrington. Lodges were represented and there were visi- tors from other parts of the country, includ- ing a number of Provincial officers. The cere- mony was performed by the retiring W.M. (W. Bro. J. H. Heywood), who was assisted by W. Bros. Thomas Hill, P.P.G.D.C., and W. H. Owen. The newly-installed W.M. invested his officers as follows :—Bro. J. T. Barton, S.W.; Bro. J. Finlayson, J.W.; W. Bro. W. Hodgkin.' son, treasurer; W. Bro. James Waldron, secre- tary; Bro. Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, chap- lain; Bro. I. Broady, S.D.; Bro. F. Garside, J.D.; Bro. G. NewbOrn, 1.G.; Bros. W. Barton, W. Chalmers, Lieutenant James Wilcock, P. L. Broady and P. 0. Bailey, stewards; and Bro. F. J. Dell, tyler. In consequence of the war, the usual banquet had been abandoned, but light refreshments were served to the brethren after the ceremony, and the usual Royal and Masonic toasts were proposed and honoured; whilst W. Bro. Steel. on 'behalf of the Lodge,
premiuted the retirizi with a beaatil74: 0141 r.x...2 jewel.

The Warrington Territorials have furnished some more names to the Nation's Roll' of Honour this week. Last week we published a list of four killed and four wounded, and the names given below have to be added this week. These names become known in haphazard manner and the list may be incomplete. Our second list stands as follows:
KILLED. Private George Higham. Private W. Stanley Rowlinson. Private Ernest Warburton.
WOUNDED. Sergeant Ford. Private John Whitfield. Private Patrick Sheehan. Private W. Milson. Private Wm. Rowland.

div.head: CORPORAL GEO.. HIGHAM.
div.p: CORPORAL GEO.. HIGHAM.
Brave Orford " Terrier's "
Dying Words.
DID HIS "SHARE.?'

Corporal George Higham, of Laburnum Villa, Orford, has been the first of the Territorials from the village of Orford to lay down his life in the cause of his country. A better known young man—he was only 29 years of age—was not to be found in the village, and his home on

bringing the asad news that George had pa9seil away. Great as must be your grief at losing a son, you must feel he has -gone doing his duty nobly, and that, although a great loss. to you personally, he has fallen helping his country to the goal of freedom. Some must go, and he has gone as a hero and patriot—For, and on behalf, of William Mortimer and Co., your truly, H. PERCY DENSHASV:"
CORPORAL GEORGE HIGTIAM, Died of wounds received in action.

Monday was literally besieged with inquiring friends and sympathisers. At the Tannery, where the late Corporal had been employed as a flesher, the feeling amongst his fellow workmen was intense, and many of them were moved to tears; indeed the receipt of the news cast quite a gloom over the whole ot the Works.
The gallant Corporal's father, who bears the same name, is one of the oldest employes at the Orford Tannery, having worked there for no fewer than 44 years.

div.head: SERVED IN THE OLD VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: SERVED IN THE OLD VOLUNTEERS.
Mr. and Mrs. George Higham, the parents, have a large family, and there still remains on active service three soldier sons.

Corporal George Higham was a single man, and had had eleven years' military experience, serving in the old Volunteers. In August last, when the war broke out, he, without any hesita- tion, joined the Territorials, and was in due course drafted off to active service. Actual fighting was no new experience to him, for he had previously been "in the thick of it," hav- ing served through the Boer War. When at home the deceased Corporal was a regular attender at the Bible Class held in the village school, at which place, by the way, he obtained his education in his boyhood days. He was an Oddfellow, being a member of the " Royal " Lodge, which meets at an inn on Orford Green. He was also a member of the WArrington Junior Conservative Club. He ardent footballer, he was captain of the Orford Tannery team some two or three years.

div.head: BREAKING THE NEWS. Pathetic Letter From Dead Corporal's
div.p: BREAKING THE NEWS. Pathetic Letter From Dead Corporal's
Brother.
It fell to the lot of his younger brother, Pte. William Iligham, who was in the same trench, to break the news of the Corporal's death to his parents.

div.head: "YOUR GEORGE HAS BEEN HIT"
div.p: "YOUR GEORGE HAS BEEN HIT"

"Dear father and mother," he writes under date March 11th, " I am writing a few lines to you. I hardly know which way to begin, bat I hope God will help you to bear the news I have to tell you. He has helped me to bear it. On the night of the 10th of March we were sent to dig trenches just behind the firing line. The company was scattered about 300 yards. About eleven o'clock word came down to the trench, Pass the word to Bill Higham at once!' I went about 200 yards down the trench and some- one said Your George has been hit.' I 'found him down on the floor. A bullet had passed through his right hand and then. through the lower part of his stomach. He held out his hand and said :

Is that you, Bill? They have got me. You know what to do if anything happens.' I said, You are all right, lad ! We will get you to the hospital as soon as we can!' They bound him up to stop the bleeding till the stretcher came. I stopped with him all the time. We took him to the dressing station, and the doctor dressed his wounds and gave him morphia. We then took him to the' hospital, and J left him fast asleep at 5.30 o'clock this morning, and he never regained consciousness.

div.head: "I AM READY TO DIE."
div.p: "I AM READY TO DIE."

"We have just given him a full Christian burial with field honours; we laid him to rest in the beautiful little churchyard near here at 11.45 this morning. There he rests. among a good many more heroes, who have lost their lives for their King and country. Whilst I stayed with him he said, 'Bill, I am ready to die! Death does not fear me. Remeraber me to them all, and also to Mr. Owen (the vicar). I wish the Lord would take me out of my pain ! We have come out here to do our share, and my turn to go has come first !! "Well, I have given you a full account of how the brave lad died, and trust that God will help you to bear it, as I am bearing it, and above all as George bore it. He told me not to upset myself, as someone must go. DYING THOUGHTS OF THOSE AT HOME. " Tell them at home not to upset them- selves!' he also said. I daresay you will get notified by the War Office, and Major Cary will send his belongings, except his clothing, home to you. He had made his will in his pay book, but that is claimed at present by the Government: ,In another letter I will send you a copy of it, as far as I can remember it. I am writing to Mr. Owen as well. He might help you to stand the painful news. The battalion has lost a good soldier, you have lost a loving son, and I have lost a loving brother. May God bless you and help you to bear the news.—l remain, your lov- ing son, Btu."

div.head: EMPLOYERS' SYMPATHY. Died "As a Hero and a Patriot."
div.p: EMPLOYERS' SYMPATHY. Died "As a Hero and a Patriot."

The following letter was received by the be- reaved parents on Monday night from Messrs. Wm. Mortimer and Co, of Orford Tannery:— "My dear Geo. Higham,—We are obliged to yen for lending us the letter from your son MI.

div.head: "ONE OF THE VERY BEST LADS."
div.p: "ONE OF THE VERY BEST LADS."
Vicar's Tribute To Fallen Corporal.

At the close of the ordinary service in the Orford Church on Sunday evening, at which there was a large congregation, a short inter- cessory service was held, during the course of which the Vicar (the Rev. G. Vale Owen) read out the names of Orford men at the Front, or who are training in preparation for bearing their pdrt in the fighting line, and specially commended the men named to the congregation for remembrance in their prayers. He also made touching reference to the death of "one of Orford's soldier lads "—Corporal Higham— who, he said, had been promoted; had been called within the veil. He had gone out, as he himself had said, to do his duty "for Empire and for the cause of civilisation," and he had been called to continue his work in a better land. He was one of the very best lads—a member of the Bible Class—and he asked the congregation still to consider him a 4 one of the Orford family for whom their prayer.; were being continued- He asked them also to think of those who were left behind, and to remember that George Higham had gone forth into an- other life "as a conqueror in triumph " "He had a large circle of friends," coneluded the Vicar, "and all who knew him loved him." Mr. John Gibson sang the solo "0 rest in the Lord," and the congregation joined in the hymn "Jesus lives!" The Vicar has received a letter from Pte. Wm. Higham similar to that which he sent to his parents. On -Monday morning there came by parcel post to the home of Mr. and Mrs. Higham sad mementos of the fallen hero in the shape of his belongings, which included a scarf sent to him by his sister at Christmas, as well as several letters which he had received from his par- ents and relatives, his memorandum book, Prayer-book jack-knife, purse, -musketry rule- book, Testament, &c. '

div.head: PTE. STANLEY ROWLINSON A Fatal Bullet Through The Lung.
div.p: PTE. STANLEY ROWLINSON A Fatal Bullet Through The Lung.

Another name that has to be added to the roll of the gallant Territorials who have laid down their lives for their.country is that of Private Willmot Stanley. Rowlinson, who is in the A Company. Prior to offering himself for active service he resided with his parents at 4, Holland-street, off Lovely-lane. He was 17 years of age, and had been connected with the Territorials about two years By occupation he was a cutter-down at the Monlas, Hall and Co.'s Works, and he was the only son of the family. As a boy he attended the Holy Trinity School It is only six weeks ago since he left the country to go into the firing line. Writing home a day or two previous to receiviii4 his fatal wound he informed his parents that he was "alive and kicking;" and hoped thak they Were all right. The Terriers, he said, hail been very busy the previous two nights, and hail to go into the firing line that night for a few days.

div.head: MAJOR EXPRESSES BATTALION'S SYMPATHY.
div.p: MAJOR EXPRESSES BATTALION'S SYMPATHY.
The news of his death was conveyed in the

div.head: PRIVATE STANLEY ROWLINSON, Died of wounds received in action.
div.p: PRIVATE STANLEY ROWLINSON, Died of wounds received in action.
following letter from Major Cary, party, 4th South Lancashires:- 4th South Lancashire Regiment, March Mtn, 19,5. Dear Mrs Rowlinson,—
IA" Corn-

I regret to have to inform you of the death of your son. Private W. S. R,owlinson, who died of wounds yesterday afternoon. He was shot in the shoulder and the bullet passed ihraugh his lung and lodged in the lower part of the spine. His case was from the first hopeless. He lingered- for several hours, and I am told by the clergyman at the hospital that his end was without pain.

Will you, on behalf of the officers, W.O.'s and N.C.O.'s and men of his company accept our sincere sympathy in your sad loss? Private Rowlinson was buried this afternoon in the churchyard close to where the battalion is billeted.
SPOKE OF HIS MOTHER AS HIS WOUNDS WERE DRESSED.

News of the gallant private's death has also reached Warrington through a communication, to a friend, from Lieutenant-Surgeon Charles D. Law, of the R.A.M.C., who wrote:— "Last night the battalion were out and Stanley Itowlinson was wounded in the shoulder. If you should see his mother try and comfort her." In a postscript the doctor adds: "Since the foregoing was written, Stan- ley has died. Please contrey my sympathy to his parents. I tended him immediately after he was shot. lie spoke of his mother to me as I was dressing his wound. Ile did not have any, pain."

div.head: PTE. ERNEST WARBURTON.
div.p: PTE. ERNEST WARBURTON.
" Life and Soul of Section " Shot Entering Trenches.

One of the latest Warrington Territorials to lay down his life at the Front was the popu- lar Private Ernest Warburton, aged 18, the youngest son of Mr. and Mrs. J. Mather, of 369, Winwick-road. Two days ago this heroic soldier's father' received the following sad letter : " Dear Sir,—l am sorry to inform you that your son, Private Ernest Warburton, was killed in action on the night of the 10th. We all deplore his loss, as he was so bright and cheerful, and the life and soul of hip section. He was buried the same night in a little churchyard, and a cross has been erected over the grave. I enclose some papers and other articles found in his possession.—Yours truly, H. GORDON ROBERTS, Officer Commanding 'IV Company, 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment." The "papers and other articles" included a laJzzt coat:la:Ls a photograph of the rrivate's

tary Hospital. They say that the patients are well looked after, get excellent food, and last, but not least, have the services of a good doctor. The wounded son told his parents that the bullet which wounded him cut his clothing clean open and entered his left thigh. "The bullets were whizzing past us something terrible,' " he added, "all the time my comrades were carrying me away on the stretcher. I had the presence of mind to put my hand on the wound and thus partly stopped the loss of blood.' The enemy were firing on the ambu- lance men all the time."

fiancee, the service Testament and a match-box. From Private William Newnes, of Forshaw- street—who is it companion of Private A. Mather, brother of the dead private, and in the same battalion, word was received on Thursday, which said he saw Private Warbur- ton shot in the spine of his back as he was going into the trenches. He died a few min- utes later, and was buried in the churchyard the same night. Private Mather himself has been in hospital since the sad day._ . _
Private Warburton enlisted as it Territorial at the Drill Hall two years ago, and had not seen active service previous to this year. He was unmarried, and worked as a plateman at
Killed in action
Messrs. Pearson and Knowles—in whose em- ploy. lbe had been for four years. His father is a 'file-cutter at Messrs. Thewlis and Grif- fiths..

As a boy he attended Orford Village School, and later became a member of the Ragged School Band—in which he remained until en- listing. Besides his parents,, Private' Warbur- ton leaves twO brothers and a sister to mourn their loss.. These two 'brothers, also soldiers, are at present training in the South.
PRIVATE ERNEST WARBURTON,

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
WOUNDED-BUT BACK AGAIN.
Private Rowland's Hurt Is, Happily, But A Slight One. •

Another of our gallant "Terriers" who sus- tained a wOimd in the service of his country was Private William Rowland, but happily his hurt was of so slight a nature that he is now back in the trenches again. Private William Rowland is a married man with four 'little children, and his home is at School-brow. He was wounded three weeks ago to-morrow,, being shot in the left shoulder. Although extremely painful at the time, the wound, happily', proved to be not at all dan- gerous and soon healed up sufficiently to warrant the surgeon in certifying Private Row- land fit for further service.

TWO BROTHERS WITH THE COLOURS. Prior to vollinteering for active service, Private Rowlands served four years with the Territorials; iirdeed, he was a time-eipired "Terrier," butt when the call-to-arms came he re-offered his services, andy they were accepted At the time he was engaged as a painter and slater in the employ of Messrs. Crosfield and Sons. He has two brothers with the colours— one older and one younger. The elder, Daniel, is attached to. the Royal Field Artillery and is a married man, with three children. The younger, Albert;-, is serving with the Warring- ton Territorial.. He is also married and has two children.

div.head: PRIVATE JOHN WHITFIELD. Shot in the Thigh Whilst Doing Ambulance Work.
div.p: PRIVATE JOHN WHITFIELD. Shot in the Thigh Whilst Doing Ambulance Work.

Private John Whitfield, whose parents, Mr. and Mrs. Robaet, Whitfield, reside at 110, Ches- ter-road, is among those who were wounded Last weak, and he now rests in Lincoln Hospital. He is only 11l years of, age, and by trade he is a bricklayer. He joined the Warrington Ter- ritorials upwards of a year ago. Being a musician, he became a member of the band of .the battalion, but, at the Front, he was acting as one of the stretcher-bearers.
It was while doing duty in this capacity on Thursday morning of last week that he stum- bled over the. body of a dead Frenchman and fell to the ground.

div.head: SHOT FROM A SNIPER.
div.p: A SHOT FROM A SNIPER.

"Almost immediately," he said, in recount- ing his experiences to his father and mother, who have, paid him a visit in hospital, "there was a flash of light and bullets came whizzing past me, and I received three wounds in the left thigh. A sniper must have got me." A letter was received from him by his par- ents on Monday morning, in which he also ex- Plained how he met with the injuries. "He supposed," he wrote, "that his parents would be surprised to hear that he had been wounded in his left thigh on the 11th inst.," but added that he was getting along fine. "Don't worry yourself about me," he went on, and finished by saying that he was hoping to gei home soon, if he could. He received a letter at dinner time and at night went into the trenches.
BULLETS WHIZZING PAST "SOMETHING TERRIBLE."
Mrs. Whitfield travelled to Lincoln- on Mon- and her husband followed on Tuesday. They speak in the utmost praise of the Mill-

know how to do enough for the wounded Tommies. At Crewe they, were snowed under with tea and cakes, fruit and chocolates, and "fags." At Chester, where also admirers gave they anything they asked for, the Boy scouts lined up and saluted as the train passed out of the station. To the writer's surprise and de- light the railway bridge at Bank Quay was crowded with people, some carrying big Uninat Jacks.
PRIVATE JOHN V7HITPIELD, Wounded in the thigh.

div.head: "HOTTEST TIME OF HIS LIFE!"
div.p: "HOTTEST TIME OF HIS LIFE!"
Warrington " Terrier " Tells of a Fierce Charge.

'.Another of the Warrington Territorials who have had the misfortune to be wounded is Private P. Sheehan, who was serving with the G" Company. He at present lies in the Springburn Hospital, Glasgo*. ,His home is in Great Britain-street, Cork, and. when in Warrington he lodged at 262, Liverpool-road, Sankey Bridges, and was, employed as a gas engine driver at the Sankey Wire Mills. He is 22 years of age, and is unmarried; and two of his brothers are also serving in the Army.
"'JABBING' AWAY FOR' DEAR LIFE!"

Writing to an old Warrington workthate. Mr. Harry Rankin, with whom he residbil, Prite Sheehan says that he went into the trenches with the Lincolns on Wcdnesday of lastsweek. "It rained something awful," he.w.rites,-"ami by 12 o'clock on Thursday morning we were waist-deep in, water and mud. . . . When the fighting came on I had the hottest time I ever had. We had so much firing to do that on the Thursday night our rifles got ret hot- On Friday morning we were reinforced by the Warwickshires and . . . . the order was passed down the line: "Prepare to charge!" cOuld not describe that charge to you if I tried, but you may gather some idea of what it is like if you can imagine a rush by sFven hundred madmen—for one is quite mad when in it—rushing at a number of other madmen and jabbing away for dear life with theiy bayonets.

HIT WITH THE BUTT END OF A 11Irt.E. ! "I escaped very well, for the fellow who jabbed me did it with the wrong end of the rifle, but he managed to break two of my ribs, lad mat is why lam in hospital.. . . But we took the 'trench, and it was nearly full of Ger,nan coad. . . . . All Friday I was lying down oa a hef.p of German bodies, fot I could not stir for pani, and on Friday night we went to the base. . . We had to leave some of the woundad on the field, for as the R.A.M.C. chaps and stretcher- bearers go for the hurt the Germans pop them off."

div.head: APPRECIATIVE PEOPLE.
div.p: APPRECIATIVE PEOPLE.
Describing the journey up from the South Coast in a hospital train, the writer says that the people at places where they stopped did rot
PRIVATE P. SHEEHAN. Wounded during a charge.

div.head: SERGEANT FORD.
div.p: SERGEANT FORD.
Wounded In Head, But Back At The
Trenches.

Sergeant Ford, 27 years of age, whose home is at 17, Neston-street, has had ten years' service in the 4th South Lancashires. He had finished twos terms when he enlisted. Writing home on March Ist he says that he got hit on the left side of the head on February 26th. The bullet took his head band away. His injuries, however, proved to be only slight, and after a short stay in hospital, he went into the trenches again on Friday, during the night. At ten o'clock on Saturday, the 27th, the Ger- mans started shelling the trenches. He says he was the only unlucky one, being hit with, a piece of shrapnel. His family, he said, must' not take it too seriously, as he thought he ,would soon be out of the hospital again. A !letter of March 4th announces that he had !come out, but was sent back again. He re- peated that he did not think his hurt was serious, and hoped they would not upset them- selves at home.
Sergeant Ford worked for fourteen years at the Longford Gas Works and was storekeeper there.

div.head: PRIVATE WILLIAM MILSON.
div.p: PRIVATE WILLIAM MILSON.
A Family of Soldiers.

Mr. and Mrs. Allison, of 101, Longford-street, have four sons and one son-in-law, all soldiers. Private William Milson, 25 years of age, who worked at Rylands Brothers, and joined the Territorials, got wounded on the 10th inst., so he writes in a letter to his mother. "I have been in hospital and am going on well," says a postcard 46f the 7th inst. "I am down at the base and quite well," states a second post- card, dated the 10th inst. Then follows another brief missive, received on Tuesday morning, saying that he had been admitted to the hos- pital, and he had received no letter from home for a long time. He had been shot in the chest and the bullet came out at his back, and he was hoping to be in England again by the time they received that letter. The other brothers serving in the Army are Private George James Allison, who had been a' Territorial six years; Private Charles Henry Milson, 33 years of age; Private George Wil- liam Allison, 29 years of age, and who joined a Welsh Regiment at Swindon; and Corporal James Milson, 23 years of -age, who is a Terri- torial in the 4th South Lancashires and is now on his way to the firing-line. Private Arthur Mills, brother-in-law, went through the Boer War. He is now engaged in driving two horses in the transport section, conveying food to the soldiers. '

div.head: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES.
div.p: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES.
Easter Saßings Cancelled.

The Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Comany, Ltd., regret to announce that the contemplated sailings for the Easter Holidays have been definitely cancelled owing to the dis- turbed conditions prevailing. The announce- ment thus made will not under the circum- stances be unexpected, and it is hoped that a restricted service may be maintained from Whitsuntide between Liverpool and North Wales.

TEACHERS ON MILITARY SERVICE. On the recommendation of the School Management Sub-committee, the Warrington iEducation Committee, at their meeting on Monday evening, decided that leave of absence be granted to Mr. Richard E. Burtt, certificated assistant master in the Wycliffe Council School, during the period of his military ser- vice, and that his nominee be paid such sums as, with the total Army or Corps pay and separation allowances, if any, received from the Government, will make up an amount equal to his full salary for the time being. Leave of absence for the same reason was also granted to Mr. William C. Entwistle, of the St. Barnabas' School, and it was decided to pay to his nominee a weekly sum of 126, tid.

div.head: VIOLATED TRUCE.
div.p: VIOLATED TRUCE.
Mr. Farier's Reply to Mr. gylands' Partisaa Speech,
Request for Proof or An Apology'.
To the Editor of " The Examiner."

Sir,—As President of that Wairington* Liberal Association, I cannot Am the par- tisan speech of the Chairman of the-Warring- ton Conservative Association at the annual meeting to pass in silence. Afterrgivitig lip i;ervice to the political trued by siyirig'that "polities were barred," Mr. Rylards imme- diately proceeds to make an unworthy and unwarranted attack upon the Liberal party generally, and particularly upon a prominent Warrington Liberal family. The speetliii a good deal involved, and in places contradic- tory, but the most offensive portion is as follows:

It had been in their minds for many tears that Germany had been making notablif en- deavours to build a fleet strong enough to challenge our own, and during all that One the Haldanes, the Brunners, the Mends, and the. Crosfields, as far as he recollected, had maintained that the " G(irman peril" wag as bogey, that the Germans loved us as brothers, an that the last nation in the world they would seek to attack was our- selves, Perhaps it was a little difficult to us to appreciate' that attitude of mind, and how it could be possible that a sensible man could' suggest that the proper course for us to take wan to scrap our Navy as the sign of our good' intentions towards Germany, with w perfect confidence that she would never hit us or seek to quarrel with us.

div.head: Weariest Part.
div.p: The Weariest Part.

It is note my purpose to follow the bad pre- cedent set by Arr. Ityknds by violating the political truce: It would be easy to defend the Liberal 4 policy in, this connection from attack, buttr confine mytPlf to what is per- sonal. Fiefore, dealing with whi.e h locNo application, tc word shout the attack on Lord Haldane. Perhaps this the meanest part of the whole, especially at a time when the Territorial Forces crefejed mainly by the strenuous toirof fiord' Haldane, are acknow- ledged by those at the‘Fitont, from General French downwards, .to be so. efficient. Perhaps the best .way to deal with this disparagement of Lord Haldane is to quote from the "Pall Mall Gazette," a source which does not gener- ally give 'quarter or praise to a Liberal Minister:

With much that Lord Haldane did as Minister for Wm- we profoundly disagreed. But Nye are, for that reason, the more ready to acknowledge that, when his work of organisation was put to the test, it gave the happiest results, and we can find no excuse for those who make him a target for malevolent innuendo. . . .

div.head: Attack on the Crosfields.
div.p: The Attack on the Crosfields.
And,now to deal with Mr. Rylands' attacks, •or as the paper quoted would term them, "malevolent innuendos," upon the Cros- fields.

Many may differ from the Crosfields in regard to the political principles which' that family has consistently upheld in Warrington for at least a century, but all Will be ready to give its members credit for filling a worthy place in the industrial, municipal and political life of the town. They have ever held their honour, the honour of Warrington, and the honour of England high; and that through long years, going back before the time that the forebears of Mr. Rylands stood shoulder to-- shoulder with the Crosfields in united efforts for political progress, and when Mr. Peter Rylands represented' in Parliament the principles which his son now attacks. It is scarcely necessary, in thinking of the present generation of the Crosfields, to recall the fact that Major Crosfield and his sister have given in -unstinted measure their time, money and energy in striving for national de- fence, and especially that form advocated by the National Service League. Whether Mr. Rylande agrees with this last or not, has he the hardihood to suggest that either of these members of this family are indifferent to the cause of national safety? But is there not just reasoii to conclude that in referring to the Crosfields, Mr. Rylands' • intention was to discredit another member of that family, namely, Mr. Arthur Crosfield, and that he was endeavouring to make party capital by disparaging Mr. Crosfield; who may be the Liberal candidate when the next election comes to be fought on party lines? It is im- probable Mr. Rylands would seek to deprecate the services of Major Crosfield, who, as every- one will acknowledge, is doing, and has done, his utmost for his country's safety.

div.head: Challenge.
div.p: A Challenge.

If I am right in supposing that this attack was made solely for party purposes, and with the intention of disparaging Mr. Arthur Crosfield; then I challenge the accuracy of Mr. Rylands' "recollections" I have been associated' with Mr Crosfield for many years, have heard the great bulk of his political speeches, have listened to the emphasis and conviction with which he has urged the vita/ importance of an overwhelm- ingly powerful Navy in view of the German menace. Never a syllable have I heard him utter that could be construed as a sugges- tion that the Navy should be " scrapped ." My belief, therefore, is that Mr. Rylands' statement and innuendos are as unfounded as they are unworthy. I therefore ask him either to make good his so-calltd " recollec- tions " and insinuations by quotations from Mr. Crosfield's speeches, or, if these are in- accurate and without foundation, to apolo- gise. It will be admitted as readily by Mr. Crosfield's political opponents, as by his sup- porters, that he always fights fairly, fights as a gentleman. All know that if, by chance, he were ever led into making any statement re- flecting upon a political opponent which was clearly contrary to fact, he would promptly make an honourable withdrawal. Will M.Y. :vlands do likewise if he cannot make good his ill-timed charges?

What Loyal Englishmen Have Agreed To Do. Party conflict has its place, and an import- ant one, in the healthy development of any people. • Out of this conflict of ideas national progress evolves. But there are times like the present, when the flare of these conflicts should subside. By general consent the lights of party strife have been ordered to be put out. All loyal Englishmen have agreed that during the war none should be for party, but all for the State. It seems a most unfor- tunate thing that any local party leader should go out of his way to rekindle these political fires, and through ill-advised, taunt- ing, and, as I believe, false statements, spread disunion and endanger the strength which can only come when politicians place their country's interest before that of party'. Yours faithfully, _ _
, C. E. PARKER. President Warrington Liberal Association. Penketh, March 16th, 1915.

Education Committee In An
Appreciative Mood.

Monday night's meeting of the Warrington Education Committee was the last of the financial year and, before separating the mem- bers took the opportunity of according a vote of thanks to their Chairman (Councillor Roberts), for his services during the past twelve months.
CHAIRMAN'S SONS WITH THE COLOURS.

The vote was proposed by the Mewl?. (Alder- man Peter Peacock), who said that they all agreed that Councillor Roberta conducted the business of the committee very well indeed, and that he had education at heart, and gave the committee not only his time but also the best of his very valuable knowledge on the sub- ject which came within their province. They were particularly gratified at his services dur- ing the past year, as he had been going through serious and strenuous times in consequence of the war. They knew that extra work had been placed on him, because his gallant sons were Rprri nrt their country The committee's debt
seconding, and said it needed no words of his to help the members to appreciate the whole- hearted manner in which the Chairman always undertook anything that was for the good of education.

div.head: COMMITTEE MOST FORTUNATE IN
div.p: COMMITTEE MOST FORTUNATE IN
THEIR CHAIRMAN.

The Rev. Canon STEVENSON supported, re- marking that during the whole twelve years the committee had been in existence they had been most fortunate in their chairmen, and he felt sure that they all realised that Councillor Roberts, not only upheld, but enhanced the record of his office. (Hear, hear.) He brought to the duties an intimate knowledge of the various ramifications of the - educational system, and they till felt that, when he spoke, he spoke with a full understanding of all he said; whilst, moreover, he was able to keep them to the point when they, were tempted to stray into various interesting paths, the temptation of which beset them all at various times. (Laughter; and applause.) _ _
The proposition was carried with applause.

div.head: BURDEN ALMOST UNBEARABLE.
div.p: A BURDEN ALMOST UNBEARABLE.

The CHAIRMAN, in acknowledgment, said he very greatly appreciated what he knew was the honest and kindly sympathy of the speakers in special directions just now. "The whole country," he added, "is going through a very serious and anxious time, and to some of us the burden is almost greater than we can bear. I hope and believe, however, that, sustained by the sympathy of our fellowmen, and by that trust in Providence which we hold, we may see this awful period terminate successfully, and that those whom we love so dearly may be spared to come back to us." (Hear, hear.)

div.head: THANKS TO THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THANKS TO THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.

The DEPUTY-MAYOR (Dr. Joseph) proposed a vote of thanks to the Deputy Chairman of the committee (Mr. A. J. Jolley), whose services, he said, had been admirable. It was, perhaps, an unfortunate position for anyone to be. in to have to propose a vote of thanks to one who was the Chairman of a Finance Committee, but, in that connection, he was reminded of the old statement of Christian doctrine to the effect that whilst one hated the sin, one loved the sinner. (Laughter.) Mr. C. E. PARKER seconded, remarking that he thought the committee were fortunate in having the benefit of the services of a gentle- man like Mr. Jolley, who was willing to give them so much of his time and energy, And who brought to educational matters such a clear head.

The proposition was carried. HOPED HE WAS NOT A DEADLY SINNER. Mr. JOLLEY thanked the committee for their expression of goodwill and hoped that he had not been such a deadly sinner often, and said that if he had he would have to do a penance after the nice things that had been said about him that evening. (Laughter.)

div.head: And Stole A Tin Of Salmon.
div.p: And Stole A Tin Of Salmon.

At the Borough Court on Monday, Patrick McLoughlin, described on the charge sheet as "a loiterer," of no settled abode, was charged with having, on the Fair-ground on Saturday nigfit, stolen from the person of William Maxwell, a 60. tin of salmon It was stated by the Chief Constable that McLoughlin accosted the old man, who had had one or two glasses of beer, and held up his stick in a most threatening manner. He then rifled the old fellow's pockets and took the tin of salmon. He admitted the offence. There was another alleged offence in Green-street which had to be inquired into.. The case wee adjourned till Thursday.

div.head: Further Charge.
div.p: A Further Charge.

When the prisoner was brought up on Thurs- day a further charge was preferred against him —that of having stolen 2s. from an old man aamed Thomas Maloney. . , Maloney said that prisoner and he had been earryin,g sandwich boards, and at the close :If the day McLoughlin asked him how much he had got. Witness showed him a 2s. piece and prisoner grabbed it and, added the witness, "was out of sight before one could say Jack Robinson."

Prisoner, it appeared from further f.viThneo. later on stole the tin of salmon, and at 12.30 a.m. came up to a watchman's fire in Butter- market-street and ate the contents of the tin, being soon afterwards arrested by Detective- Sergeant Holland.
Piisoner, against whom there were previous convictions, WAS committed to prison for six months, with hard labour.

div.head: BELGIAN GRATITUDE.
div.p: BELGIAN GRATITUDE.
Kindness Received at the Infir-
mary Acknowledged.

Mr. J. H. Smethurst, chairman of the Board of Management, at the Infirmary, has received a letter from a number of Belgian wounded, who lately stayed for treatment in the Military Ward. The following is a translation of the letter:—

Mr. Chairman,—Being certain that ,you will meet among the members, of the committee some sympathetic translator more familiar with the French language, I take the liberty of using the latter rather than English to express .you our hearty thanks for the charming hospitality that we enjoyed in your Institution. We shall not soon forget the tepder care and devotion of the doctors, the matron; and the nurs..?s.

By a thousand tbuching attentions, and by the variety of pleasant recreation, you suc- ,.eeded in making our minds of conquered and exiled men forget the too painful sorrows that oppress them. These sentiments, awakened in unfortunate circumstances for our people and our nation, are not such as will soon pass/ away; they are engraved in the hearts of the people who are destined to suffer and do not permit the kindnesses received to be forgotten. rnforting Feeling. ting feeling for a people that very proud of its aspirations • Ting in the accomplishment +ties, to feel at it side a great •• • . • •nsents to share its fate, and, •, • the coming liberation, shows

and most cordial hospitality. We have appreciated a great expression of this feeling among the inhabitants of Warrington, and this not only with regard to Belgian wounded, but also with regard to the Belgian civil population who are reeeiving the benefits of your kindness, we are happy to be able to express to you our very sincere and affectionate thanks.
Sorry not to be able to express in your own language all our gratitude.—We beg to remain, yours very respectfully, ' H. GHYSELINCK.

div.head: COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS.

WEDNESDAY. Before Mr. Roger C. Parr and other magistrates. A Costly Stop.—Frank Wood, of Edward- street, Compstall, near Stockport, was fined 10s. and 10s. 6d. costs for allowing a heavy locomotive, of which he had charge, to remain stationary on a bridge at Walton. _

Working An Unfii Horse.—Thomas Massey, of 3, Melville-street, Warrington; and Thomas Driscoll, of 53, Leonard-street, Warrington, were fined 10s. and costs and 20s. and costs, respectively, the former for working' a horse whilst in an unfit state at Sankey Bridges on March 4th, and the latter for causing it to'.l3e worked.—The evidence showed that the horse had sores on its shoulders and that the lad, Massey, when spoken to by Inspector Dee. of the R.S.P.C.A., stated that the other defendant told him to take the horse out.—Driscoll said that the sores were perfectly dry when the horse was taken out of the stables, and he thought a little light work would do it no harm.

div.head: WHAT THE WAR TEACHES.
div.p: WHAT THE WAR TEACHES.
The Vital Need for Zam-Buk.

The war has brought home to officers, men, and the public generally, the fact that Zam-Buk is a real friend in need. Letters received daily tell how valuable Zam-Buk has proved not only for healing the cuts, wounds and bruises, inci- dental to life in the trenches, but for mending and preventing sore feet after arduous marches, and warding off frost-bite. " The War Office Times" have been to some pains to investigate the matter, and the vie-x- -they express on the value of Zam-Buk should have great weight. Referring to the vital need for sound feet, the journal says : "Zam-Buk is the most effective alleviat3r of pain, not only for feet troubles, but for many other ailments and accidents to which officers and men on land and sea are liable. The war has not only enhanced Zam-Buk's reputation for " first-aid " purposes, but it has established and emphasised the fact that a box of Zam-Buk is an indispensable adjunct for every , soldier and sailor. "We have tested Zam-Buk and round it splendid both as a curative and remedial agency for many purposes. We should like to see one or two boxes of this excellent first-aid sup- plied to every man in the Expeditionary Force. Such a step would, in our opinion, add greatly to its efficiency."

This expert- opinion on the indispensability of Zam-Buk for soldiers and sailors must im- press civilians who are every day liable to mis- haps. Accidents will happen, and skin and scalp troubles will crop up in every family. But by keeping Zam-Buk handy and usifit it'Promptly, danger and anxiety are soon banished. A 2/9 box of Zam-Buk, which contains nearly four times the 1/10. size, is especially useful for family use.

div.head: THREE GENERATIONS OF
div.p: THREE GENERATIONS OF
SOLDIERS.
An Orford-lane Family's Record.

- It would be hard to beat the record for patriotism of the. family of •Knox, of 158, Orford-lane, Warrington. There are four sons all soldiers, their father was a soldier, and their grandfather was also a military. man. The father, who died on the 30th of December, 1013, was Quartermaster of the King's Royal Rifles, Liverpool, and his father before him ,had an honourable military career. The eld- est son, William, is quartermaster-sergeant of the, Royal ,Engineers; while the second son, George, is a warrant officer in the Royal Marine Artillery; and Thomas, the third son, holds the rank of " sergeant-instructor in the Indian Volunteers, and has offered his ser- vices, if required, for the trenches. The fourth son, John, who enlisted some eight Years ago, when 17 years of ago, is now in the trenches in France, and when he has a chance takes the opportunity of informing his mother ." by postcard of .his doings. His latest communica- tion was received on Tuesday of last week, and in it the gallant soldier informed his mother that he was well.

div.head: RIVAL COMMITTEES.
div.p: RIVAL COMMITTEES.
Mr. Kingdon Declines to Accept
An" Olive Branch."
OLD ISSUE AGAIN RAISED,

At the monthly meeting of the Education Committee on Monday evening, Mr, Holman Kingdon reverted to the question which he brought forward at the last meeting, viz., the relationship between the Education Depart- ment and the Health Committee of the Cor- poration in regard to the appointment of offi- cials. It will be remembered that, at the February meeting, Mr. Kingdon tu3ked to be allowed to retire from the chairmanship of the Medical Inspectiain Sub-committee, be- cause, as he said, "an intolerable position" had been created through the selection by the Health Committee of a new whgle-time dental officer without consultation with his commit- tee, ..who, nevertheless, would have to be re- sponsible for superintending the work of that official .and for its effective carrying out. He then contended that the. appointment was one in which the Education Committee were essen- tially interested, and in which the Medical Inspection Sub-committee shotakl most cer- tainly have had a voice. He further stated that although the appointment was one which most directly concerned the sub-eommittee over which he then presided, and that, 'despite that fact, the first official intimation the sub-com- mittee had had that the new dental officer was appointed came that night, and that, officially, the. committee which was to be responsible for the new officer's work, had only. just learned his nathe and qualifications. He submitted that if the ,committee were to be Asponsible for the work -of officers, such as the school dentist, they should have some control . over. the appointment Of them.' ,

div.head: WHO SHALL APPOINT?
div.p: WHO SHALL APPOINT?

Mr. KINGDON re-introduced the subject at Monday night's meeting by moving the follow- ing :—" That, whereas the Education (Admin- istrative Provisions) Act, 1907, imposes on the Local Education Authority the duty of mak- ing provision for the Medical Inspection of school children, and this duty has been dele- gated to the Medical Inspection Committee, this committee is of the opinion that all ap- pointments of officers for the purpose of carry- ing out the medical inspection and treatment of school children, excepting the appointment of the principal school medical officer when that officer is also to be the Medical Officer of Health, should be made by the Education Com- mittee." In doing so, he repeated that he did not think it was a business-like arrange- ment that the Education Committee, or any of its sub-committees, should he responsible for the results of the work of officials whom they were not allowed to appoint. If the, mem- bers passed his proposition it would mean that they were going to run the committee on busi- ness lines; they would be trying to the best of their ability to apply in the matter of the internal administration of the education of the town the same principle as was now being recommended to the nation at large. Mr. JAII3.IAN seconded.

HOLDING OUT "THE OLIVE BRANCH." The MAYOR. (Alderman 'Peter Peacock) said there was a suggestion made at the last meet- ing of the Health Committee that there should be a kind of "feeler" put out to see whether the Medical Inspection Sub-committee would be satisfied with an undertaking that when such appointments as the one in question were made in future, the whole of the members of the sub-committee would be invited to attend the Health Committee meetings and help in the making of the appointment. He, person- ally, thought that would be a happy solution to the difficulty, and, if the Medical Inspection Sub-committee favoured the suggestion, it would be 'put into proper form by means of a resolution.

div.head: AN UNACCEPTABLE OFFER.
div.p: AN UNACCEPTABLE OFFER.

Mr. KINGDON said that the offer was abso- lutely unacceptable to him, although he did not wish to speak for, the other members of the sub-committee. He pointed out that the Medical Inspection Sub-committee .had no re- presentation on the Health Committee, and consequently had up to that night had no "feeler" put out to them, either official, semi- official, or otherwise. At. any rate, the "feeler" had not ,reached him. Perhaps it was what the Americans called a "tickler." (Laughter.) The DEPUTY-MAYOR (Councillor Joseph) said he had always been in favour of a. joint com- mittee; it would provide the best way out of difficulties such as the present one. Mr. JARMAN : How many members of the Health Committee are there?
The CHAIRMAN (Councillor Roberis) : Twelve. Mr. JARMAN : And how many of the Medical Inspection Committee? The CHAIRMAN: Either twelve or thirteen.

THOUGHT IT A FAIR MODUS VIVENDI. Mr. tresoN said that he had been one of those who had sought a joint committee such as that suggested by the Mayor, and he, and others, had understood that when an appointment, such as the one referred to, was to be made the Medical Inspection Sub-committee would be invited to send representatives to the Health Committee's meeting. The whole of the pre- sent difficulty had arisen because that course was not pursued. The Education Committee were reduced to this position: That the whole of their .officers, whose salaries they paid, were appointed by another body. The committee had no control over their appointment or dismissal, although they found the salary and bore the burden of the responsibility for the officials' work, and he contended that if the Council conferred responsibility on a committee they must also give it liberty. They could not tie and fetter men and then expect them to be responsible for results. He took it the Mayor's suggestion would meet the wishes of the major- ity of . the Education Committee, and would form a fair modus vivendi, upon which they could base some understanding and agreement. Things could not go on as they had been going. He could not consent to be responsible for results when he had no authority at all in the matter of the making of appointments and when he had no control over those who were to do the work.

div.head: WOULD DO AWAY WITH THE COMMITTEE.
div.p: WOULD DO AWAY WITH THE COMMITTEE.

Councillor PEMBERTON said he was in favour of having the Medical Inspection Sub-commit- tee done away with. The Medical Officer of Health • was the medical officer for the whole town and for everybody in it, including the children, and, in this matter of health, it would be far better to have one department only.

The CHAIRMAN thought a suggestion of the kind put forward by the Mayor would have been welcomed, for he felt that it might form the basis of a friendly and business-like settle- ment. The olive branch was being held out. Mr. KINGDON : Is this offer going to deal only with the officers under the Medical Inspection Sub-committee, or the whole of the officers appointed? The MAYOR: With the schools. Mr. KINGDON : Then I refuse to accept the offer, so far as I am concerned.:

The CHAIRMAN said ,he would have preferred that the matter be deferred until they had received a communication from the Hea Committee, when the offer, that they undw:- stood would be contained therein, could be con- sidered on its merits., He thought that was the most business-like way' to deal with the matter. Mr. B. T. FAIRCLOUGH suggested that the mat- ter should be deferred until the next meeting.

div.head: NOT A BUSINESS PROPOSITION.
div.p: NOT A BUSINESS PROPOSITION.

Mr. C. E. PARKER said that he took a great deal of interest in the work of the Medical Inspection Sub-committee, but he would not care to be re-appointed upon the committee on the old understanding. He had no feeling in the matter, but, as Mr. Kingdon had said, what had taken place was not in the nature of a business proposition; moreover, it was not sen- sible, and it did a great deal to take away the interest of the members from their work. ,If things were to go on in accordance with the old understanding it would be better for The co-opted members, to withdraw entirely andslet the members of the Education Committees entirely selected out of the Town Council. Councillor WILKINSON said that if he were a member of the Medical, Inspection Sub-com- mittee he would take up the same position as Mr. Kingdon had taken; he would either have the privilege of making the appointments of
