div.p: STOCKTON HEATH

United Band of Hope Concert—The closing concert of the session was held in the Wesleyan Schoolroom on Monday night, the Rev. G. Curtis presiding. The first part of the programme con- sisted of a cantata entitled "Britannia's Re- view of the Band of Hope Army," which was splendidly given by the members. Miss Elsie Whitfield made an ideal Britannia, with Reggie Grounds, Evelyn Todd and Bessie Gerrard as attendants. The " army " consisted of a num- ber of Welsh, Irish, Scotch and English boys and girls, who looked vc•y pretty • in their national costumes. National songs were sung by Bessie Clarke, Hilda Taylor, Sarah Gamble and Arthur Walton. Recitations were given by E. Travis, L. Sandford, E. Williams, A. Ramsbottom, M. Rarasbottom, I. Clarke, E. Brookes, A: Spencer, 0. Ditchfield; J. Williams, R. Grounds and E. Todd. Other -items included songs by Miss Eva Tanner (Temperance Queen), who was deservedly -encored; a similar compli- ment being paid to Daisy and Rennie Summers, who sang very effectively "I don't want to play in your yard." Other songs were given by Miss L. Brookes and Ruby Powell. The humorous sketch, "Paddy's Pledge," by mem- bers of the Warrington Temperance Guild Sketch Party, created much amusement. The characters were taken by the Misses A. Little- wood, E. Tanner and A. Hamer, .and Messrs. N. Fernley and F. Jones. Mr. G. A. Whitfield acted as accompanist.

div.head: SEMI-DIRK STREETS.
div.p: THE SEMI-DIRK STREETS.
Places Where The Reduced Lighting Is Objectionable.

The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held on Tuesday even- ing in the Council Schools. In the absence of the Chairman, Mr. F. Pearson presided. The other members present were Messrs. J. Hallows, A. Bottomley, C. Hallows, W. Mclntyre, J. Whitley, F. Warburton and J. McDermid, with Mr. W. E. Hough (deputy clerk), Mr. S. Wright (surveyor), and Mr. E. Bradshaw (clerk to the Parish Council). •

div.head: An Eyesore to Vanish.
div.p: An Eyesore to Vanish.
The correspondence included a letter from the County Surveyor stating that the hoarding at Twenty Steps Bridge would he removed in June.
The Chairman said they had been waiting for that for many years. There was another hoard- ing in the Square which ought to go.
Reduced Public Lighting.

The Clerk produced the- order which the Lighting Committee had received respecting the reduced lighting of the streets. He said the Police Superintendent had Waited upon him and had explained that what he wanted was that the brilliant lights should be dimmed. Mr. Howe, chairman of the Lighting Cora- wittee, reported that he received the order from Mr. Hough, and he went ta see the authorities, and they gave him instructions as to what they thought right to be done. As a result the com- mittee had decided to leave unlit every third or fourth light. Brilliant lights, he understood, must either be lowered or made invisible from above by painting the tops. and the manager of the Gasworks had arranged for that to be done in the case of the street lamps. The Military Authorities • held very strong views on, the matter.

Mr. Hough stated that there were places in' the Manchester district where nothing was done: The Chairman said there was no uniformity in the matter. When they went to some places they found them most brilliantly lighted. Mr. Mclntyre said that at one point in Chapel-lane, .which was: considered dangerous, the lamp had been re-lit. He added that in cer- tain other places the reduction of the lights was very objectionable, tend he thought some representation might be made in this respect. The Deputy Clerk said if the committee would name any such points he would have attention called to them.

div.head: Modlfication of Bylaws.
div.p: Modlfication of Bylaws.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board referring to the suggested alterations in the bylaws. Mr. Hough said the committee would probably adopt the usual course of appointing a sub- committee to go through and modify the bylaws. The Chairman said the matter was brought up a few meetings ago, the suggestion being made that they should, perhaps, adoPt some new by- laws, such as might be more easily adhered to by builders.
It was decided that the Building Committee, the Lighting Committee and the Surveyor be appointed to deal with the matter. ,
The Clerk's Salary.

It was decided that the remuneration of the Clerk be the same as last year. viz., .225. Mr. A. Bottomley• contendea that the sum was not sufficient for the duties the Clerk had performed. Mr. Hough, however, suggested that the sum named would do for this year. The Building Committee had no report.

div.head: To Fight Huns—Not Flames.
div.p: To Fight Huns—Not Flames.

The Fire Brigade Committee reported that, at a meeting on March 3rd, some alterations .were deemed necessary • at the fire station, whilst several of the firemen having joined the Army, it was necessary to reorganise the brigade. The minutes were approved.
A "News "-ance.
Mr. Pearson called attention to the state of the public streets consequent on the blowing about of the placards, which newsboys left about.

Mr. Whitley said it was not the local boys who stuck the placards about, it was the boys from Warrington. The attention of the police had been called to the matter, but they said the public wanted to know what was going on.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

Fifty Years a Forester.—The remains of the late Mr. William Simpson, farmer, ivh.) died on March 11th, were laid to rest in Stretton Churchyard on Sunday afternoon, the Rev. ad Hon. C. F. Cross officiating. The principal mourners were the deceased's sons, Messrs. Henry, William, Fred and Samuel Simpson, and the funeral was also attended by a number of grandchildren and friends. Messrs. E. Owen, J. Smith, W. Lawson and F. Cottrell acted as bearers. Mr. Simpson, who was a well-known and much-respected resident, had reached his 79th year. Born in Stretton parish, he lived there until recent years, when he re- moved to Sankey. He was a member of the Ancient Order of Foresters for 50 years. A number of wreaths were sent by members of the family and friends.

div.head: RIVAL COMMlTTEES—continued.
div.p: RIVAL COMMlTTEES—continued.

the officials for which his committee were . re- sponsible, or he .would resign. Councillor BROADHURST thought the best thing the committee could do would be to accept' the offer put forward by the Mayor, and, in future, meet the Health Committee, in . the manner suggested;

Mr. WACK-ER : It was suggested as g 86p that might quieten the committee. Councillor WILKINSON said that the idea of the Health Committee with regard to. the sug- gestion that the two cOmmitt?es should einifer was "We will give it thought !" That was as far as it went.

div.head: MOTION CARRIED.
div.p: THE MOTION CARRIED.

Other members- having spoken, Mr. Krmalpv said he did not feel disposed to withdraw his proposal, and, so far as he ,was Concerned; unless the Town Council were prepared to give the Education Committee the right. to make any appointment that Came within the scope of the work that they were sUpOosed to do, and for which they. were responsible, :he was not inclined to take any interest or share in the work of the committee.
The proposition was then put and carried.

div.head: LYAI M.
div.p: LYAI M.

Additional Scavenger.—The Council on Mon- day evening acquiesced in the proposal of Coun- cillors Lockyer and Parker—that an additional scavenger be employed. Cleaning of Roads.—By request, the Surveyor (Mr. D. Mort) reported to the Council on Mon- day the length of the roads to be kept clean by their respective employes.

Tar-Macadam Contract.—On the motion of Councillors Gotobed and Cowper, the Council unanimously resolved, at Monday's meeting, that a contract for the carrying on of tar- macadam work be prepared. Footballer Recruits.—H. Daniels, of the Wed- nesday football team, has this week enlisted. From that club he is the fifth to do so. The Saturday club has so far provided about fifteen units of His Majesty's Forces. Forthcoming Liberal Party.—On Tuesday, March 23rd, the Lymm Women Liberals hope to enjoy a tea—followed by an attractive enter- tainment—in the Primitive Methodist School- room. Gentlemen are cordially invited. Overseers Re-appointed.—At Monday's special Council meeting Councillor -W. G. Groves and Mr. Samuel Walker Gould were unanimously re-gected Overseers for the ensuing year—on the motion of Councillors Gotobed and Ingham. On The Sessions Bench.—At the Lymm Petty Sessions, held on Wednesday Morning, there were on the Bench: The Hon. John E. Cross (in the chair), Vice-Chancellor D. Stewart Smith, Messrs. John Coxon, H. Holden and T. J. Ridgway.' Matron's Thanks.—Sister Colburn, matron of the Red Cross Hospital, wishes to express through the medium of "The Examiner" her hearty thanks to all who so far have so kindly sent gifts to her institution. All have been fully appreciated by the inmates. Headmaster Welcomed.—Mr. W. Hawkins, having obtained respite from his military, duties after seven arduous months, was ac- corded a marked . welcome on Monday—when he resumed his interrupted duties of Grammar School headmaster. These had been relin- quished on Saturday by Mr. C. C. Parez.

Councillors Who Attended.—At the special meeting of the Lymm Urban District Council, held on Monday evening at the Council Offices, there were present: Councillors T. H. War- burton (in the chair), F. Lockyer, W. G. Groves, C. Cowper, A. Maclntyre, R. H. Gotobed, G. H. Parker, S. Critchley and F. Ingham; and Mr. William Mullard (clerk). Mr. George Williamson also was present. Chances Of Football Cup.—The Lymm Wed- nesday 'football team hope to visit Manchester on Wednesday to oppose the Post Office team of that city. If they defeat that team, they will tie with a Stockport club for the cup and medals—in Which case a most exciting match would doubtless terminate the League cup fixtures. The Lymm team is however, gradually losing members owing to recruiting.

Street-Lighting In War-Time.—" That for the preseneonly every other street lamp be lighted and the tops blackened; and that lamps at the cross-roads and other large lanaps be only shaded—arrangements to be left to Councillor Cowper as manager." This motion was car- ried unanimously at Monday's special Council meeting, on the proposition of Councillors S. Critchley and W. G. Groves. Four Disabled Fighters.—At "Brookfield " the Red Cross Hospital—arrived last Friday four more temporarily disabled warriors. They are Sergeant Prentice, East Surrey Regiment; and Privates Stovell, Leicestershires; Bass, Army Sertice Corps; and Bushell, 2nd Lancasters. Of these, two are suffering from frost-bite, one from horse kick to shin, and one from varicose reins (operated on in France). All progress satisfactorily, along with their fourteen fellow-sufferers.

Lioness Dies At Lymm.—At the Pepper-street Football Ground on Sunday, aTrived "Buff's Bill's" American circus and menagerie. Begin- ning the next day, a procession round the town- ship and several largely-attended performances were given. The circus left on Thursday morn- ing. • Just 'as the circus .arrived a fine lioness died—and the hide has been • exhibited. The cause of its death is unknown, but its native trainer thinks the recent passage from Ireland may have "upset her."—A Lymm man was announced to enter the lions' den with the trainer on Wednesday evening. He did not do so, however..—Owing to the presence of the circus, thei Wednesday footballers had this week to postpone their match. " Tommy " on Prayer lyleetings.—Private Henry Brooks writes home from France to Lymm: "I think we shall be all right if we keep ourselves fit. You cannot wonder at the prayer meetings held in England for us at the Front. It is dreadful out here. . . . There are four or five of our fellows (i.e., Cheshires) in hospital with wounds, but I am glad to say they are not serious. I had to bandage one young . man the other night, but he has gone to .England now, and I think he will soon be all right: . . . I don't think you are getting' all our letters. . . . Hope to be with you soon, as I don't think it will last much longer." Soldiers' Lively Morning—private Jack Guest, of the Village, Lymin, writes home from the firing-line to a friend: " . You must not be getting all my letters. . . . We were in the trenches yesterday (Friday), and I would rather be in them than where we are now. This place has been shelled again. this morning. We had to get what we could and get out as soon as we could; we had to go in the fields for about an hour and a half in the rain. We have got back in the billet now, but there is no telling how soon we shall have to go out again—they may start again any time. Yesterday when we were out they shelled the hospital and killed four or five. They will do anything to kill a few men. Yesterday two others were hit—one killed and one wounded— in the trench by snipers. . . . You dare not put your hat above the top, or else they have a shot at you. . . . To-day we were talking about the days when we could go to the foot- ball match. I hope it won't be long." Cyclist's Two Offences.—George Mills Seddon, agent, of Laskey-lane, Thelwall, was summoned to Wednesday's Lymm Sessions for having obstructed the highway on Penny-hill, on Wednesday, March 3rd, by leaving a motor- cycle and sidecar 'standing there, and for not having a licence. He admitted the offence.— Sergeant Davies told how, at half-past six, he had seen the cycle standing almost in the centre of the read opposite the Church Inn. It was then dark, and there were no lights on the machine. In the inn he saw defendant, who said he did not think it dangerous—as there was a lighted lamp near to. Asked for his licence, Seddon said he did not know whether he had it with hint or not; he then produced an expired one, but said he had another at home—and agreed to send it to the police on the following Friday. The police, however, had to call at the house .twice before obtaining it. They then found he had taken it out six days after being questioned.— Defendant said he had not known the lieence had expired, and wrote to .Mr. Potts' im- mediately he found out. His cycle lamp he had turned out because he was very short of carbide.—The Chairman characterised the first offence as a gross bit of negligence, for which defendant '.was fined half-a-crown. He also said that there was' no excuse for not renewing the licence, and 'a fine of ss. and Be. 6d. costs was imposed.

div.head: "HAD IT VERY HOT." But "Lymm Boys stuck It Very Well."
div.p: "HAD IT VERY HOT." But "Lymm Boys stuck It Very Well."
SHELL TERRORS.

Lance-Corporal John 11. Moston's latest letter from the , trenches reached Mrs. G. Davies at his former home on Booth's Hill, only two days ago. He says :—" We are alive and kicking. We had it very hot in the trenches on Thursday—l thought the last had come! Shells were bursting so near to us that I was covered with slutch twice'.

" I cannot explain how it was only by saying it was like hell on earth. I was very glad when I know that no one was hurt or killed, and shall never forget the third time in the trenches as long as I live. The Lymm boys stick it very well, firing away all the time?'
IMPORTANT RESIGNATION
Of Secretary_ to Belgian Reftige.es'
Committee.
We understand that Mr. W. Mußard has this week resigned his position of secretary to the Belgian Refugees' Committee.—Why P

div.head: WAR AND FUSTIAN-CUTTING.
div.p: WAR AND FUSTIAN-CUTTING.
Township's Principal Industry At
Piesent Unaffected.
Fustian-cutting is Lymm's chief industry, about 100 workers being employed at it. There are five shops—two belonging to Mr. Henry Moston, two to Mr. C. Cowper, and one to Mr. H. Daniels.

Though the work has, of course, been some- what slacker since the outbreak of war, thus necessitating some of the employes taking periodical respites from their regular duties, we understand that at present none of the fustian-cutters are out of employment.

div.head: NO LYNEM NIEN 'WOUNDED:
div.p: NO LYNEM NIEN 'WOUNDED:
Though All Have Been In Action.
LATEST NEWS.

Two days ago word was received from Private Stanley Gibbs (of the sth Cheshires), whose home is at Henry-street, Lymm, saying: "We had a lively day yesterday in the trenches. All the Lymm boys were in action, and the German shells were bursting all over us. Best of all, not one of us was hurt. We could not hear one another speak for the rifle fire. We are out in a field to-day, and; it is like midsummer. Private Gibbs is a "range-finder." From him this week have reached Lymm two or three letters.

div.head: Hospital Front Blown In.
div.p: Hospital Front Blown In.

"Yesterday we had twenty-four hours in the trenches," he wrote on Friday. March sth, "and the Germans blew our hospital front in and killed six men—one out of our company. There will be very few of the peonle left in this vil- lage now; most of them are leaving to-day. . . . I shall be glad when it is all over. . . . We are a great deal safer in the firing line than in this village, because the Germans shell it every day. . ." "The people where we used to go have left the village now," writes the Private on WedneS- day, March 10th, "and I have to settle down to stew again. The joiners. &c., have been build- ing some wooden huts. It is a very nice job; I wish it would last till, the war .was over— which I think will not be very long now.

div.head: " Our Batt.'s " Concert.
div.p: " Our Batt.'s " Concert.
"Our liattalion rave a very good concert last nircht. We have all'sorts of games in our spare time. . .
Found in Cantured Trench.

"We are going into the trenches to-night for twenty-four hours," writes Private Gibbs still later. "Another man of our Battalion was killed last night. . . . I have got a German officer's stick, which --as found in a German trench that was capt--,-,d in . It is all carved with different fonires. I shall try to bring it home with me—l don't think they will let me send it. If not, I shall cut it into three nieces and pack it in my kit bag. . . ."

div.head: WAR-WORN GERMANS. Lymm Territorials' Views and Experiences.
div.p: WAR-WORN GERMANS. Lymm Territorials' Views and Experiences.

"We are in the beet of spirits," writes Pte. Henry- Brookes, of C Company of the sth Bat- talion of the Cheshire Regiment, to his mother, Mrs. James Taylor, who lives at 1, West Hyde, Newfield, Lymm, and then goes on to speak of the pleasure with which the Lymm lads serving along with him, have received copies of "The Examiner," which have been forwarded by friends at home.
Allies Winning on Land and Sea.

"Both on land and sea," he adds, "the Allies are getting the best of the Kaiser's once-mighty army, and his long-laid plans are crumbling to pieces. I believe that letters which have ap- peared in the Cheshire papers have given the _impression that our Battalion has been cut up. I wish to contradict that; there is absolutely no truth in the statement. nor is there any founda- tion/for it. Up to date (March 11th) we have enli had about sixteen casualties, and of ,these but three have been fatal. . . The most dangerous thing we have to contend with is the shrapnel. Mainly, we have to get our sleep in the daytime, for every man has to be alert in the night, for the enemy's attacks generally take place under cover of the darkness. 1 may say that if the enemy make up their minds t.) entertain us to a night attack, they always get an overwhelming reception. . . . - Our Regulars Are Grand. -

"Our 'Regulars' are grand, and are most amusing company in the trenches; in fact, they keep us, so to speak, rich in the matter of enter- tainment. . . . We have every morning to quit the village in which we sleep o' nights. when we, are not in the trenches, because the Germans will insist on baby-killing with . their sometimes explosive shells, which, by the way, do not come over to us so numerously as they used to. . . . The rockets sent up at nights on both .sides are sufficiently numerous to re- mind one of a visit to :-Belle Vtie, Manchester, and anyone popping his head over the top of the trench whilst these firework displays are on is pretty certain to receive 'the ration of lead which means death.' Wounds in the head, I need hardly say, are very dangerous, but from a wound in the body, provided it be below the heart, the patient in most cases recovers. Value of First Aid u Work.

"I have had to attend to a few terrible cases since we came out here . . . and I feel glad that I went in for first aid work. If a man is wounded in the trenches in day-time he has to be tended on the spot, for it is impossible to take him down to the dressing station—which is generally about a mile behind the firing line— until night.. The most dangerous time is reliev- ing time—when the old party go out of the trenches and the new party come in. Many a, time on their way the men have to throw them- selires prone in the mud, so that they may not be seen when the lights are thrown up. Both sides indulge in these pyrotechnic displays, with the idea of detecting attacks, which May be expected any minute throughout the night. . . . A Nerve-Trying Job.

"There are some very nerve-trying jobs, in the firing-line, and one of the worst of these is that which has to be undertaken by 'the listening patrol,' as it is called. It consists of men, who, under cover of night, have to steal out of our trenches and endeavour to get near enough to the German lines to gain information of value, and one can easily guess how hazardous this duty is when he learns that very often the trenches are little mere than fifty yards apart. . . . The weather has been very trying, but I am glad to say that it is improbing now, and that it makes better the prospects of the ad- vance, which we are expecting to make every day. Our artillery and aircraft are playing la prominent part in this war, and the two corn-

bined play havoc with the enemy. Some days you hear little save the noise of our great guns doing work of so deadly a nature that they have, won the mastery over our foes. It is plain to see that the Germans are getting war- worn and exhausted, and so we try to cheer them up—(writes "Tommy" in sarcastic vein)— with a few ragtime melodies and ,sentimental songs, which are rendered with great gusto by the Cestrians."

div.head: GERMANS FED UP!"
div.p: GERMANS FED UP!"
Lymm Territorials In Optimistic Vein.

Yesterday Private Jim Taylors letter reached his mother at 1, West .Hyde, Lymm C' Company, sth Cheshires, France. am in the pink at present, but have been busy just lately and could not find time to write. ,

"We afe doing, fine, although it is hard work. But it cannot last long, The Germans are beaten now,' and we can see it and can do as we like with them. It's not 'paper' talk we tell you—because we don't See any papers over here. Please send us more 'fags.' We live on smoking here to pass our spare minutes away. Also more chocolate—it's the best stuff to eat over here, and when we see other chaps chewing it it makes our teeth water. . . .
RED CROSS ACCOMMODATION.

div.head: Will It Be Increased?
div.p: Will It Be Increased?

We hear' that!•a :dainitation' of ,the Working Men's Committee, waited upon the matron of the Red Cross Hospital on Thursday night with .- reference to the possibility of increasing the accommodation of that institution. It will be recollected that last week, we drew atteation to the fact that the accommodation of the Lymra
Hospital—unlike its neighbours—was not being increased, and asked the reason for th* dilatoriness in the matter.

div.head: VOLUNTEER DEFENCE.
div.p: VOLUNTEER DEFENCE.
Public Meeting To Be Called By Urban Council.
GREAT CHANGES?

The principal business of a special meeting of the Urban District Council on Monday evening was the consideration. of the advisa- bility of raising a force for home defence, to be affiliated with the Central Volunteer Train- ing Corps (which, of course, already exists in. .Lymm) and to _form part of the Cheshire Vol- unteer Regiment. • Mr. George Williamson attended in conse- quence of the Council of the local corps hav- ing held a meeting last week. It had been decided to approach the Council about calling. a public meeting, with the object of -affiliating with the rest of the county—as suggested by the Lord Lieutenant. On behalf of the local corps, Mr. Williamson explained this proposed step to the Council. After due discussion and the asking and answering of a number of questions, 'Councillor C. Cowper 'Proposed that •w.publie meeting be called by the. Chainnati,(Councillor T. 11. Warburton) in accordance with a circu- lar produced, the arrangements to be left to Mr. Williamson and the Chairman...
Councillor S. CritehleY seconded, and the motion was carried unanimously.
The date of. the meeting is not yet known.
SUPPORT FROM RATES?

The Clerk (Mr. W. MuHard) read a letter from the Clerk to the Ashton-on-Mersey Urban District Council with regard to the cost of the equipment of the corps coming front the rates. and suggesting that the local authorities should approach the Local Government Board for their consent to the expenses of equipment. It was resolved that the matter should be further considered by a private 'committee.

div.head: RECRUITING AGENT.
div.p: RECRUITING AGENT.

A letter from Captain Linaker with regard to acting as, agent for recruiting was also read. It was decided to let the matter lie on tho table. - In the meantime Mr. Williamson is acting as the Captain's agent.

div.head: " OUII RIG GI AS."
div.p: " OUII RIG GI AS."

Private Percy Clare writes: "March 13th (Saturday) We came out of the trenches last night We had a rather hot time yesterday, and were firing on the enemy for a long time. Our big suns gave them some snuff.

"The Germans were shelling our trenches— well, trying to do, but they did not manage. The shells dropped all round very near to us, but we got none hurt, thank God! It was an awful row—all- the guns going off at once. But we took it rather coolly; we are gettirg used to it now.

In Trenches At Night. "It is like the sth of November in the trenches at night. The Germans send star- shells—which do us no harm, only they light the place up just like day. We have similar shells, too.
"We are all quite well and happy;. and I think we Shall soon have the war over, now the Fighting Fifth have got at them."

div.head: "EVERYTHING WELL!"
div.p: "EVERYTHING WELL!"

Pte. Joseph Clare writes word 'received on • . Thursday morning : "Keep on smiling! Every-.. • ' thing is going on well, but we had a rough time of it on the 12th in the. trenches We were not - half giving them something to be going on with, and their shells were bursting all rotind.---- us,_but we managed to pull through.

"It made us -get a bit excited at first, but after we had fired a few rounds we got used to it and had just the same as you have seen in the papers—like hell on earth for a few minutes. But we took everything coolly. It was the first time we had had a chance of having a pot at them. "Don't worry! All of us are all right and fit."

div.head: BETTER WE_VTIIER Greall,‘ Cheers Lynim " Tonunies In Trenches.
div.p: BETTER WE_VTIIER Greall,‘ Cheers Lynim " Tonunies In Trenches.

Sergeant H. Clare, of the Drill Hall. Lymm, writes cheery letters home, saying how the boys are progressing at the Fr )nt. A letter received from him on Sunday said it was lovely spring weather there, and the roads and fields were drying up—so that they were getting rid of the mud' a little. All had got, quite accustomed to the trenches. Also they had had another issue of cigarettes and tobaCco. All the Lymm men were quite all right, and a little while ago he had seen Captain Ridgway, who looked fine!

Duties Exceedingly Well Done. Three days ago a letter arrived which the Sergeant had written a week before. "I have great pleasure in sending you the very best news concerning ourselves," he wrote. "All our men are in the best of health, and .are doing their duty well, indeed they do every duty in the trenches exceedingly well. Not Cut Up. " COntradict any rumours you hear about the Lymm men being cut up! "I never felt better in my life before. The food continues to be good, and we have plenty of cigarette's. We have all had a pair of socks given us, sent from 'the Queen and Women of the Empire,' along with a note." On Sunday the Sergeant 'wrote:— " We came out of the trenches last night again, all safe and sound."

div.head: TIMES IN WHICH WE LIVE.
div.p: THE TIMES IN WHICH WE LIVE.
CHILD LABOUR TRAGEDY.
" Saddest Sight That Eye Can Rest Upon."

div.head: "WAR NEWS."
div.p: "WAR NEWS."
SPECIAL FOR "THE EXAMINER.'

The insatiable thirst for the latest war news, the eagerness to read the scraps that an un- willing Press Bureau bands out from time to time, has produced quite a revolutionary effect upon the mind of the average person to-day. The individual who scarce opened the pages of a daily paper. before August, Ibl4, now in- dulges in his morning and evening editions, and heroically reads the same "Official Bulletin" /twice per diem, as though he were "mugging-u!)" for some examination. The wading through, the hair-raising and soul- stirring articles of the multitude of special correspondents attached to each 'paper is another daily act of penance, which those who have not answered their country's pill inflict upon themselves ; and having read them, the mind wonders how one small bead can weave so much, around so little: The public mind is bent on reading war news; and the'art of getting up a newspaper, however fine it was in the piping times of peace, has become superfine to a degree. The cries of the newsboys give evidence of this public craving for war news. "All the latest winners," is only heard at rare intervals; and quite a shudder strikes the hearer as an urchin, in a moment of forgetful- ness, calls out—" Winner of the Waterloo Cup!"
Attendant Evils. The sale of newspapers has grown to such alarming proportions that quite a smile steals over the countenance as the cutting down of the morning papers to a single sheet is recalled.

But this demand for news has brought with it a full train of attendant evils. Papers are called for morning, noon and night; and some- one must be employed in hawking them. The inevitable ;result is the greater :employ- ment of boy labour. Boys, even of tender age, are engaged in satisfying the public- greed for news. To the heedless and the thoughtless, this means nothing. The arrival of the morning paper at 7.0 a.m. is an expected and regular occurrence. The special edition purchased at 10.0 p.m. calls for no questions about the welfare of the urchin who sells the paper. But it means a great deal. It bids fair to grow into a national menace. That paper pushed through the letter box an hour before break-fast meant the rising of a tired little youngster at 5.0 a.m. His morning round continues till school time; and the dinner hour means fhnning with a noon edition to certain customers.

Doze In School. Afternoon school is "a sleep and a forget- ting"; and then comes the evening round. And so without a respite, however brief, the little silent sufferers toil on to slake the thirst for war news.

The evening papers are responsible for even more evil. Engage one of those ragged young urchins in conversation for a few minutes. There one stands shivering in the door of a public-house, crying " Spesh till" at 10.30 p.m. What a tale he tells in this age of. "Children" Acts! School closed at 4.0 p.m. A lump of bread stuck in his fist—his clogs and stockings left at home to save 'Wear, and to excite pity, and he is yelling "Five o'clock" at 4.30 pan. At intervals of an hour he returns to get a bundle of the' next edition. And so in cold and wet, half-clothed and ill-fed, he prepares him- self for an early grave, a life of crime, or some other evil. Poor children ! Ask any teacher in, your schools what be thinks. The farmer who fain would exploit the boy of thirteen, rob him of the heritage which years of striving has left him, and cut down the pittance of his workmen with cheap labour, is at least giving the school boys healthy and productive employment. But what of the sad-eyed, weary slum child, as he dozes in his desk at school? It is. one of the saddest sights that the eye can rest upon; and it is to be seen daily in almost every elementary school.
S. C. J.

div.head: WHAT BUDDHISM LACKS.
div.p: WHAT BUDDHISM LACKS.
Story of a Great Faith Told at
Adult School..

Professor G. Currie Martin continued his highly interesting and instructive series of lectures on "The Lessons of the Great Reli- gions" on Sunday, when he dealt rith. Budd- hism. The lectures are being given under the auspices of the Warrington and District _Adult School Union and last 'Sunday's lect or'!' was delivered .at the Stockton Beath Adolf School, where also the last of the 'series—which will deal with the faith of ancient Persia—will 'lie .given to--norrow evening. There was a good attendance on Sunday, and the Professor began by showing that Buddhism was an outgrowth of Hinduism. In the words of Professor Barnett, it! was "an atheistic, nihilistic, Hindu -idealism." The life of the founder was then briefly sketched, stress being laid on his sincerity, and strength of purpose, as well as on his spiritual vision of reality. The nature of the eight-fold path of Buddhism was then explained, and Matthew Arnold's "Light of Asia" recommended as a simple introduction to the subject. The difficult pro- blems of the Buddhist doctrines of the .soul and of Nirvana were discussed, and illustrated so as to render their meaning intelligible to the Western mind. The ideal, the Lecturer said, was to reach a condition of tranquility of soul, freed from all confusion. The later developments of the religion were then traced to the desire for an object of worship, and the longing of the heart for a personal presentation of Deity. Hence arose the thought of the Buddha as 'Saviour and the possibility of the disciple himself becoming a Buddha. The progress of the faith -in the Far East was traced in interesting fashion, and its present- day comlitions in Burundi, China and Japan were touched upon. As compared with Chris- tianity, Buddhism lacked a clear doctrine of God, an historiclncarnation, and a Otisfactory doctrine of salvation. '

Montaigne remarks that " Every several nation bath some names which, I wot not how, are somethites taken in ill part." Naturally, my friend Miss Altna never ceased to deplore trie circumstances that gave her a name which " dated"' her so unmistakably, and many now helpless little victims of the present craze (I alreaay know of two called Ypres). will one of these days have the like feeling of regret. and resent- ment. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCEL 20, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCEL 20, 1915.
FUTURE OF EUROPE. Germany Will Concede Peace —On Terms.
HER BENEFICENT PLANS.

A few weelis ago Mr. A. Mounfield gave to our readers the translations of two articles from German newspapers, in which Ger- many's purposes were revealed with startling frankness. The writer of one of those articles, Herr Maximilian Harden, has been writing a similar effusion for a German news- paper published in New York. If it is in- tended to influence American opinion, it shows a curious lack of perception and humour. It is, however, quite in a piece with the utterances of the Kaiser and his spokes- men, and reveals the same implicit claim that the rest of the world has no voice in the ar- rangement of its own destiny. The closing words, however, are distinctly modest. That a typical German leader like Herr Harden should suggest that England after the war may be a Power of equal strength and equal rights with Germany shows that someone has been thinking seriously about the British Navy. Here are sonic extracts from the article : " Not as weak-willed blunderers have we undertaken the fearful risk of this war. We wanted it, because we bad to wish it and could Wish it. May the Teuton Devil throttle those whiners whose pleas for excuses make us ludicrous in these hours of lofty experience. We do not stand, and shall not place ourselves before the court of Europe. Our power shall create new law in Europe. Germany strikes. If it conquers new realms for its genius, the .priesthood of all the gods will sing songs of praise to the good war. . . . We wage it .from the lofty point of view, and with the conviction that Germany, as a result of her achievements and in proportion to them is justified in asking, and must obtain, wider room on earth for development and for work- ing out the possibilities that are in her. . . . The terms of a peace treaty that does not ensure this would leave the great effort iinre- warded. Even if it brought dozens of shin- ing billions into the National Treasury, the fate of Europe would be dependent upon the United States of America. " We are waging war for ourselves alone; and still we are convinced that all who desire the good would soon be able to rejoice in the result. HOW THE KAISER WILL END THE WAR.
" I can imagine Germany's war lord, when Calais is captured, sending the fleets and armies back home, and quietly saying to our enemies: -

" You now have felt what Germany's strength and determination can do, and here- after you will probably weigh the matter well before you venture to attack us. Of you Germany demands nothing further. Not even reimbursement for its expenses in this war —for those it is reimbursed by the wholesome terror which it evoked. Do you want any- thing of us.? We shall never refuse a chal- lenge to a quarrel. We shall remain in the Belgian netherland, to which we shall add the thin Strip of coast up to the rear of Calais (you Frenchmen have enough better harbours, anyway); we terminate, of our own accord, this war which, now that we have safeguarded our honour, can bring us no other gains we now return to the joy of gruitful work, and will grasp the sword again only if you attempt to crowd us out of that which we have., won with our' blood. .Of a solemn peace confer- ence, with haggling over terms, parchment, and seal, we have no need. The prisoners are to be freed. You can keep Your fortresses if they do not seem to you to be wdrthless, if the rebuilding of them siill seems, worth while to you. To-morrow is again a common .day.'

div.head: BELGIUM'S WARM BLAZE OF ADVANTAGE.
div.p: BELGIUM'S WARM BLAZE OF ADVANTAGE.

" To the Belgians we are the Archinin and the Tenant of the. Pool of Hell! We would remain so, even if every stone in Louvain and in Malines were replaced by its equivalent in gold. That rage can be overcome only after the race, praised by Schiller's fiery breath, sees its neighbours close it hand and draws advantage from intimate relations with them. kntwerp not pitted against, but working with Hamburg and Bremen; Liege, side by side with Essen's' Berlin's and Swabia's gun fac- tories Cockerill in combination with Krupp; iron, coal, woven stuff from old Ger- many and Belgium introduced into the mar- kets of the world by one and the same com- mercial spirit; our Kameran and their Congo —such a warm blaze of advantage has burned away many a hatred. " Only, never again a withered Iteichsland ! (Imperial territory.) From Calais to Ant- werp, Flanders' Limbur4, Brabant, to behind the line of the MCIII3O forts, Prussian! (Ger- man princes no longer haggle, German tribes no longer envy one another) ;, -the Southern triangle witk Alsace and Lorraine—and Lux- emburg, too, if it desires—is to be an inde- pendent federated State, entrusted to a Catholic noble house,. • Then Germany would know for what it shed its blood. " We need land for our industries, a road into the ocean, an undivided colony, the assur- ance of a supply of raw materials and the most - fertile well-spring of prosperity—a people industrious and efficient in its work. " Here they are: Ore and copper, glass am] sugar, flax and wool. But here,, too, there once lived Jan and Hubert van Eyck, Rubens, the reveller Ruysbroek, and Jordeans of the avid eyes. Here there always lived—to be sure, in twilight—Germania's little soul, fluttering imagination.

div.head: AND ENGLAND-.
div.p: AND ENGLAND-.

" And is there not.here, too, that which— all .Coo stormily and, as a rule, in all too harsh a tone of abuse—every German heart yearns for, a victory over England ? On the seas such victory cannot be quickly won, in- deed; can, indeed, never betwon without great sacrifice. But with the German Empire, whose mortars loom threatening from one coast of the Channel, whose flag floats over the two greatest harbours of Europe and over the Congo basin England would have to come into a friendly agreement as a Power of equal strength, with equal rights."

div.head: WORKERS' WEEKLY PENCE FOR INFIRMARY.
div.p: WORKERS' WEEKLY PENCE FOR INFIRMARY.
A Splendid Subscription in Spite of the War.

div.head: WAGE-EARNERS DONATE OVER £l,OOO.
div.p: WAGE-EARNERS DONATE OVER £l,OOO.

Despite months of war, and all the con- ditions that it has brought in its train, the working ,men of Warrington last year sub- scribed the sum of £1,087 Bs. led. to the local Infirmary by means of the weekly levy to which they have gladly subjected themselves, or as the result of various concerts and other money- earning attractions which, through their representative committee, they organised and carried through. Under all the cirtuinstances it is a fine total, and one of which they need not be ashamed, especially in view of the heightened cost of living, which has, naturally, hit the worker first of all. Moreover it is only £6 2s, 3d. less than the total contributed in the twelve previous months, when the world was at peace and when the purchasing power of the working man's sovereign w6s much greater than it is now " The fact that they have sub- scribed so liberally and so consistently in such trying times said the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock)—at the annual meeting of the Work- ing Men's Committee in connection with the. Infirmary, which was held in the Town Hall on Saturday afternoon—" reflects the greatest credit upon them. 7

MOST DIFFICULT YEAR FOR SUBSCRIPTIONS. His Worship presided over the meeting in question and, others present included Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, C.V.O. (president of the Infirmary). Mr. J. H. Smethurst (chairman of the Board of -Management), Mr. Roger C. Parr (hon. treasurer), Mr. F. Aylmer •Frost (member of the House and Finance Com- mittees), Mr. G. Walker (vice-chairman of the Working Men's Committee), and Mr. J. H. Hampson (secretary). . A number of letters of apology were read.— rho Rev. __John Yonge, who is now " con-

valescing " at Buxton: wrote congratulating the committee upon their work, and added a word in praise of the manner in which the work of the Infirmary had been carried on, work .which, like theirs, had been so gratifying in its results. —Mr. John R. Ransome hoped the committee would be as successful in the future as in the past; and Mr. J. Fairelough regretted that circumstances rendered it impossible for him to be present.—Alderman Thomas Burton, the chairman ,of the committee, also regretted inability to attend owing .to indisposition, and wrote The past year has been the most difficult • year for raising subscriptions of any dur- ing the life of the committee. When we consider .the number Of heroic. young Men who have left town during the year to take up arms against the most outrageous and brutal nation that ever disgraced civilisa- tion, we are proud of all who have gone to save our country from the ravages of such brutes. This is streing language, but I don't think it too strong, when we consider the atrocities perpetrated. in Belgium. Had there ,been no war, thef4e men would have been following their ordinary employ- ment, and mast of them contributing a small sum every week • to tile Infirmary, which would have shown a much improved balance .sheet. However, I think the com- mittee have done exceedingly well in the cltcumstances. A letter of apology was also received from Mr. W. Peter Rylands..
COMMITTEE'S GOOD FINANCIAL POSITION.

Since the last annual meeting, said the Mayor —in the course of a brief opening speech—the committee had, along with the whole of the country, been passing through the most troublous times in tin' history of the world. Yet, notwithstanding those troublous times, the committee were, in a good financial position, and the amount collected slniwed an increase of £7B is. id. on the sum raised in 1909—the first mar in which the -contributions received direct from the works exceNled the sum of 1;1,000. He understood that it was the ambition of the committee to raise the sum of £1,500 by subscriptions, and they had gone .a good way towards realising that ambition, in spite of the war, for they had raised 0,087 Bs. hod. When he looked through the report of the Enfirmary committee of another large town—a town he would not name, hut one which had a population of 126,000—he noted that the amount collected among the workers was only £7oo—as against £1,067 raised in the previous year—which was very poor as, compared with the £l,OOO odd collected in Warrington with its population of only 85,000. The liberal sum raised in Warrington was characteristic of the working men of the town. who had made up their minds to do their duty in this respect. Whatever happened they were determined not to neglect their own institution. (Applause.) The Infirmary, during the past year, dealt with no fewer than 12,177 patients, at a cost of £5,313 12s. 10d. ' Included in the number of patients were 4,860 accident eases and 1,274 in- patients, whilst no fewer than 809 operations had been performed.

£1,113 9s. Bd., as 'against £1,215 17s. sd. in 1913; Infirmary . Special War Fund, £4O; St. John Ambulance. Brigade, Warrington Corps, £4 7s. 5d.; War Refugees Fund (prclceeds of concert given by Mr; and Mrs. A. 11. Crosfield), £lO4 18s. Bd. Mr. Hampson also drew attention to the fact that the accounts showed a slight reduction in the amount contributed front the works, but pointed out that a lot of the works had not only contributed Ito the Infirmary, but to the War Funds also. He particularly referred to the handsome increase in the amount contributed by the employes of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, which. totalled £47 19s. 2d. during the first seven months, the subscription for the corresponding period of last year having been .only £7 17s. 2d. Several members of the committee had left to go on active service, among them being the Mayor's son. (Applause.) They wished them all a safe return. ' (Renewed applause.)

div.head: WHY NOT £2,000 A YEAR FROM THE EMPLOYES?
div.p: WHY NOT £2,000 A YEAR FROM THE EMPLOYES?

With regard to working men's subscriptions, he would like to coiumend to other firms the system which had been adopted by Messrs. Crosfield. lie wmild like to see the governing body aim at getting a sum of £2.0110 a year from the employes. When working men went to work in the morning they never knew whether they might not require the services of the Infirmary before evening. Even if they did not require the services of the institution them- selves they knew that, by subscribing, they were helping those who did—that they were helping in a good cause: In conclusion his Worship expressed the pride he felt in having been elected president of the Working Men's Committee., HOW THE MONEY WAS DIVIDED.

The lion. Secretary then submitted the statement of accounts, which showed that the amount raised by the employes at the various Works and places of business was, as stated above, £1,087 Bs. 10d., as, against £1,093 us. 21d. in 1913. In addition, the committee Were in- terested in a large number of special efforts which brought the total amount raised to £1,280 ss. Bd., as compared with £1,233 16s. 6d. in the previous year. After deducting £l7 Os. 11d, for expenses, the sums distributed were: Infirmary and pispenskiry ordinary account,

div.head: WORKERS HAVE THE WELFARE OF INFIRMARY AT HEART.
div.p: WORKERS HAVE THE WELFARE OF INFIRMARY AT HEART.
In moving the adoption of the annual report,

Mr. George Walker said that he was very glad that the amount raised was so large as had proved to be the case, and when the war was over he had no doubt that they would reach the £1.500. It was a pleasure to meet the 'members of the Working Men's Committee and to note how sincerely they 118(1 at heart al. welfare of the Infirmary. In their secretary they had a most indefatigable worker, and one who look the deepest interest in his work. In conclusion, Mr. Walker ,moved the adoption of the accounts, as submitted by the secretary. Mr. W. .Daintith 'seconded, and the accounts were adopted.

div.head: "THE FIRST INSTITUTION IN THE TOWN."
div.p: "THE FIRST INSTITUTION IN THE TOWN."

Sir Gilbert Greem;ll-, -being called upon by the Mayor to say a few words, began by paying a. tribute to Alderman Burton for the great in- terest he took in the work of the Infirmary, work which he had dearly at heart. Continu- ing, he said that the amount of money which had been raised among the working men of the town was most satisfactory, especially in view of the fact that "a great deal .of money had been diverted to other good objects in connection with the war. He was glad that they had, in the press of calls upon them, not forgotten their own local institutions. "The Infirmary," con- cluded Sir Gilbert,." is the first institution in the town, and we must all of us remember that, and we must further remember that it must be kept in a state of the very highest efficiency. I believe that it is as good an infirmary as any in the country. (Hear, bear.) We have an ex- cellent building; it is well looked after; and the amount of voluntary aid given to the institu- tion is something extraordinary. We still look to the working men for that support, which I know they will give, and as long as we have the help of every section of the community I have no doubt that the institution will continue to flourish." (Applause.) Mr. Roger C. Parr also spoke briefly, remark- ing that everybody who had an interest in the Infirmary must feel deeply grateful to the work- ing men of Warrington for contributing so mag- nificently to its funds. The work of organising the collection of contributions was really more important than the actual giving, because people were very often ready to contribute, but required to have their efforts directed through the proper channels. (Applause.) • ONLY £lll LESS, DESPITE THE WAR. Mr. J. li. Smethurst said be was very pleased to see that the finances had worked out so well, for everybody recognised the difficulty of obtain- ing money for such objects as infirmaries nowa- days. He proceeded to pay a tribute to the assistance which the representatives of the Working Men's Committee rendered in the man- agement of the Infirmarx, and said that the work of the institution was growing very rapidly. It was undoubtedly the besecharity in the town and district, and it was increasingly, nay, unceasingly, used f y the people of War- rington. Dealing with • the finances, Mr. ,Sme- thurst said that last year they did very well, as on the total amount they were only' a matter of 4311 down. That was due to the special effort of the Old English Fair Committee, which resulted in t,(>0() coming to the institution as extraordinary income. (Applause.) The In- firmary was an absolute necessity, and it ought not to be necessary for the management to go cap i I hard, in any begging spirit, to anyone and say, "Of your charity, give us something." Last year he reminded the WorkiniMen's Com- mittee that if they continued to provide more money, they might hope some day to have a con- valescent home in connection with the. Infirin- ary. During the past few months, owing to the fact of their haying wounded soldiers in the hospital. they had had experience of two con- valescent homes. Sir (albert Greenall and Mr. Roger C. Parr kindly placed their houses at the disposal of the Board, and the treatment meted out to the soldiers who stayed there was such that the hospital authorities could see the very great improvement in their physique. They could, therefore, think what it would mean if the Infirmary had a convalescent home to which. working men, their wives, or their children, might be sent after they had spent several weeks in the Infirmary. (Applause.) Mr. F. A. Frost bore testimony to the hard and conscientious work done by members of the Working Men's Committee and by their repre- sentatives on the governing body. There was hardly a meeting of that body but he got some valuable suggestions from the workers' leie- gateS. A short time ago it was suggested that the rules should be altered so that the workers should have six direct representatives, instead of four. He was convineed that the ninre eepie- sentatives the workers got the fewer complamts 'they would have, and -Then the meetillg at which the matter would be considered tame round, -he hoped to be p-nsent to support the proposal to increase the m meu-s -zepre- sentation.

div.head: MAYOR RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT.
div.p: MAYOR RE-ELECTED PRESIDENT.

The election of officers was next proceeded with, and on the proposition of Mr. George Walker the Mayor .was unanimously elected president of the Working Men's Committee. His Worship, in returning thanks, thought that the time was ripe for suggesting to all
employers that their men Should pay .a penny a week apiece to the Infirmary.
OTHER OFFICERS.

Alderman Burton wrote that owing to the state of his health he could not undertake any office during the year, but it was felt that it would be -too great a loss if he wee allowed to retire, and he was unanimously re-elected. The following' officers were also re-elected:— Vice-chairman, • Mr. G. Walker; honorary auditor, --Mr. C. _ Jackson Holmes; honorary secretary, Mr. J. 11. J. Hampson.. The honorary surgeons were thanked, it being observed that but for them the institu- tion would often be in a quandary. Their work was of the highest importance, and was freely given.

div.head: IF EVERY WORKER GAVE A WEEKLY PENNY –
div.p: IF EVERY WORKER GAVE A WEEKLY PENNY -

Mr. Watsoir referred to the question of systematic weekly- contributions, and said that if an arrangement could be made for the deduction of one penny per week from the wages of every employe on behalf of the Infirmary, £2,000 a year would at once be raised. He believed about half the firms in the town already adopted that plan. Mr. G. E. Knott explained that at the works of Messrs. Rylands' Bros. a scale of deductions, graded according to the amount of wages, waN in force, and yielded. very satisfactory results, without hardship to anybody. Votes of thanks. were heartily accorded to the officers of the' committee: to the honorary surgeons of the Infirmary, and to the Press, the Chief constable, Messrs.- Peter Walker and Son, Ltd., Warrington Musical Society, Cros- field's Band; and Mr. A. W. Turpin, manager of the Hippodrome, for assistance rendered during the year'.

div.head: CHARGE FOR THE POLICE AMBULANCE.
div.p: THE CHARGE FOR THE POLICE AMBULANCE.

Mr. Watson mentioned a case in which a man who met wii h an accident necessitating his removal to the infirmary, had received a bill for ss. for the use of the police ambulance. Ile regarded that as a hardship, and thought the Infirmary should either have aik. ambulance of its own or a standing arrangement with the Chief Constable that the charge • Should be •made through the infirmary, and not upon the patient concerned. The Mayor said the charge was made to cover the cost of the hire of the horse, but if a patient could not afford to pay., the- Corpora- tion did not press the matter. Mr. Watson: The person who comes to col- lect the accounts does not say it is not press- ing.

Mr. Walker referred to an accident which happened at the works with which he was connected and said that although the police ambulance arrived threequarters of an hour late and the injured men had already been sent to the Infirmary, he was 'surprised to receive a bill for ss.

Mr. Smethurst asked that tye account to which lir. Watson had referred should be sent to the Infirmary. . The Chief. Constable acted very fairly in these matters, and when he, knew that a. case was absolutely for the In- firmary, no charge was made.

div.head: COST OF EDUCATION.
div.p: THE COST OF EDUCATION.
Do the Ratepayers Get Value for Their Moue.)

Giving his report as representing the Com- mittee on the local Education Committee, Mr. George Walker said he could.not hold out any particular hope as to when the maximum education rate would be reached.... Warrington was suffering from. the bad effects of a policy pursued in t he past, when the people refused to have a :41)001 Board. The increased expendi- ture, however, was not due to the building bf new schools. He did not 'believe the building of schools was costing 2d. in the 2 to-day, because the loans were spread over a number of years. Members of the Town Council occasionally ex- pressed regret that more of the cost of • educa- tion was not borne by the taxpayer rather than by the ratepayer To him (the speaker) it seemed all the same whether he paid with his right hand or with his left. The only difficulty was that if they put mare on the national ex- chequer they Vould probably not have the same interest maintained in education locally as, wheri the payment was direct through the rates.

div.head: Education Worse Than 30 Years Ago. .
div.p: Education Worse Than 30 Years Ago. .

Mr. Walker 'went on to say that it had been suggested that the ratepayers got value for the money they spent on education, but said that he very much doubted Whether an adequate return was received for the vast expenditure. He had watched the matter closely, and Was sorry to say he did not think they got value for money. He maintained that the education given now, if they viewed it with reference to the three Ws, was not a patch on what it was 30 years ago. He wished he had brought to that meeting three applications he recently received for a junior clerkship; they would have provided 'a little bit of fun. The handwriting would have proved an eye-opener, and the spelling a perfect puzzle —in fact, worthy of Pitman., (Laughter.) Al- though experts in education thought they were making rapid strides, he believed there was too much attempted and too little done. (Hear, hear.). There did not seem fo be the thoroughness in the ground ,work that was essential to good education: •

div.head: " Awfully Neglected " Subjects.
div.p: " Awfully Neglected " Subjects.

The primary subjects were awfully neglected. When he -Walked through some of the schools in the town he enuld see nearly as many ways of holding a pen as there were scholars in the class. (Laughter.) He could even see them writing with the nibs, without any wooden stem at all. and not the slightest notice was taken of it. in his. boyhood days they were taught in school that all pens were to be held at a certain angle and in a certain way; but that teaching had gone out entirely. When he appealed to a headmaster, he (the headmaster) said handwriting.ok'as not cpnsidered essential now, because there were typewriter. (Laugh- ter.) They were trusting sadly too much to mechanical means, and he ventured to think •that a nice penman was an acquisition in an office even to-day. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: Millions Spent For No "Earthly Use."
div.p: Millions Spent For No "Earthly Use."

The speaker concluded by saying that he honestly thought the educational chaos was as bad to-day, only in another form, as it was 20 years ago. Re had not the least hesitation in saying that some of the millions spent on education might just as well be poured down a grid for what earthly uSe they were. Education to-day was not Sufficieritly practical. It was not on the right lines,, and he doubted whether the teacher was .drawn from the class which had the most influence.

Mr. W. E. Stout agreed with most of Mr. Walker's remarks as to the quality of educa- tion imparted in the present day, and said that it was very different when be was a boy. Even at an old woman's school which. he first attended he learned more than many boys seemed to learn under the highly paid educational staff of to-day.
The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding.

div.head: TRANSFERRED TEACHERS.
div.p: TRANSFERRED TEACHERS.
Commencing Salary As For A New Appointment?

The miontes of the school Management Sub- committee, presented to the Education Com- mittee for approval. at their monthly meeting twit ritomlay I` \Tiling, contained the following item t—" It was resolved that if a teacher already serving in one of the-schools under the committee applies for, and is nppginted to, a position in another school under the.scommittee, the commencing salary for that appointment shall be as for a new appointment, but any teacher desiring exemption from this regula- tion must, before applying for the appoint- ment, make application to the committee, and the committee may consider Whether the special circumstances of the case justify any variation from the regulation.. Mr. J. Upson urged the Chairman of the sub- committee to withdraw the minute, on the ground that it did not accurately represent the result of the committee's :discussion on the matter.
('hni titian (Counc)llor :Robert s) agreed. Conon Stevenson, Ihe chairman of the ,o 1 committee in question, agreed to withdro w the minute,

div.head: BOYS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: THE BOYS OF TO-DAY.
Is Allegation of Deterioration . Justified By Facts?

div.head: TEACHER'S REPLY TO CRITICS.
div.p: TEACHER'S REPLY TO CRITICS.

Our elementary system is now being severely tested on the battlefields of Europe and on the high seas, and who shall say we have not the right to be very proud of the result? Almost every General remarks upon the intelligence, courage, resource and Initiative of our troops--who are, for the most part, the product of our elementary schools!

These striking words were spoken by Mr. J. E. Morgan, in the Wycliffe Memof fat Hall last Friday evening. The occasion was the annual general meeting of the Warrington and Dis- trict Teachers' Association, and Mr. G. New- burn (retiring president) occupied the chair. . Mr. MORGAN, having been installed as Presi- dent by the retiring President, and having had a cordial reception, proceeded to give his "address." He first dealt with, the -charge of inefficiency which, be said, was being repeat- edly brought against the product of our elementary schools.. He quoted from Arnold Freeman's book, "Boy-life and Labour": "It seems to be a commonly accepted view that the responsibility for the manufacture of ineffi- ciency lies to a great extent with the elemen- tary school." It had also been stated by Sir IT. Hibbert (chairman of the Lancashire Edu- cation Committee) that boys were not turned out of school so well equipped in reading, writing and arithmetic as formerly. But Mr. J. L. Paton (high-master of the Manchester Grammar School) said: "I have 450 boys who come from the elementary schools. Do I find them perfect? No! There are no signs of wings sprouting beneath their shoulders.

One Great Advance!. Do I find them worse than they used to be? No; certainly not. It is one of the mistakeq of grown-up men, especially when they become employers of labour, to think that in their time all boys were paragons of perfection. I think that the boy coming"from the elementary school is far more .wideawake than he used to be, and, above all, far more interested in his work."

The one great advance we can claim, said Mr. Morgan, is that the attitude of the boy towards his school-work is quite different from what it used to be. He used to loathe it all, and when he reached the age of exemption he * threw his cal; in the air, and said: "Catch me ever going near that place again!"

div.head: Warrington Manager's Defence.
div.p: Warrington Manager's Defence.

A former manager of a Warrington school Had made a spirited defence of the teacher and dealt with points we can fully endorse— lack of parental control; late hours at which children are seen about the streets; a curricu- lum which is far too full,. and in some places abolition of corporal punishment, with a con- sequent weakening of teachers' authority.

div.head: Teachers' Many Difficulties.
div.p: Teachers' Many Difficulties.

The teachers, the speaker continued, were now working on far different lines in school— in a state of transition between old and new methods. Some of the children had been trained partly under one method and partly under another. The new methods could-not be said to have thoroughly established themselves. But before the results of their school-work were criticised there should be borne in mind many unfortunate circamstances against which the schools had to contend. (I-Lear, hear.) Probably not one-third of the scholars came from homes which supplemented school efforts. Children were sent to school dirty and insnffi- Aently clad. Out of school employment was also an obvious drawback. Boys were engaged in their_ spare time as Milk-boys, paper-boys, and errand-boys; and girls at 'domestic duties, and 80 on. Persistent exposure to all weathers and lack of time for proper meals were not conducive to satisfactory school results. Again, the site of classes (60 to one teacher) was a great barrier.

Mr. S-torgan then dealt *ith remarks recently made at a meeting of the Chamber of COM- meree, to the effect that boys, when they left school, did not seem to know any more than they .used to do; that there was a lack of ap- preciation of the advantages of to-day, and lack of manners and behaviour to elders. He maintained that a statement of that kind was easy to make, but difficult to proVe or dis- prove, because so much of a child's knowledge could bo directly tested, but lay dormant— ready to be called up when needed. Unless they had vocational teaching, where a boy's ability could be judged by the practical skill he showed in Making boots, clothes, &c., they ' would always find people ready to offer criti- cism of that kind on their work.

div.head: .Boys Ought To Know More.
div.p: .Boys Ought To Know More.

. 'At the same time, boys ought to know more —considering that the school age had been raised several times and that half-time was not so prevalent as formerly. The scholars were also provided with better school books, and the teachers were more highly qualified. But, as tg lack of appreciation of these advan- tages, surely the answer lay in the growing npluber of students to be found in evening continuation schools and secondary schools! A -point often lost sight of was that the cream. of their scholars passed through secondary schools and took Civil Service and similar ap- pointments—with the result that, the local employer had to be content with only. second- rate scholars. It was from, these, very often as .units, that the work of the teachers was judged.

_ _ - The Chief Wrong. • But lack of parental control was the chief wrong—tto much pocket-money and the conse- quently frequent visits to picture-shows, where films were shown such as were calculated to breed utter disregard of parental authority. Want of discipline certainly did net occur within the schools; and, moreover, it was ob- tained without the employment nf harsh measures, as formerly! (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) • .

div.head: PATRIOTIC PROFESSION. .
div.p: PATRIOTIC PROFESSION. .
Twenl3-fhe Per Cent. of the Teachers "Join Up."

Mr. P. IL LoxiisuAw (secretary) reported an- other successful year; and, amidst considerable applause, mentioned that 25 per cent. of the Warrington men teachers had joined the colours.—The roll of honour will be found on another page of this issue.

div.head: £25 A MONTH TO THE WAR FUNDS.
div.p: £25 A MONTH TO THE WAR FUNDS.

Mr. J. l.rsos presented a highly satisfactory report as treasurer. The finances of the asso- ciation were in a flourishing condition, for the year's receipts totalled £231 2s. 3d., and they had a handsome balance in hand. Up to March Ist the teachers of the town ,had subscribed about £l6O to various war relief funds—(ap- )lause)—the receipts, since they commenced ,subscribing, having, averaged more than £25 a month. .1 grant of £lO had also been made from the Reserve Fund. Roughly, the follow- ing subscriptions had been made:—Prinee of Wales' Fund £l3O, West 'Lancashire Hospital ,122., Infirmary Wounded Soldiers £23, "School- master" _Belgian Fund £32, and local relief cases £l2; leaving a balance in hand of about £lO. (Applause.)

div.p: Beechnes Plll5
of the dominant position held to-day by
MAKING MEN OF 'EM.
Recruits' Busy Days and Nights.
Pte. T. Heaton, of the 4th Battalion of the West Riding " Regiment, writing last week-end to a friend in Warrington, tells of his experi- ences whilst undergoing training.

The recruit's time, he says, is kept quite full up, and no pains are spared to turn him into an efficient soldier as speedily as possible. His company have to take part in two night attacks per week; besides marches in the day time and night guard duty at least once a week. But the men do not complain, for they know that it is making better and more useful .men . of them.

Pte. Heaton appends a specimen time-table of a (lay's work, when a.night attack is thrown in. tp with the lark, he says, they set off for a route march at 8 o'clock in the morning, taking some refreshments with them. At 3 p.m. a 'halt is called and dinner is partaken of, after which tomes a short period of rest. By five o'clock the men are "padding the hoof" again, each man carrying with him sufficient food to last him the night through. Arrived at a strategic posi- tion, suitable for the purpose of the sham night attack they trench themselves in, and sor9,e- times whilst waiting for the enemy' they are able to snatch a little sleep. Frequently, how- ever, the night attacks are delivered-early on, and the "victory " won, the men Are able to march back to their quarters by midnight, tired out, but conscious of the fact that they have acquired much knowledge and experience that will be of service to the 'old country shortly. Despite their arduous duties, the writer adds, the men keep in the best of health.

The Hay-box Cooker. A demonstration of the uses of the "hay-box cooker" was given at Battersea Polytechnic lately. That used cost 10th; it was a packing case lined with newspaper, divided into two compartments and packed tightly with old hay. When the dish to be cooked (in a metal or earthenware saucepan) has been brought to a boil, it is put into a nest scooped in the hay, covered with a flannel, packed over with a hay pillow; the lid is put on, and another flannel put over. It will then cook itself without further assistance. Dishes shown cooked in this way were porridge, put on overnight for the morning's breakfast, rhubarb, ham, meat stew, and soup.

div.head: " SORTES GRAMMATICAE."
div.p: " SORTES GRAMMATICAE."
Rev. L. J. T. Darwall Discovers Latin War-References.

Under the heading of " Sortes Gram- maticae," readers of the " Saturday. West- minster Gazette" have been discussing for the last week or two "how marvellously apt have been some of the passages recently quoted by our scholars in the public Press." One or two correspondents have thus been led to turn up their "own classical library, reli- giously preserved since 'Varsity days." Herein they have found quite a collection of ancient references remarkably applicable to the present war. " What store of wisdom and fortitude"—exclaims one epistolist—"can we draw in these favoured days, if we but choose, from the pure and deep cool wells of ancient Rome!"

. The Rev. L. J. T. Darwall, vicar of Walton (who is known to readers of the "Westmin- ster" as a skilled writer of classical verse) contributed the following to Saturday's issue of that periodical: "The old Eton grammar on which I was brought up would, I think, yield even more sates than the later Latin primer of your correspondents. sAs, for instance: (I).Descrip- tion of the Crown Prince: Qui natum haberem tali ingenio pneditum ("such as (lisposition," as ..laggie Tulliver said) ;-• (2) The plight of Belgium : Mihi nec seritur nec metitur; (3) German Kuhn'. : Nomine granimaticus,•re bar- barus; (4) The king's journey to the Front: Audito regem Doroberniam profieisci; (5) Regiment of Bantams: Perpusilli vocantur nani; (6) Germans trying to influence Amer- ican opinion: Hine spargere voces in vulgum ambiguas et %turret.° conscius arma. And the last sentence of the Syntax might be the Kaiser's own last word: (7) V:e miser° milli, quanta de spe deeidi.—There are plenty more I have ventured just to give these as a speci- men."
The translations of the above Latin quota- tions are:

(1) That I might have a son endowed with such genius (or disposition); (2) It is neither sown nor reaped (for me); (3) Polished in name, in reality unpolished (or barbarous); (4) It having been heard that the King is going to Dorobernia; (5) The very small ones are called dwarfs; (0 Conscious of scattering hence among the multitude lying words, and of provoking war; (7) Woe is me; how I have been deceived in my hopes

The integrity and honour of the French ladies is unimpeachable. When it is remembered that the Germans occupy twelve departments of France, and that the atrocities committed there have been even more terrible than in Belgium, because they could more easily be kept from the knowledge of the world, it must be recognised that the ladies are not lacking in material for their grim and horrifying task.
The pleats are stitched down -as far as, and sometimes a little below the knee, and there the pressing will be required. This design is also ,very suitable for the slim young girl.
Tailor-mades Lead.

Despite the war and its • attendant ills, Lon- don salons are; holding their usual exhibitions of spring fashions, but shorn of their wonted brilliance, these events have lost their chief attractions.. The changes brought about by the war are strikingly evident, in the few even- ing dresses, shown, and in the sombre note struck by every model. Pride of place has been unanimously accorded to tailor-mades, and next in order is the all-in-one day gown, which is frequently of . wool faille. This beautiful material will be worn until well on in the spring, and the lighter accessories consisting of material-muffs, and collarettes, go well with it. Men's suitings are to have a. vogue, more especially the striped cloths, for on account of the amount of khaki worn, tailors have acoumulated stocks of these goods, and are very wisely using them for women's hard-wear suits. Navy blue serge has lost none of its prestige, and is usually trimmed with wide silk braid in military style.

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.

The London Season. The theatres and fashionable restaurants in the Metropolis are doing remarkably well, in spite of the war, and their crowded doorways do not suggest that there is a scarcity of people in a position to spend money on amusement and entertaining. Possibly there will be more social diversion of a 'private and informal kind this year, because so many public events associated with the " London Season" have been aban- doned. There will be no University Boat Race, no fashionable cricket at Lords, no meetings of the Coaching Clubs, no Military Tournament, no river carnival at Henley, and no great balls given by the leading hostesses in Society. It is generally expected that May and June, when the "London season" in ordinary years is at its height, will synchronise with the climax of the war., when a determined effort will be made by the .Allied Armies in the West to thrust back the Germans from France and Belgium. The loss of life will, be awful, and preparations are being made in this country to receive an enor- mous number of wounded. The war has been so long at a deadlock in France and Belgium, that people are apt to lose sense of its seriousness, but it is to be feared that this will be brought home to us in the near future, and it will then be recognised that it will be no time for dancing, racing, frivolity, or other exhibitions of light- hearted gaiety. Economy in Fuel.
The high wiater price of coal will this reason probably be felt by many more markedly than for some years past, owing to a variety of causes. -

Asa means of assistance it may interest readers to know that in those places where wood blocks are employed for paving purposes the old pieces which are taken up during periods of renewal can, generally speaking, be purchased from the Corporation of the town in which they occur at the very reasonable price of about Os. per cart load. The blocks, being creosoted, burn well, and will be found of material assistance in using up the " slack " or dust -which, in More or less quantity, accom- panies all coal. A fire made up of this com- bination will keep in, without attention, for several hours. The small " hips"c. are exceed- ingly handy for starting a tire._ Altogether the use of these wood blocks will prove of considerable service and economy.— "Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

Split Pea Soup. Soak over-night one cup of dried split peas. In the morning put them on to boil in three pints qf fresh, cold water. Let them simmer until dissolved, adding enough water as it boils away to keep three pints of liquid in the kettle. Keep it well scraped from the sides of the kettle. When soft rub through a strainer, and put on to boil again. Add water, stock, milk or cream to make it of the required con- sistence, and stir into the soup while boiling, and just before taking up a smooth batter made of a tablespoonful of flour and three-quarters of a teacupful of cream, or made with water and half a tablespoonful of butter. Salt to taste. It may be varied by adding half a can of tomatoes before straining, or by boiling with the peas a small onion.

div.head: COMING OF SPPING.
div.p: THE COMING OF SPPING.
MY DEAR CHILDREN,-

Hurrah! The sun has condescended this week to shine •a little brighter and more often than of late. A splendid sign! DOC'S' it not herald the coming of Spring? Yes; presently everything will be happening—in the country- side—as described in the beautiful Spring song I give below.
The message of Spring is easily understood.

It is just this: " Wake up!" Everybody must "Put a move on "---if you understand what that means. The English Army understanaS it at any rate. It has been celebrating the coining of Spring by making an advance and vetting rid of ten thousand of the enemy. I understand it-4 am just arranging some very tine " corners " for you to read by and by. !And I hope you understand it ,too.
Your loving
UNCLE NED
