div.head: Sarah Bernhardt.
div.p: Sarah Bernhardt.

Sarah Bernhardt has shown great spirit and courage •in face of the calamity that has befallen her. It is said that during the terrible nine 'days of suspense, when her physical sufferings were intense, she Dever lost hope or patience. The leg was amputated above the knee, but the patient is already pro- nounced convalescent. There is no doubt that this wonderful actress has done more than anyone else to popularise the French language, literature and dramatic art, in the • ,inany- countries she has visited.

div.head: Modified Skirts.
div.p: Modified Skirts.

Some of the modified, new wide skirts are scarcely more than two yards round the ankle, but they suggest greater fullness. The appear- ance of width is due to gored side pieces, that are made to flare out slightly at the hem. The skirt appears to be quite straight, for it has panels in front and at the back, and these give it the perpendicular lines to Which everyone has grown accustomed. At the same time the shape is quite newt For those women who are above medium height, and slim in figure, the modified box-pleated design should have many charms; it is the most attractive of all the new models. There are, as a rule, six pleats, two of these are placed on each side, one in front, and the sixth at the back. This model also conserves the straight effect, but the pleats to be a success must be arranged as flat as possible, and as they show a tendency to get out of place, will require frequent pressing.-

Leek Soup. Put into two quarts of boiling water half a dozen parboiled potatoes, 4oz. of bread, 2oz. of dripping, and 21b. of sliced leek; boil for an hour, then add lb. of rice. Boil all together for another hour, and serve. This is a pleasant change, and is very inexpensive, besides being nourishing.

Celery Soup. ' Wash six good heads of celery thoroughly in salt and water. Peel two onions and cut them up small with the celery. Stew for two hours in some stock, with loz. of pearl barley and a small bunch of herbs. Before serving, season the soup with pepper and salt, and remove the herbs.

div.head: HERE AND THERE.
div.p: HERE AND THERE.
Made Sure.

A young ruan took a lady acquaintance to a steeplechase meeting and • she insisted on placing a bet on a,horse. The hOrse did worse than to come in last. He turned around and ran the other way. "Well, you lose your bet," said the man. " The horse you had your money on is wining the wrung way!" "It shows that a woman's instinct can't go wrong!" she answered triumphantly. " I backed him both ways!"
War Economies. The two servants met in the tram. "Does this awful war make much difference to you, Mary?'"
"The missus says we've got to economise. so we're to have margarine with meals in the kitchen." "Doesn't she have it. then?"
"Not her. She says it doesn't suit her diges- tion. But there's nothing wrong with her digestion. We know that. For as often/as not we send her up the margarine and have the butter ourselves."

div.head: Good Catch.
div.p: A Good Catch.

Some time ago a fearless young lady rider, when out with Lord Fitzhardinge's hounds in the country below Almondgbury, so renowned for its rhines—those great broad trenches brim- ming with water which have furnished a bath for many a Nimrod—went plump into one of them which she tried witl. more pluck than prudence. For a little while she seemed in some peril, when a young hunting farmer came to the rescue and gallantly drew her, dripping with water, out of danger The young lady's nerve, however, was proof against even such a ducking, for she was no sooner on terra firma than she said ,archly to her deliverer, "This is not hunting—it is fishing!" " Yes„ miss," was the reply, "I have done a little angling in my time, but it is not 'often one has. a chance of landing so large a fish." •

div.head: WHAT HE HAD LEARNT.
div.p: WHAT HE HAD LEARNT.

Proud Father: "Welcome back to the old farm, my boy! So you got through college all right?" Farmer's 'Son: "Yes, father." Proud Father: "Ye know I told ye to study up on chemistry and things so you'd know best what to do with different kinds of land. What do you think of that medder there, for instance?"
Farmer's Son (joyfully) : " Crikey! What a place for cricket!"
"LOVING THEM."

Here is a pretty little story of a poor child's gentle and loving nature In front of a shop stood a perambulator, in. which a baby was sleeping with a tiny puppy —Whose nose was nestling comfortably close to the baby's cheek. By the perambulator stood a little ragged girl, looking terribly thin and ill- kept, but very happy. Gently and tenderly she was stroking the sleepers. "Are you taking care of them?" asked a passer-by kindly. " No, ma'am," the little child answered with a 'beautiful smile; "I am only loving them." Only loving them! If we all showed ;such love to others there would be little quarrelling and selfishness among us.
THE GLADDEST TIME. I like it in the morning when The sun shines in across my bed And seems to kind of whisper then
" Get up, you little sleepy head." And just outside my window, where A limb sticks upward from a tree The sparrows often sit and stare And nod their heads and chirp at rue.

I like it in the evening when The sound all seem so fur away, And all the men go home again Who had to work so hard all day, For then toy muvver- always sings And dresses in her nicest gown. div.head: Sweated Khaki Women Weavers.
div.p: Sweated Khaki Women Weavers.

Men working on munitions of war, and in trades connected with the war, are earning exceptionally good wages. Not so the women, probably from their lack of organisation. In the North, the greater part of the khaki used .for the soldiers is. woven by women and girls, and others make the uniforms; men being employed only in the cutting out. Many women are at the present moment greatly overworked, but they show their patriotism by not complaining, or striking. For weaving a piece of khaki sixty yards in length, some employers give eight shillings and sixpence, a high wage; for many women do the same work for three shillings and fourpence. If Govern- ment fixed the price to be paid, the workers as well as the contractors, sweating would not be possible.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information in Popular Language.
Alcohol and the Nervous System.

When alcohol is taken into the body, there is no tissue that escapes its baneful influence: The more highly organised the tissue, the more susceptible it is to any poisonous agent. There- fore for the delicate cells of the nervous system alcohol has a special predilection. The terrible effects of alcohol upon the nervous system are %strikingly apparent in the brain degeneracy It produces, as evidenced by in- sanity. Statistics gleaned from all Parts of the world-show positively that at least fifty per cent of all insanity is due to alcohol.—George Thomason, M.D.,. L.R.C.P., in March "Good Health."

div.head: PleuriLy.
div.p: PleuriLy.

Pleurisy means inflammation of the pleura or lining of the lungs; it is a common form of chest complaint, and may be acute or chronic. It generally arises from exposure to cold, hence is prevalent during told weather. There are two kinds, " dry pleurisy " and " pleurisy with effusion." In the case of dry pleurisy, says a writer in " Farm and Home,'! which is on the whole the milder form, the chief sign is a sharp pain in the side vhen breathing. Fever May or may not be present, the breathing is more rapid and of a catching character, and there is a short, dry ,cough. .This form of pleurisy may be limited to a patch of the lung, or may extend over the greater part of one or both sides.- In general with treatment it goes in a short time, and complete recovery takes place. Pleurisy with effusion is more severe than the above, though the symptoms at first are lunch the same, the pain abating as the effusion takes place. The patient at first lies on the sound side, but as the disease progresses he finds more comfort on the back or affected side; sometimes he cannot even lie down, and must be propped up. In most cases the recovery is complete. The treatment varies according to the severity of the attack. The pain is relieved by poultices or fomentations though many doctors now use icebags to the side, and this generally soothes the acute pain. The patient must remain in an even temperature and take light, nourishing food. In the case of pleurisy with effusion blistering and 'the use of saline purgatives are often useful in diminishing the fluid. Should all else' fail, what is termed aspiration is performed, that is draining away the floid•by means of u needle. To bring about convalescence requires care' and patience, and if a .second attack it would be wise to be examined by the_ doCtor periodically in order to make sure that phthisis 'does not develop in the lung.
A SPRING SONG. (By JOIIN LEA-)

Down the lane are cowslips growing; In the woods the thrushes sing; O'er the fields the soft winds blowing, Calls us out to greet the Spring. Such a gust is surely welcome! Open wide the garden gate, And come with me By lane and lea To welcome her in royal state.

See from yonder bed of nettles Comes a fly on gauzy wing; Now he soars and now he settles, Half asleep, to meet the Spring. Tender leaves along the hedgerow Peep abroad in doubt and fear, As though to cry To passers-by .`"Oh, is the Springtime really here?"

Sunshine on the green fields lying Spreads a carpet for our feet;. Zephyrs down the valley sighing Bring a perfume rich and sweet; Sedges, by the river waving, Murmur "No more winter (bear !" And all around Each sight and sound Cries "Yes! the Spring is really here!"

div.head: CURIOUS ARAB CUSTOMS.
div.p: CURIOUS ARAB CUSTOMS.

An Arab on entering a house removes his shoes, but not his hat. lie mounts his horse upon. the right side, while his wife milks the cow on the left side. In writing a letter he puts nearly all his complimei“:s on the outsnb. his head In tiq be wrapped up Ivarm, e yen in slim- mer, while•his feet May well eniniga 12,9 nuked in winter. Every article. of e filch is liquid he weighs, but he measures wheat, bar- ley, and a few other articles. 11. reads and writes from right to left.

lie eats scarcely anything for breakfast, about as much for dinner, but, after the work of the day is done, he sits down to a hot meal swim- ming in oil, or in boiled butter. Ilk sons eat with him, but the females of his' house wait till his lordship is done. He rides a donkey when travelling, his wife walking behind. lie laughsout the idea of walking in the street with his wife, or. of ever vaeating his seat for a woman. • lie knows no .use for chairs, tables, knives, forks, or even gpoons,PPS they are wooden ones. Bedsteads, bureaus, and fire- places are also wooden as a rule.

div.head: HOW GERMANY HAS ESCAPED THE FUEL
div.p: HOW GERMANY HAS ESCAPED THE FUEL
FAMINE.

Some extremely interesting particulars . are given in .a recent issue of a motoriiitg journal regarding the manner in which Germany has escaped the predicted fuel famine. The fact of the matter is that Germany is not ,now using' ,—outside the army and navy—either petrel or benzole for running .any 'motor Vehicles; yet there are now ample quantities of; fuel throughout the Empire, and taxi-cabs, 'buses, and commercial vehicles are everywhere in operation again. Germany has been and is still getting petrol. For example, petrol f:nom 'Roumania) still reaches her, and 0 VVI• sea; supplies get into the country somehow., And it is also true that flu' home production of benzole has been greatly increased, but the great bulk of it is, as is the case with the petrol, reserved for military . purposes. Some months ago when the °fuel position becapie acute, it would appear that the whole cheniial skill of Germany was organised to discover a substitute for petrol—one that, could be pre- pared in plentiful quantities friim material in the country. Now this substitute has been :found, and it is in general use. It gives With- in a fraction the same power and consumption as petrol, viz.:. five-sixths, and does not require any alteration • of the engine or carburetter. All that has been done is to fit an exhaust heat- ing jacket to each carburetter. The petrol substitute Germany is using contains 80 per cent. alcohol, 20 per cent. benzoic?, and an addition of about 200 grammes per gallon of naphthalene, a solid hydrocarbon; of which they have great quantities in their chemical works. This is benzole; is an easily soluble hydrocarbon, and presumably it adds greatly to the calorific value of the mixture. • .The alcohol alone has a low ealorific value: one therefore the benzole and naphthalene are added partly as enrichers. The form of alcohol that Germany is Using, it muy be pre- sumed, is potato spirit. The benzole gets over the' starting difficulty resulting frOM the 'low vapour pressure of alcohol. Prom the point of view of the future of efficient and cheap petrol substitutes, this is all very interesting.

div.head: FIELD OF SPORT.
div.p: FIELD OF SPORT.
NO CUP FOR WARRINGTON.
The Unexpected Happens and Salford Clear Off Old Scores.

div.head: HOME TEAM'S FEEBLE DISPLAY.
div.p: HOME TEAM'S FEEBLE DISPLAY.
Notes by " Centre."

"It is the unexpected that always happens" said the old phrase-maker, and once again has he been justified, for the result of Saturday's cllp-tie was anything but what was anticipated. Here were Warrington face to face with the most momentous match of the season, and having as their opponents a club they had already " licked " three times this winter. What more natural than to expect that they 'would "(10 it on" their opponents upon this, tile fourth time of asking? But they did not; nor, indeed, did they ever look a bit like loing it from the moment the ball was kicked Off, Their recent "return to form" was con- Kllicuous by its absence; they seemed quite in- capable of doing the right thing at the right moment, and the tables were completely and crushingly turned upon them. True, Salford showed a degree of skill and determination that they had not before evinced at Wilderspool this season, but Warrington, at their best, should have. been capable of holding them, even if not of beating them. But, unaccountably, the home tenth's forth crumpled clean up, and, if ever a thirteen were whipped all along the line, they were that thirteen.

had been more than wiped out. Thomas, Rees and Woods indulged in a fine passing movement, which finished up with a most determined on- slaught on the Warrington line. Scrum fol- lowed scrum with increasing violence right on the line, and do what Warrington would they could not get away. At last May, taking advan- tage of a first-class opportunity, managed to score a clever try. And that was how the score stood when the referee's whistle signalled the change over—Salford's unconverted try to War- rington's penalty goal. In the second half Salford's superiority, already plain • enough to see, became more marked still, and soon after the restart Mesley placed his side further ahead, dashing over at the corner. A little later a raid on the home goal led to John scoring, after a smart clearance by Young, whilst, about a minute from the end, Mesley again nipped over the line, the result being that when time was called the score-board told the following doleful tale: Salford, 1 goal 3 tries (11 points); Warrington, 1 goal (2 points).
WARRINGTON'S INEFFECTIVE EFFORTS.

Ineffectiveness dogged the whole of War- rington's play. Even the usually effective Jolley was at times painfully ineffective, whilst the whole of his play was singularly mediocre by comparison with what his brilliant displays of the past have led us to expect of him% The home forwards worked hard, true enough, but their work; too, was . ineffectual, lacking com- bination, and containing but little that was brilliant or enterprising. Bombardier Chesters, who tby the way was accorded quite an ovation when he took the field, by no means repeated the fine display which he gave sWhen he was last able to don the Wilderspool colours. Daintith and Young never worked with such perfect lack of understanding, and the_three-quarters rarely did the right thing a`t the right moment. Tranter began badly and did not seem able to get over his initial mis- takes, and Bradshaw was anything but a brilliant success, whilst Taberner also *as decidedly below par. Brookes was about the one man in the team who really played up to expectations, and to his fine defensive work the fact that, the adverse total was not a bigger one is largely due. The victors were, perhaps, best served by Mesley and Callender, the former being full of dash, and "as tricky as they make 'em." The Salford Captain was also always in the picture, and John and May were a useful and resourceful pair of halves, infinitely better than their vis-a-vis. Of the forward, pees and 4Woods were undoubtedly the pick, but the Whole sextette worked hard and effectively: Launce was not brilliant at full-back, but he never really let his team down. On the day's play, undoubtedly the best team won.

It should be said that Warrington were handicapped for the greater part of the second half through the absence of Cox, who was ordered off by the referee for alleged rough play, a decision which was not accepted quietly by the spectators.

div.head: CROWD OF OVER SIX THOUSAND.
div.p: A CROWD OF OVER SIX THOUSAND.

A record "gate" -had assembled to gloat over the fourth and final discomfiture of Salford, but, after the first few minutes, there was not a gloat left in them, and it was a saddened and silent crowd that melted away when the final whistle blew; indeed, hundreds did not wait that long. No fewer than 6,200 persons paid for admission at the turnstiles, the receipts being about £l6O ---`f an' werry nice an' all," as Sam Weller would BuY. Mainly, Salford's superiority rested with their forwards; they were the trickier and the Speedier pack, and they -prevailed in most of the seruniming work, of which there was an un- usually large amount, especially just before Sal- ford 'scored their opening try and towards the end of the game. Then Salford's front-rankers were better supported by their rear lines than. Were the Warrington vanguard; indeed, the pro- uounced feebleness of the Warrington centres INs one of the chiefest contributor L factors to the Weaste men's decisive victory. Warrington °Defied with a stiffish and useful breeze in their favour, and they were the first to become dan- gerous, but the sting was soon extracted from their attacks, and for pretty nearly sixty out of the eighty minutes during which the game lasted they were defenders rather than attackers.

WARRINGTON "DRAW FIRST BLOOD." Somehow but little confidence was instilled into the crowd ,by reason of the fact that the first points fell to Warrington, and the applause which greeted them had not about it that ring of exultation which denotes the certainty of vic- tory-to-come. The points came from a penalty 4warded against the Visitors for a patent ,in- fringement. of the rules, and Jolley; taking the. kick, landed the ball straight between the up- Vghts in grand style. The set-back seemed only spur the Salford men on to greater efforts, hd very soon afterwards the adverse balance

div.head: NOW THE, , SPORTSMEN!
div.p: NOW THE, , SPORTSMEN!
Kitchener Still Wants " More Men."
AND " IT'S UP TO YOU!"

At the close of Saturday's big cup-tie at Wilderspool, after victors and vanquished had been cheered off the field, a brief recruiting meeting was held, and it was strikingly notice- able that by comparison with the thousands who had watched the mimic battle for supre- macy on the playing pitch, the number who stayed behind to listen to the call of King and country was painfully small. But, if the bulk of the huge pleasuring crowd did not, this small section of it contained men of the right spirit, for hardly had the last note of the call for more men for the war died away before one lusty young fellow stepped ~ forward, amid cheers, with a cheery "Well, here's for Num- ber 1., sir," whilst others, animated' by the true British spirit, trod on his heels in their anxiety to hand in their names, what-time the Band of the South Lancashire (P.W.V.) Regiment played the National Anthem.

div.head: MORE WILL HAVE TO JOIN!
div.p: MORE WILL HAVE TO JOIN!

The. meeting was first addressed by Councillor OssonNE (the president of the club), who, after congratulating the Salford team on their suc- cess, began with the blunt, practical statement, "Men, more of you will have to join the Forces !" He went on to tell what the players had done Already, he said, the Northern Union had sent a hundred and ten teams of players to swell the no-longer "thin, red line," Yes, 1,410 players had doffed the jersey and joined the khaki. There was one club—all honour be to it !—that had contributed all its players—they had joined masse. (Cheers.) As to the Warrington Club. no fewer than 25 players had enlisted, together with soine hundreds of spectators. The appeal that afternoon', was beipg more particii- larly made on behalf of the Artillery which Lord Derby was raising, and which was to have its Warrington section, to complete which 35 men were that day required. Surely it was not expecting too much to get 35 men out of such a crowd as had gathered to see the play that afternoon! Join at once and show how much you appreciate the services of our re- spected neighbour, Colonel Lyon. If Not Voluntary Then - -

If the young men did not come forward vol- untarily a certain amount of compulsion would have to be put upon them, for men must be got. "Come along, men !" concluded the sportsman-councillor, "surely there are eligible men among you sufficiently 'sporting' to offer their services without being compelled?" "Here's one," remarked a member of the 'crowd, "but they won't have me because I have got no teeth !"
A QUESTION-ANSWER WANTED!

Colonel LYON, of Appleton, who is to com- mand a section of the new artillery brigade, invited the crowd to ask themselves: "How long is the war to last?" and said that the answer, to an extent, was in their own hands for the war could only be finished when the country and her Allies bad got suffici:mt men to end it. Like the blunt, gallant soldier he is, the Colonel soon got to the point and he dii not mince words about it. Lord Kitchener.'

he said, "has told you that we have to be pre- pared for a three-year war. At tll3 rate we have been going on these last seven months, it looks more like lasting ten years. But, assum- ing it is only going to last three years, we want more men, and. still more men, and some of you chaps must be amongst those men, so make up your minds straightaway and come and play the man's part."

div.head: Every Able-bodied Man May Have To Go.
div.p: Every Able-bodied Man May Have To Go.

Many were the men who had already been sent, but another half-million were immedi- ately required and next year another Million would be wanted, and they wourd have to be forthcoming; indeed, if the war went on longer than was anticipated, it would be a case of every able-bodied man in the country having to go, and that was all there was about it! This country was used to volunteers; it did not understand pressed men. All the gallant men at present at the Front were volunteers; they were not compelled .to give their _very, very valuable seivices and they were better men in consequence. "We don't want conscripts!" thundered the Colonel, amid applause, "We want volunteers—and we shall get them." "Want 'em :with teeth, don't you sir?" queried the previous interrupter. "With teeth!" replied the Colonel. "There are plenty of young fellows with teeth, anci they'll get all the sharper for practice on bully- beef and biscuit. (Laughter and applause.) 0

div.head: Last Appeal for Volunteers.
div.p: The Last Appeal for Volunteers.

"We have now arrived at the time when the last appeal ill be made for voluntary service; this is one of the last chances you will have of doing what we hope you will do now." The Colonel went on to speak of the value of artillery in the field emphasising the support and, consequently, the courage it was able to give the infantry and said that, the more men this country had behind the guns, the easier was the victory for the men who shouldered the rifles. Three otheK towns were raising batteries in this new artillery brigade—Widnes, Wigan and Ashton-in-Makerfield—and surely Warrington was not going to be behind those places! (A Voice: "Not likely; but they won't have men without teeth!")

div.head: CLUB'S CONTRIBUTION.
div.p: THE CLUB'S CONTRIBUTION.

The MAxon. (Alderman Peter Peacock), who, .wearing his chain of office, was accorded a flattering reception, said that if all the young men in Warrington who could enlist would enlist, many valuable lives would be saved. One man in August last was worth six men to-day, and one man to-day would be worth three or four men a few months hence. Out of 80 playing members, the Warrington Club had sent twenty-five into the ranks, and if the young men—the spectators—of Warrington had responded in the same proportion War- rington would have had cause to be prouder of them. "We ought to get all the young men to go !" said his. Worship. "We ought to make them go, even if we do it by ' kidding ' them into it, or worrying them into it. Every fit young man has a duty to do to-day and he must do it, or !" Surely Warrington could complete a battery in the new artillery brigade! If the young men did not volunteer then indeed, had the time come when con-
scription—with all that about. it that was so distasteful to the English mind—would have to be enforced.
TO MEN WHO LOVE KING AND COUNTRY.

Alderman TINNION also addressed a few words to "men who love their King and country." He began with a compliment to Cglonel Lyon. "I admire the Man who has addressed you," he said, "he's a soldier, every inch of him; one of the men that England may well be proud of. And he asks you, his fellow men, to rally round him. I know what your answer will be !" (Applause, and a Voice: "Here's one, sir!") The greatest need the country had, tolday, continued the Alderman, was artillery- men, and now was Warrington's opportunity to get together a battery composed of War- ringtonians only. This war was a more serious thing than many of them appeared .to think, and if it had not been for their splendid Navy the people in this quiet country would have tasted some of the worst hor,rors of war. The " Terriers " Doing Splendidly. "The Warrington Territorials," the speaker concluded, "are doing splendidly—(loud and prolonged applause)—but they cannot give of their best unless we get this 'battery and other ,batteries of artillery to support them. That's (why I appeal to you- to do your duty and do it now! I say that it is a disgrace to think that we have over 2,000,000 Of young men capable of 'bearing aims who are not yet doing so. This war is' not half over, and it will never be ov'er until every young man in the country realises that it is his duty to do his share. Come on, young' men, and do all you can for your
(Continued in preceding column.)

div.head: POSITION AND PROSPECTS OF THE LEADING CLUBS.
div.p: POSITION AND PROSPECTS OF THE LEADING CLUBS.
Notes by " Linesman."

On Saturday there was one match played in the Warrington and District League tourna- ment, and Fairfield *United made the journey to Newton to meet the Congregationalists with a much depleted team, Hunter, Lewis and Tay- lor being absent. NOt much can be said of the play because of its scrappy nature. Good play was lacking by both teams. Fouls and argu- ments between players were numerous, and this interfered with the game generally. The.result w4s a drawn game, each team scoring twice.

As there are now only six Saturdays remain- ing on which to fulfil the remaining fixtures for the present season, the race for the champion- ship of the League, coupled with the semi-final and final ties for the " Starkey " Cup, does not allow for any more vacant dates, especially ,amongst the five top clubs, and peilhaps it will be interesting to the readers of these columns and the supporters of the clUbs to give a list of the remaining fixtures to be played : Fairfield United, with 25 points, have six matches to play as follows :—Home: EarleStown St, John's Mission, Hollins Green, Longford United and St. Barnabas'. Away: Earlestown St. John's Mission and St. Barnabas'.

Orford White Star, with 25 points, have six matches to play as follows :—Home: Warrington Central; Longford United and Grappenhall. Away: Earlestown Y.M.C.A., Warrington Cen- tral and Grappenhall. The Earlestown St. John's Mission; with 22 Points, have six matches to play as follows : Home: Fairfield United, Warrington Central and Grappenhall. Away: Fairfield -United, St. Barnabas' and Grappenhall. The Longford United, with 20 points, have seven matches to play, as follows :—Home: Elm- wood Congregationalists, Newton Congregation- alists and Grappenhall. Away: Newton Con- gregationalists, Earlestown Y.M.C.A., Orford White Star and Fairfield United.

St. Barnabas'„with 18 points, have six matches to play as follows :—Home: Paddington, Earles- town St. John's Mission, Fairfield United, War- rington Central and Grappenhall. Away: Fair- field United.

Arising out of the protest by the Earlestown Mission against the referee awarding a goal to the Orford White Star team, which was Iniought by the former club before the Liverpool Associa- tion Committee, the latter upheld the decision of the Warrington League Committee, by accept- ing the referee's decision as final. With re- spect to the Mission players leaving the field of play before the close of the game and without the referee's permission, the Liverpool Com- mittee suspended three of the Mission players for fourteen dais, dating from March .15th.

The. Hon. SecretarY of the League has. re- ceived a communication from the Secretary of the Liverpool- Association upholding the deci- sion of the League Committee not to allow the Walton Club to take part in the " Starkey " Cup Competition. •

Mr. F. Andrews, hon. sec. of the Walton Club, writes to say that his club was not dis- qualified through having broken the iules of the competition, but owing to a special clause being added after Walton had joined and made progress in the competition. Entries for the competition were' desired and Walton entered and paid entrance fee, 2s. 6d. The list of players was duly sent in; and Walton got a bye in the first round. For the second round the Walton representative was told that Walton must become affiliated with the Cheshire Association and again the club com- plied; and the draw for the second round wa Walton v. Earlestown Y.M.C.A. The latter club gave Walton a walk over. Walton having thus reached the semi-final, were told that the competition rules had only just been returned from the Liverpool Association .with a clause added that the " Starkey " Cup, com- petition was to be open only to Warrington and District 'League Clubs. "I considef,'" says Mr. Andrews, "that Ur rules they started with should hold good to the end."

The Great Sankey team are making a bold bid for the championship of the Widnes and District Alliance, and to-day they have a stiff task on hand, when they will oppose the Calder and Mersey Lads on the Calder ground. Should the Great Sankey Lads succeed in annexing both points there is every proba- bility they will retain the chief honours of the Alliance.

In the North Cheshire League the fight for second position is very keen., and McKennal's are due to visit Stockton Heath this afternoon. Should the "Heathens" prove successful their prospects will be very good for obtaining the medals for runners-up.

tracks for the visitors' goal, Scott clearing at the critical moment. Long secured the ball and raced along on the right, and centred at the proper moment. Millward availed himself of the opportunity thus offered, and scored for the United with a splendid shot. Following this the home team had the best of the exchanges, and after several shots had been cleared, the Congregationalists equalised from a scrimmage in the visitors' goal. From the centre kick the Congregationalists still continued to have the best of the game, and showed gookcombination, Potter saving well on many occasions. At the end of twenty-five minutes' play the Congrega- tionalists succeeded in gaining the lead. The visitors retaliated. After a good run on the wing by Boscow, the latter's final effort was very weak and easily cleared. Half-time: New- ton Congregationalists, 2 goals; Fairfield United, 1 goal.

The visitors, now having the aid of the wind, were seen to better advantage, and Long sent in a splendid- shot, but the home goalkeeiier tipped the ball over the bar. This was not im- proved upon, and following 'even play in mid- field the visitors attacked strongly, and after several shots at close quarters the ball was sent through and the scores made equal. The Con- gregationalists played desperately to gain the lead, but could not beat the' visitors' defence. Towards the close of the game play was inclined to be of the rough element, but at the call of time the result was :. newton Congregational- ists, 2 goals; Fairfield United, 2 goals.

div.head: " STARKEY " CUP COMPETITION. Re-played Tie. EARLESTOWN MISSION v. PADDINGTON.
div.p: " STARKEY " CUP COMPETITION. Re-played Tie. EARLESTOWN MISSION v. PADDINGTON.
After having played a drawn game, the above tams again opposed each other on the ground of the former.

Mission: H. Wallas; Winders and A. Eaton; Alldridge, F. Eaton and Theobald; W. Wallas, Jones, Bothwell, Waywell arid Sherlock. Paddington: Harrison; Marsh and Holmes; Griffiths, Taylor and Pritchard; Garnett, Hol- croft, Wrench, Summers and Darbyshire. Referee, B. Howell.

The visitors won the toss and Rothwell set the ball in motion and sent a wide pass out to Sher- lock, who raced towards the visitors' goal, when Holmes intervened and cleared well up the field. Wrench, securing the leather, the visitors in- vaded the, home quarters, and from a well- judged pass,. Garnett received and opened the score for th,e visitors, after three minutes' play. Following this reverse the home forwards were aggressive, but Taylor relieved finely. The home team returned to the attack, Theobald feeding his forwards well, and from a combined movement by the home forwards the ball was sent past Harrison, and the, scores equalised. From the centre kick Wrench was prominent with good passes to Garnett, but the home llnlf- back line were playing keenly and succeeded in breaking up the attempt of the visitors. Eventually the ball was transferred to the visit- ors' end, and the home team gained the lead, Jones doing the needful. Fa a while the home team kept the, yisitors on the defensive, and gained several fruitless corner kicks, Holmes and Marsh defending finely. Harrison , made several fine saves, but at length Rothwell got through, and passing to Waywell, the latter beat Harrison and °registered the third goal. Half- time: Mission, 3 goals ) Paddington, 1 goal. The visitors opened the second portion strongly, but were met by a pair of stout defenders in Winders and A. Eaton, and had to retire to mid-field, where the game was evenly and keenly contested. Unfortunately, Summers, of the visitors, was heavily charged by Winders and had to retire. Owing to their strength being reduced the visitors adopted the one-back game, and this led .to many free kicks for offsite, but at length Rothwell got through and scored an easy goal. From now to the close of play several unpleasant incidents occurred, ~which spoilt the game. Result: Earlestown Mission, 4 goals; Paddington, 1 goal.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCHES.
ELMWOOD-AVENUE CONGREGATIONAL- ISTS MARRIED v. SINGLE.

Owing to the Congregationalists having no League fixture, a match was arranged between the Married and Single members of the club, the following players taking part:— Married: Ashton; Holt and Patterson; Hazel- dine, Finch and Dutton; Kendrick, J. Phoenix, sen., Jackson, Brown and Wright. Single: Hunt; Joe Phoenix and Mellor; Gib- son, W. Ashton and Clayton; E. Kendrick, W. Phcenix, Jim Phoenix, Wells and Littlewood. Referee, Mr. J. Garfitt.

The Married players had choice of ends, and defended the top goal, and the game opened with a rush by the Single, Wells and Little- wood leading the attack, and this was repulsed by bolt. Following even exchanges in mid- field the Single's returned to the attack and T. Kendrick scored after ten minutes' play. After, this reverse the Married applied pres- sure and Hazeldine was prominent with long shots and a good effort to break through' lie passed on to Dutton. who equalised. Patterson gave away a penalty kick, but Wells failed to convert. Half-time: One goal each. Upon resuming play was evenly contested for a time, and then the strenuousness of the game began to tell on the Married players, and the Single had much their own way; and goals were scored by Kendrick, Wells, W. Phcenix and W. Ashton. Final score: Single, 5 goals; Married, 1 goal.

div.head: NOM II CHESHIRE LEAGUE.
div.p: NOM II CHESHIRE LEAGUE.
Second Division.
BROADHEATH LADS v. STOCKTON HEATH

The above teams met on Saturday at Broad- heath. The home team were not able to put their best eleven into the field, and the visitors were short of the gervices of Hooper, their goalkeeper. The visitors won the toss and the home team kicked off, and were soon aggres- sive, Humbled kicking into touch. Then Nor- ton gave a nice pass to Cook and the-latter called upon Rylance to clear. Marsh securing, he got past the backs and then shot straight into the goalkeeper's hands. Cook was again dangerous, when Chesters nipped in and cleared, and a few minutes later the visitors got to close quarters with the home defence and Bentley shot wide. At the visitors' end How- ard sent in a good shot, which Rylance put over the bar. The corner-kick was cleared, and Bentley, securing the ball, beat the oppos- ing backs and scored an easy goal. Encouraged by this success, the visitors played up strongly, but the home backs defended well. Good play by Lloyd and Marsh on the visitors' right fol- lowed, and the former increased their lead. As. the interval was approaching the home team retaliated and attacked .in determined fashion. • Howard reduced the arrears. Half- time: Stockton Heath, 2 goals; Broadheath, 1 goal.

In the second portion the visitors had the wind in their favour, but for a while play was of the quiet order. The home team livened up a little and. paid a visit to the Stockton Heath goal, but Rylance cleared and the visiting for- wards raced to the opposite end and were awarded a penalty kick. Bentley missed, and shortly after West, with a good opening, shot very wide of the uprights. The home team made several raids on the visitors' goal, but the backs proved equal to the occasion and each side gained corner-kicks, which proved futile Towards the close the visitors attacked again, and Bentley scored the third goal. The closing stages were very tame. • Result : Stockton heath,, 3 goals; Broadheath Lads, 1 goal.

(Dedicated to the Stay-at-Home Rangers.)
All the brave boys under canvas are sleeping, All of them pressing to march with the van, Far from the home where their sweethearts are weeping; What are you waiting for, sweet little man?
You with the terrible warlike moustaches, Fit for a colonel or chief of a clan; You with the waist made for sword-belts and , sashes, Whe're are your shoulder-straps, sweet little man?
Have we a nation to save? In the first place Saving ourselves is the sensible plan,— Surely the spot where there's shooting's the worst place Where I can stand; says the sweet little man.
When the brown soldiers conic back from the borders, - How will he look while his features they . scan? How will be feel when he gets marching orders, Sigried .by his lady-love, sweet little man?
0. W. HOLMES.

In ,Massachusetts 50 Years ago what we call a " nut, " they called a "sweet little man." During • the , Civil - War some .of these smart youths like ours Went gladly to the Front— some ,again lagged behind. Then the Poet, Oliver Wendell Ifolnies, asked them the . above pointed questions—questions which some of our young men . who are still civilians must also face and answer.

div.head: "HEAVY BAPTISM OF FIRE."
div.p: "HEAVY BAPTISM OF FIRE."
Private Leonard Gough Writes of His Experiences.

Private Leonard Gough, another of War- rington's gallant Territorials, has written a couple of interesting letters to his parents, who reside at 19, Mill-lane. lie _is attached to A Company (No. 1 Platoon), and he has played his part in the recent fighting. Helped to Remove the " Casualties." Writing, under date March 2nd, he says "I have been into the trenches and in the firing, and I am very sorry to say that we have had one killed and four wounded out of our little lot, so far. It was my duty to assist in the removal of the "casualties." My word, it was an experience! Wehad a heavy baptism of fire . . . . and are expecting to leave the trenches in a day or two for a rest. Up to the present our Arthur has not come up here. but I do not suppose it will be long before he does. Since we have been here we have had fairly decent weather, and that has made things easier for us all. . . . To-day I had a letter that I sent to our Arthur, last October, returned to me, it being stated that he could not be found, but the authorities state that he has not been reported a casualty, so that is good news. Comforts That Are Required.

• • . • When I went into the trenches I was with our Albert's chum; a man who was with him in India. . . . If you send me anything at any time, do not send clothing, but send tea, cocoa, sugar, sweets, or anything in that line. We get plenty of shirts, &c., and also tobacco and cigarettes Every night you are in my thoughts, and I hope God will . . . . give me strength to fight bravely in this great war and to do what is set out for me, with a stout heart. May we soon all be together once more!"
Resting After The Fight.

In a letter written five days later—viz.: on March 7th—the plucky " Terrier " says "We are at present at our camp, having a few days' rest after our turn in the trenches. We returned from the firing line last Thursday, after a spell of six days. Arthur and I are together again, and I expect that next time we go up he will be with us. We are both 'alive and kicking,' and are feeling 'in the pink.' An Unforgettable Experience.

"My first time in the trenches was an ex- perience I shall never forget, and bringing the wounded and the dead from the trenches under heavy fire is exciting, I can tell you! One day we were shelled out, and I felt rather queer. Of course, towards the end of our stay in the trenches, I got used to it, and the next time I go to 'carry on I shall treat it just as if I wer4 going to work. As you will have read is your papers, our boys gave a good account, of themselves the first time they were under fire, and they will continue to do so in the future. . I have had the pleasure of seeing the . . . Prince of Wales, who was walking through this place last Friday."

div.head: FOOTBALL BEHIND THE FIRING
div.p: FOOTBALL BEHIND THE FIRING
LINE.
Warrinwon " Terriers" Win A Couple Of Exciting Matches.

Among the gallant lads employed by the St. llelens Cable and Rubber Company who have gone to the Front with the Warrington Terri- torials is Pte. Joseph Bond, son of Mr. and Mrs. Fredk. Bond, of 5, Worrall's-row. When the call for men came he was among the first of the local "Terriers" to volunteer for active ser- vice, and he proceeded to the South of England for his war training. Pte. Bond is well known in local Association football circles, having played in goal for the Sankey Club on numerous occasions.

div.head: Three Days and Nights in the Trenches.
div.p: Three Days and Nights in the Trenches.

In the course of a letter, dated March 13, to Mr. W. Watson, of the Cable Company, he writes that he is in the best of health, and adds: "I suppose you know that we have been in the trenches for a period of six days. When I say we,' I 'mean the Battalion have, for we went in in two lots, each lot remaining in the trenches three days and three nights. My lot had it lively journey going down and coming back, as we were under shell and rifle fire the whole of the way, added to which we were up to our knees in mud. Talk about perspiring. Why, that march was worse than work! Although the going was both dangerous and hard, we could not help laughing at each other floundering about to keep our feet. . . . Almost As Safe As Being At Home.

"Once we got in the trenches- it was almost as safe as being at home. At the moment of writ- ing we are in what we call a rest camp, and whilst we have been here we have played two football matches. What's more the Warrington Terriers' won them both—the first by three goals to one, and the second by two goals to one. Our boys played like trumps . . . and they relished the game. I may add that I was

goalkeeper for our side. . . . I should be pleased to hear from any of the workpeople, for it puts new heart into one to know that he is not forgotten by those who knew him at home. Tell all my old workmates that I wish them, one and all, the best of luck, and that I am living in hopes of seeing them all again before long."

div.head: WARRINGTON " TERRIER'S "
div.p: WARRINGTON " TERRIER'S "
PROPHECY.
"War 'Ol ill Re Over By July." He Says.

"We .are right amongst it here," writes Lance-Corporal Percy Ford, of C Company of the 4th South Lancashires (the Warrington Territorial Battalion), to Mr. Watson, of the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Company, by whom he was employed up to the time when he offered his services to his country.

div.head: Five Hours Under Rifle Fire.
div.p: Five Hours Under Rifle Fire.
His letter is dated Thursday of last week, and, after making the announcement quoted above, he continues: •

"We have had a good breaking in, as 'at the first time of asking,' we were under rifle fire for over five hours. The weather here is awful; in fact, We are up to the eyes in mud. The Ger- mans have fairly made a mess of things round here, every house having been ransacked. But we are paying them back! As you will notice, I have had the luck to be made a lance-cor- poral, so you will guess that I am 'on the job.' . . . We are naturally, not given much liberty here. We are only allowed out from 4 till 8, so we have not much time to 'play the game.' Here is a good tip: 'The war will be over by July.'"

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELDS BATTLE-CRY. SilONl Them What Warrington Lads Can Do!"
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELDS BATTLE-CRY. SilONl Them What Warrington Lads Can Do!"

Writing to his parents, who live at 16, Leonard-street, Private IL Glover, of D Com- pany. 4th South Lancashire Regiment, gives a thrilling description of a visit .to the firing line, for the purpose of digging trenches. After warning his 'parents "not to believe any rumours that are going about in'Warrington at present that we have been in action and have got cut up," the gallant Private says: "On Friday we had a lively job. We had to go dig- ging trenches behind our firing line.

div.head: Then the " Fun " Started.
div.p: Then the " Fun " Started.

"We had to walk about four miles before we got there, but when we got into rifle range. the 'fun' started. The Germans throw what we call star-lights.' and they light up all the place. It is a fine sight. If you have time you have to drop flat on to the ground. About half an hour after we left the town we had to walk in single file every now and then, and then one of these lights would go up. We would then have to drop flat, get up, start running, and get down again. It took us nearly two hours to go about a mile. We got in a narrow lane, and the bullets were coming thick over our heads.

div.head: Sheltered in a Ditch.
div.p: Sheltered in a Ditch.

"We had to get in a ditch, until there was a chance to make another dash. We left the road, and rushed across a big field. There was some mud about, but for 300 yards we walked on boards, or, rather, I should say, nearly crawled on them. We were 'two-double' all the time. We then left the boards, and had to make a dash behind our reserve trenches, up to our knees in mud and water. Then we were led out to where we had to dig the trenches. Bullets "Coming Like Bees."

"The bullets were coming over us like bees. Major Crosfield came along and shouted 'Come along, lads, show them what Warrington lads can do.' For half an hour we had to work like - to get a cover from the bullets. I worked like one possessed. My hands are sore with dig- ging. We were at it for six hours. We had three wounded and one killed-. There was a barn in front of us, and the bullets seemed to be concentrated on it. When we had nearly got the trenches finished, I had a narrow•escape.

div.head: Close Call.
div.p: A Close Call.

"I was sitting talking to a chap opposite me. when a bullet came flying over his head, and saw him jump down quick. As luck would have it / jumped down, too, and I heard the bullet bit something I thanked my lucky stars that I did jump, because it was my overcoat that it had dropped on, and I was sitting near it. Major Crosfield, I believe, told one chap next morning that we were a lucky lot to come out as we had done. Scenes of Destruction and Desolation.

"We had to pass a village to get to the firing line, and it was in a state. Everything . . . had been wrecked. Every rarmhouse on the way was destroyed, and it did look desolate. Not a building in the village ,was left un- touched, except a big house that stands by itself above all the others, and it is a mystery to every one why it has been left. This must have been a fine little town in peace time, with a nice square and a bandstand in the centre."
-Before enlisting Pte. Glover was in the em- ployment of Messrs. Jackson's, pawnbrokers, Orford-lane.

div.head: WARRINGTON WESLEYANISM.
div.p: WARRINGTON WESLEYANISM.
More Members Reported At Quarterly Meeting.

The quarterly meetinc, of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit was held in the School at Latchford last week. There was a record attendance; all ministers being present, to- gether with representatives from all parts of the circuit. Tea was provided by the ladies of the Latchford Church, and the subsequent meeting was presided over by the Rev. W. T. Derry. It was decided to place on permanent record the unique services rendered to the Wesleyan Methodist Church by. the late Mr. John Bennett. Tribute was paid to his humility of character, his sincerity, and his ever ready generosity. Votes of condolence were passed with the relatives of the late Isaac Hay- 'ward, the late Mr. Barlow, and the late Rev. Frank Ashton.

The Chairman presented the numerical state- ment, which showed a small increase of membership as compared with the previous quarter. The Society Stewards (Messrs. Withinshaw .and Hickman), rei)orted the finances to be in a, satisfactory state. The Revs. W. T. Derry, A. J. Morton and H. Dixon were thanked for their past services, and unanimously invited to remain another year. All accepted the invitation. _

The• Stewards reported that the Rev. Percy Imeson, now of Doncaster. had been invited to succeed the Rev. H. Williamson, and had accepted the invitation The Rev. A. A. Fullar, of Bolton, was provisionally invited to succeed the Rev. A. J. Morton in 1917.
Miss Hartley, •Mr. W. Silcock and Mr. Watson were elected representatives to the Synod.

The Chairman reported that the Free Church bit Winwick had been taken over from the Free Church Council. There Was a debt of £3OO upon it, but, in answer to a very generous challenge from Mr. C. E. Parker, he and the Stewards, with Mr. Meldrum, had conducted a lightning campaign through the circuit, and in less than a fortnight the whole of the money had been raised and the Winwick Church was now entirely free of debt.
The repo4 was received with great satis- faction.

Mr. Barlow reported that all the trust property in the circuit was in a healthy con- dition financially, and almost free from debt. The missionary contributions showed an advanc,e on the previous year, but the Guild membership bad fallen slightly. The next quarterly meeting was fixed to be held at Penketh 'in June.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
NIIRTII AND MERRIMENT AT THE HIPPODROME.

It goes without saying that this week's splen- did Hippodrome programme is practically one long and 'delicious laugh—for a celebrated "Sim Peterman" company tops the bill with two excruciatingly funny "rambles "—" The Hair- dresser" and "The Stationmaster." In each of these Bob Stevens excels in the title-role, whilst an expert company contrives that there shall not be a dull moment throughout their performances. "Britannia's Honour" is a most imposing and rousing patriotic spectacle, in a series of fine tableaux. The costumes and musical effects are of the first order. Miss Alice Gibbs is an artiste "extra" to the programme and "extra" in talent. Her finely-rendered solos are much in demand, but the greatest success is her jodelling—which earns vociferous applause, and for which she is consistently recalled. Lois Conn is a great favourite with "her" cornet, and furnishes the surprise of the even- ing—which it would not be fair to divulge. George E. Carnell is an ." Electric Light" of peculiar brilliance, and has an excellent reper- toire. A specially good war-issue of "The Gaumont Graphic" is also thrown on the screen.

div.head: WAR-PLAY AT THE ROYAL
div.p: WAR-PLAY AT THE ROYAL
COURT.

At the Royal Court this week, a stirring war play makes a positively irresistible appeal to lovers of melodrama. Entitled "In Time of War," it is from the pen of that past-master in stage sensationalism, Mr. C. Watson Mill, and it gives a vivid picture of some of the horrors and heroism which distinguish the present great conflict. Incidentally it makes several powerful recruiting appeals and so, after all, may be serving a much more useful purpose than that of merely entertaining people. It is full of the most exciting incidents, and is most realistically staged and acted. Particularly thrilling are the scenes in which the German soldiery attack a hospital and a wireless station, to the accompaniment of the sharp cracking of musketry, the boom of the guns and the bursting of shells and with dbbris falling all around Of course, a love story runs through the piece, and a telling one it is too; culminating to salvos of applause, from the audience, when the hero is saved from a par- ticularly tight corner by the pluck and brains of his wife—a situation of which so practised a playwright as Mr Mill makes the very most, and which is calculated to bring down "the most irresponsive house that ever was," as Mark Twain said.

The play is most spiritedly played, Mr. Stephen Langton making a dashing and daring Captain Squires, and declaiming with powerful emphasis the telling and manly appeals for "more men and still more," put in his mouth by the author. Miss Alida L. Lindon gives a fine reading of the part of/ the heroine, and Mr. A. Balfour Mackey assumes the role of the cunning and treacherous German spy, Baron .Goffenhelm, with such effect that he receives the stage(villain's best reward in ample measure of hisses. Mr. Claude Agnew is also a big suc- cess as an overbearing German prince, and Miss Ida Mackey impersonates a princess- turned-spy with great effect. Miss Lily Morrell as a- Red Cross nurse and Messrs. Douglas Earle and J. B. Murray as typically fearless and large-hharted " Tommies," introduce a delightful vein of humour. "In Time of War" is a seasonable drama and people who like drama will " go nap on it." as the phrase runs.
For- Next Week.
That talented actress, Miss Ethel Van Praagh, and Mr.- J. Edward Whitty will next week appear in "A Place in the Sun," a new play which has scored a big hit wherever it has been shown.

div.head: GRAND THEATRE RE-OPENING
div.p: THE GRAND THEATRE RE-OPENING

The Grand Electric Theatrti, Bridge Foot, which has been renovated and made up-to-date and cosy, and will now compare favourably with any similar place of entertainment, will be re-opened on Monday, under the manage- ment of Mr. C. L. Ashton, who promises patrons an unbroken series of high-class and interesting programmes. The first performance in the newly-furnished hall will be given on Monday afternoon next, when the proceeds will be devoted to the Raddon Court Red Cross Hospital. The per- formance will be under the patronage of the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), Lady Harmood Banner, Colonel Moggridge, Colonel and Mrs. Lyon, and Colonel and Mrs. Mocatta and, no doubt, there will be a record attend- ance.

div.head: CAPITAL COAIEDV AT THE STAR
div.p: CAPITAL COAIEDV AT THE STAR
KINEMA.

Special Keystone nights proved a remarkable attraction on Monday and • Tuesday "Laugh- ing Gas," "Caught in a Cabaret," "The New Janitor," "The Face on the Bar-room Floor" and "The Masquerader" moving large audiences with uncontrollable laughter. "Lancashire Suspension Bridges" and " Pathes' Animated Gazette" two fine cduda- tional films were also shown.

"The Colleen Bawn " that great Irish favourite—topped a record bill on Wednesday, whilst a gripping drama, "The Eleventh Commandment: will to-night doubtless account for assemblies every whit equal to those of Thursday and yesterday Certainly fine picture drama should not be missed by a single devotee of the film _ _ Big Films Next Week. _
On the first three nights of the week a filmed version of "East Lynne" will occupy premier place in a fine programme, whilst on the last three nights "Kismet" will form the " star "

HOSPITAL SUNDAY.
Good. Collections in Local Churches and Chapels.

In practically all the places of worship us Warrington and district last Sunday, special collections were made on behalf of the War- rington Infirmary, whilst at most of them eloquent appeals on behalf of the deserving charity were made from the pulpit andl rostrum.
All the returns have not yet been made, but we understand that the total collection will amount to a very satisfactory sum. .

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

For Distressed Belgian Med icos.—Padgate • people had a great treat on Thursday evening, when, in the Wesley Hall, Mr. Arthur litim- phreys,• the well-known tourist travel-agent, lectured on "Notes from the War-Country. Dr. Murray,: Of Penketh, presided, and de- scribed the terrible condition of the Belgian doctors and chemists, and explained that the British Medical Association had requested al/ its divisions to contribute to the Belgian Doctors' and Pharmacists' Relief Fund. The. local medical men had contributed generously, but Dr. Bennett, the chairman of the division, thought he ought to make some special effort in the matter, and had arranged this gather- Humphreys gave a most lucid and instructive lecture, describing vividly his ex- periences of being held up in Switzerland at the beginning of the war with a party of tourists, and their subsequent difficulty in get— ting back to England. A magnificent series of slides were put on the screen in a. perfect manner by Mr. Jones (of Messrs. Hill and Co., who kindly provided the lantern, gas, &c.). Views of the Swiss mobilisation were especially interesting, ;whilst those of .Belgium, illustrat- ing many beautiful buildings before and after bombardment, created a deep impression.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman, the Lecturer and Lanternist was proposed by Di. Bennett, seconded by the Rev. Chamberlain (curate- in-charge) and supported by the Rev. A. J. Morton, who explained that the Wesleyan body were only too pleased to grant the use of their hall for such a worthy object.—A sum of over .t.lO will be forwarded at once as a result of the lecture, which, considering the awful state of the weather, is highly satis- factory.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Forty Years a Forester.—On Monday after- noon in the Sankey Churchyard, the funeral took place of the late Mr. John Baker, aged 88, who had farmed in Sankey for forty years. Ile retired from business about fifteen years ago, since when he has been living with his son, Mr. J. W. Baker, at Penketh, where he passed away early on Friday morning of last week. The interment ViVts in the family grave.. The chief mourners were Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Baker, Mr: and Mrs. T. Baker, Mrs. Cook (daughter), Mr. Leo Cook, Mr. J Baker and Master T. Baker (grandsons), Mr. T. Cook, Mr. Hector Ireland, Mr. P. Dumbill and Mr. J. Dumbill (nephews). Wreaths were snt by members of the family, and by Mrs. Butter, worth and Mrs. W. Taylor.

div.head: HAD NOTHING TO SAY.
div.p: HAD NOTHING TO SAY.

At Monday's Police Court, John Briggs was charged with having been an absentee from the 3rd Battalion of the King's Liverpool Regi- ment, since Saturday, March 6th.—P.C. Bennett said he met Briggs in Wilderspool-road, and asked him what he was doing, but the man had nothing to say.—An escort, it was stated, was on its way to Warrington, and to this Briggs. Was ordered to be handed.

WARRINGTON BLUE COAT CHARITY SCHOOL. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the Trustees of the above School will, at their next Quarterly Meeting, on the 19th day of April next, proceed to elect three Children (one Boy and two Girls) to Vacancies now existing in the Institution. No Candidate will be eligible unless an application on his or her behalf (forms of which may be obtained from the Clerk, at his Office, 3, Winwick-street), shall have been made to the Clerk to the Trustees at least fourteen days previous to the day of Meet- ing. In electing Children, the Trustees make Orphans their first choice. Those deprived of one parent come next in consideration, and after them the children of parents who have the greatest number and the slenderest means. Dated this 18th day of March, 1915. HENRY GREENALL, Clerk to the Trustees.

A SURE Sllol'. Sequel To A Stone-Throwing Challenge. At the County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. Roger C. Parr and other magis- trates, William Matthews and William Hamp- ton, both of 54, Grafton-street, were charged with being concerned in the theft of a fowl valued at 55., at Burtonwood, on March 14th. The evidence as outlined to the Court by the Superintendent, was to the effect that one of the men wa§ seen to leave a fowl-house at Tan- House Farm with a hen under his coat, whilst the other man stood in the road near by and looked on. They Were caught by Mr. Arthur Cooper (son of the occupier of the farm), but they broke away and made off in the direction of Warrington. Mr. Cooper got the assistance of his brother, and mounting their bicycles, the . pair went in pursuit of the prisoners, whom they overtook on the canal bank at Dallam. Mr. Arthur Cooper is a special constable and, with the assistance of his brother, he took the two men into custody and brought them to Sankey Police Station. On the way Matthews said that he threw a stone at the hen and lamed it and the other man went over the fence to fetch it. The men were locked up, and when charged, Matthews said "We are willing to pay 12s. for the hen; never mind 55.!" The other man said nothing. They were taken before the magistrates and re- manded on bail. They came to Warrington about three years ago, and had been employed at Whitecross Works. Hampton was married and had four young children, and the other man was his brother-in-law, was single, and lodged with Hampton. There was nothing against the men before this. One of the prisoners told the Court that "it was a joke more than anything." He said to his friend "I don't think you can throw a stone and hit one of those fowls. His friend threw and did hit the bird and then he said that they had better shift it or they might get into trouble." The men were bound over and ordered to pay the costs. ANGLING. Warrington Working Men's Association. N.A. CENTRE. After a winter of poor sport the close season is upon us, with a set-board which, as far as Icompetition goes, is the poorest for several lyears. Mr. F. Jolley is the only one to grace the hoard with anything like decent fish. I suppose it is all through the wretched week: ends we have experienced since January. The number of members visiting our fisheries has not been a dozen in any one week-end, so that may account for a deal of the scarcity of specimens. Now that the fence months are upon us and members of the Warrington district who al- ways have observed them will find it much harder to, keep within bounds, when they are troutine,,, at the Gowy with worm and an eel takes it. It will take no small amount of courage to return eel or pike to the water when members know that they are spoiling their own coarse fishing by doing so, but this ' thing will have to be done, no matter what are the consequences. Members .are beginning to grumble at the laws meted out to them by the P.F.P.L., and- the sooner they legislate for the angler in a manner that will prove satis- factory to all the better it will be for all concerned. To put matters in a nut-shell, they want to protect coarse fish, and at the same time they 'are destroying thein by forcing mem- bers to return pike and eel to waters where they are already doing considerable harm. If we pay the piper, surely we should choose the tune! Tickets for the Walton Reservoir are now being asked for, and members may have same on application at the club-houses. The best trout taken by a member up to the present weighed 11b. 90z. and fell to Mr. E. Brookes. All cards are now in the Secretary's hands and members should call for them at once scr as to assist all Secretaries in fixing the correct number for the season. A. S. " BOGEY " BILLIARDS. Devotees of billiards are offered an interest- ing variant of their favourite game in "bogey billiards," which, as its title implies, is founded on the performances of "Colonel Bogey," whose name is familiar to. all golfers. To each hole on the billiard table is assigned a definite value. The full course consists of 18 holes or pockets divided into three series. The game is an intensely interesting one for two, three, or four players, and has a unique advantage over all other games played on a billiard table, in that anyone who has a table at his disposal can, as at golf, find enjoyment in a round by himself versus "Bogey." The inventor of the game is Mr. D. Irvine Watson, this year's 'holder of the Single-handed Championship of the English Bowling Associa- tion. Sound Reasoning. "I feel pretty sure that the moon is of mw e importance to us than the sun." "How so?" "You see, the moon shines at night, when we are certainly, in need of light, while the sun only shines in the daytime, when we have all the light we want."
